HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
HTTP is an application-layer protocol.
HTTP defines communication between clients and servers.
HTTP uses a request-response model.
An HTTP client sends a request.
An HTTP server sends a response.
A request and a response are different protocol messages.
HTTP defines message semantics independently of the programming language implementing the client or server.
PHP can implement HTTP server behavior.
JavaScript can initiate HTTP requests through host APIs.
C can implement HTTP clients and servers.
C++ can implement HTTP clients and servers.
C# can implement HTTP clients and servers.

HTTP is not PHP.
HTTP is not JavaScript.
HTTP is not HTML.

HTTP can transport binary data.

HTTP/3 operates over QUIC.
HTTPS is HTTP transported with TLS protection.
TLS and HTTP solve different protocol responsibilities.
TLS provides transport security properties.
HTTP defines application request and response semantics.
Using HTTPS does not make an application logically correct.
Using HTTPS does not provide application authorization by itself.
Using HTTPS does not validate application input.
An HTTP request contains a method.
An HTTP request identifies a target.
An HTTP request contains protocol metadata.
An HTTP request can contain header fields.
An HTTP request can contain a message body when permitted by the request semantics.
An HTTP response contains a status code.
An HTTP response contains header fields.
An HTTP response can contain a message body.
The request method communicates the requested operation semantics.
GET requests retrieval of a representation.
HEAD is similar to GET but requests no response content.
POST submits data for processing according to the target resource's semantics.
PUT requests creation or replacement of the state of a target resource according to the supplied representation.
PATCH requests partial modification according to the patch representation and server contract.
DELETE requests removal of a resource association according to server semantics.
OPTIONS requests communication options for a target resource or server.
TRACE performs a diagnostic loop-back operation where supported.
CONNECT establishes a tunnel according to HTTP semantics.
Not every HTTP server supports every method.
A server can restrict methods available for a resource.
GET is a safe HTTP method according to HTTP semantics.
HEAD is a safe HTTP method.
OPTIONS is a safe HTTP method.
TRACE is a safe HTTP method according to protocol semantics.
A safe method requests read-only semantics from the client perspective.
Safe does not mean that a server performs literally no internal activity.
A server can log a GET request without violating GET's safe semantics.
GET should not be designed to request destructive state changes.
HTTP defines idempotent methods.
An idempotent method has the same intended effect when an identical request is made multiple times as when it is made once.
GET is idempotent.
HEAD is idempotent.
PUT is idempotent.
DELETE is idempotent according to HTTP method semantics.
OPTIONS is idempotent.
TRACE is idempotent.
POST is not inherently idempotent.
PATCH is not inherently idempotent.

Idempotency does not mean every repeated response must be byte-for-byte identical.
Deleting an already deleted resource can produce a different response while DELETE remains idempotent in intended effect.

A 5xx response is not automatically HTTP 500.

Storage defines how state survives, how state is identified, how state changes, who may change it, how concurrent changes are controlled, how corruption is detected, and how valid state is recovered after failure.
A reliable storage design knows which state matters.
It knows which copy is authoritative.
It knows when a write is actually complete.
It knows what can be rebuilt.
It knows what must never be silently discarded.
It validates what it reads.
It verifies what it writes.
It preserves evidence when something goes wrong.
And when the required state cannot be established from evidence, it reports that state as unknown or unavailable rather than inventing one.

A rhetorical question is asked for emphasis and does not always require a literal answer.
Repeating information already established in a conversation may be unnecessary unless clarification is requested.

Inter-process communication, or IPC, is the exchange of data, signals, or synchronization information between separate processes.
Processes normally have separate address spaces.
One process cannot ordinarily access another process's memory directly.
IPC provides controlled mechanisms for processes to communicate.
Common IPC mechanisms include:
Anonymous pipes.
Named pipes.
FIFOs.
Unix domain sockets.
TCP sockets.
UDP sockets.
Shared memory.
Message queues.
Signals.
Semaphores.
Memory-mapped files.
Platform-specific IPC facilities.
Different IPC mechanisms solve different problems.
Do not choose IPC merely because a mechanism is familiar.
Choose the smallest mechanism that satisfies the communication requirements.
Before selecting IPC, determine:
Which processes communicate?
Are they on the same machine?
Can they be on different machines?
Is communication one-way or bidirectional?
Is communication request-response or asynchronous?
How much data is exchanged?
Does message ordering matter?
Does message delivery need acknowledgement?
Can messages be duplicated?
Can messages be lost?
Does communication require authentication?
Does communication cross a privilege boundary?
What happens when one process exits?
What happens when communication fails?
What latency and throughput are required?
What platform support is required?
IPC is an interface.
Treat it with the same discipline as any other interface.
Define:
Message format.
Message boundaries.
Ordering.
Error behavior.
Connection lifecycle.
Size limits.
Timeouts.
Authentication where required.
Authorization where required.
Versioning where required.
Do not let two processes depend on undocumented assumptions.
A pipe is a byte stream.
An anonymous pipe is commonly created by one process and inherited by related processes.
Typical uses include:
Parent-to-child communication.
Child-to-parent communication.
Connecting command-line programs.
Redirecting standard input.
Redirecting standard output.
A pipe does not inherently contain application-level messages.
If a process writes:
HELLO
then:
WORLD
the reader should not assume two reads will return exactly those two writes.
Byte streams do not preserve application message boundaries.
Define framing if messages matter.
A simple line-oriented protocol can use:
MESSAGE\n
This works when:
Messages cannot contain unescaped newlines.
Maximum line length is bounded.
Encoding is defined.
More complex protocols can use length prefixes.
For example:
4-byte length
followed by:
payload bytes
The receiver reads the length.
Validates it.
Then reads exactly that many payload bytes.
Do not allocate memory from an untrusted length field before validating its range.
length = 4294967295
must not cause an enormous allocation merely because the field is syntactically valid.
Set protocol limits.
A reader must handle partial reads.
Requesting 100 bytes does not guarantee one read operation returns 100 bytes.
The operating system can return fewer bytes.
Continue reading until:
The required amount is received.
EOF occurs.
An error occurs.
A timeout or cancellation condition occurs.
Do not treat a short read as automatically meaning the complete message arrived.
Likewise, writes can be partial.
A request to write 100 bytes can write fewer than 100.
Handle the actual number of bytes written.
Do not assume one write operation transmits the entire buffer unless the API explicitly guarantees it for that operation and size.
Standard input and standard output can form an IPC interface.
A parent process can launch a child process and communicate through stdin and stdout.
This is often a useful design for small tools.
Parent sends requests through child stdin.
Child sends structured responses through stdout.
Child sends diagnostics through stderr.
Keep protocol output separate from diagnostic output.
Do not write arbitrary log messages into stdout if stdout is carrying machine-readable protocol data.
Use stderr or another logging channel.
Otherwise the parent cannot distinguish:
Protocol response.
Debug message.
Warning.
Status text.
This can corrupt the interface.
Exit status is also communication.
A child process can return an exit code.
0 = success
nonzero = failure
The exact meaning of nonzero values should be defined if callers depend on them.
Do not encode large amounts of information into exit codes.
They are small status channels.
Use stdout, stderr, files, sockets, or another mechanism for detailed results.
An exit code is not a substitute for structured error information when structured information is required.
EOF has meaning.
For a pipe or socket, EOF commonly means the other side closed its writing endpoint or connection.
Do not interpret EOF as an empty message.
Empty payload and closed stream are different conditions.
Handle them separately.
Named pipes and FIFOs allow independently started processes to communicate through a named operating-system object.
On Unix-like systems, a FIFO can appear in the filesystem.
One process writes.
Another reads.
FIFOs can be useful for simple local communication.
They also require lifecycle management.
Consider:
Who creates the FIFO?
Who owns it?
What permissions does it have?
What happens if it already exists?
What happens if no reader exists?
Who removes it?
Could an attacker create it first?
Do not blindly trust a filesystem object because it has the expected pathname.
Validate ownership and permissions where the IPC boundary is security-sensitive.
Named pipes on Windows provide a different platform mechanism with similar high-level purpose.
Do not assume Unix FIFO behavior and Windows named-pipe behavior are identical.
If software is platform-independent, define a platform-neutral IPC abstraction.
Implement platform-specific mechanisms behind it.
The externally visible semantics should remain consistent where required.
Unix domain sockets provide socket communication between processes on the same Unix-like system.
They can support:
Stream semantics.
Datagram semantics.
Local request-response.
Local services.
They avoid external network routing.
Filesystem-named Unix sockets can use filesystem permissions as part of access control.
Do not assume filesystem permissions alone provide all required authorization.
Peer credentials can sometimes be obtained through operating-system facilities.
Use them where appropriate.
Unix domain sockets can be useful when:
Processes are independently started.
Bidirectional communication is required.
Multiple clients connect to one local service.
A socket-style interface is convenient.
Do not use TCP localhost automatically when a local-domain socket better matches the requirement.
Likewise, do not use a Unix domain socket if cross-machine communication is required.
TCP sockets provide a reliable ordered byte stream between endpoints.
TCP can be used locally or across networks.
TCP does not provide application message boundaries.
Define framing.
TCP does not provide application identity merely because a connection exists.
Authentication may still be required.
TCP does not prove the peer is authorized.
Transport connectivity is not authority.
A TCP connection to:
127.0.0.1
is local network communication.
That can reduce exposure.
It does not automatically make every local client trusted.
Other processes running under other users may be able to connect depending on system configuration.
If the service performs privileged operations, authenticate or otherwise enforce the required local authority boundary.
Binding to all interfaces:
0.0.0.0
or:
::
can expose an IPC-style service to the network.
Do not change a local-only service to all-interface binding casually.
That changes the security boundary.
Configuration should make the binding explicit.
UDP provides datagram communication.

Delivery.
Uniqueness.
Connection establishment.
A UDP sender can send a datagram that never arrives.
Datagrams can arrive out of order.
Datagrams can be duplicated.
Applications using UDP must tolerate the behavior required by their protocol.
Do not build reliability assumptions into UDP merely because local testing rarely loses packets.
Local IPC can still use datagram sockets where their semantics are useful.
Choose based on required behavior.
Shared memory allows multiple processes to access a common memory region.
This can provide very high throughput.
It also introduces synchronization requirements.
Shared memory gives processes shared bytes.
It does not automatically provide:
Mutual exclusion.
Consistency.
Ownership.
Crash recovery.
A shared-memory structure needs a defined layout.
Header.
Version.
State.
Sequence number.
Data length.
Data.
Do not let separate processes independently assume structure layout without a stable contract.
Binary shared-memory structures can be affected by:
Alignment.
Padding.
Integer width.
Endianness.
Compiler ABI.
Structure packing.
Version differences.
Do not map an arbitrary native C struct into shared memory and assume every build will interpret it identically.
Define representation deliberately.
If all communicating processes use the same binary and platform, native layout can sometimes be acceptable.
Know the constraint.
If interoperability matters, use an explicitly defined representation.
Shared memory requires synchronization when multiple processes can access mutable data concurrently.
Possible mechanisms include:
Process-shared mutexes.
Atomic operations.
Sequence locks.
Ring-buffer ownership rules.
Single-producer/single-consumer designs.
Do not access shared mutable data concurrently without a synchronization model.
Race conditions cross process boundaries just as they cross thread boundaries.
A shared-memory flag such as:
ready = 1
is not automatically sufficient synchronization.
Memory visibility and ordering matter.
Use synchronization primitives appropriate to the platform and language.
Do not invent a home-grown lock from ordinary integer reads and writes unless the required atomic and memory-order semantics are established.
Shared memory can outlive a process depending on the mechanism.
A crashed process can leave:
Stale objects.
Stale state.
Locks.
Partial records.
Ownership markers.
Recovery behavior must be defined.
Do not assume shared state is valid merely because the memory object still exists.
Version and validate persistent or semi-persistent shared structures.
A message queue communicates discrete messages.
This can simplify framing because the mechanism preserves message boundaries.
Message queues can provide:
Asynchronous communication.
Buffering.
Priority.
Multiple producers.
Multiple consumers.
The exact semantics depend on the queue implementation.
Do not assume all message queues guarantee the same behavior.
Determine:
Maximum message size.
Queue capacity.
Persistence.
Delivery guarantees.
Acknowledgement behavior.
Blocking behavior.
Failure behavior.
A full queue requires defined handling.
Possible policies include:
Block.
Wait with timeout.
Reject.
Drop according to explicit policy.
Apply backpressure.
Do not silently discard messages unless loss is an intentional property of the system.
Backpressure occurs when a producer generates work faster than a consumer can process it.
Without backpressure, queues can grow until memory or storage is exhausted.
Bound queues where appropriate.
When full, make behavior explicit.
Backpressure is part of IPC design.
Do not solve overload merely by making buffers enormous.
Large buffers delay failure.
They do not remove capacity limits.
Signals provide small asynchronous notifications to processes on Unix-like systems.
Examples include:
SIGTERM.
SIGINT.
SIGHUP.
SIGCHLD.
Signals are not general-purpose data transport.
Use them for events that fit signal semantics.
Request termination.
Notify configuration reload.
Notify child process state change.
Do not try to transmit large structured data through ordinary signals.
Signal handlers have severe restrictions in many environments.
Only async-signal-safe operations can safely be performed directly inside a POSIX signal handler.
Do not perform complex application logic inside the handler.
A common design is:
Signal handler sets a flag or writes to a safe notification mechanism.
Normal event loop observes the notification.
Normal code performs the work.
This keeps complex behavior out of asynchronous signal context.
Do not call arbitrary allocation, logging, or locking code from signal handlers unless the platform guarantees it is safe.
Signals can interrupt blocking operations.
System calls can return interruption errors.
Handle interruption according to API semantics.
Do not treat every interrupted call as permanent failure.
Likewise, do not retry blindly if cancellation or shutdown is intended.
Signals can be coalesced.
Do not assume one signal delivery corresponds exactly to one logical event unless the mechanism guarantees it.
If event counts matter, use a mechanism designed to preserve counts.
Semaphores provide synchronization and counting.
A semaphore can represent available resources or coordinate processes.
Producer adds an item.
Semaphore count increases.
Consumer waits.
Consumer removes an item.
Do not use a semaphore without defining what its count represents.
A binary semaphore can provide lock-like behavior.
A counting semaphore represents multiple available units.
Do not confuse semaphore state with application data.
The data still needs its own representation.
Mutexes can sometimes be shared between processes.
A process-shared mutex requires explicit platform support and correct initialization.
Do not assume a normal thread mutex automatically works across processes.
Crash behavior matters.
If a process dies while holding an inter-process mutex, other processes can deadlock depending on the mechanism.
Robust mutex facilities can help detect owner death.
Recovery still requires application logic.
A dead owner does not prove protected data is consistent.
The process could have died halfway through an update.
After detecting owner death:
Inspect or recover protected state.
Restore invariants.
Then continue if safe.
Do not simply unlock and assume everything is valid.
Memory-mapped files can provide shared or persistent communication.
Multiple processes can map the same file.
Changes can become visible according to mapping and synchronization semantics.
Memory-mapped files share many concerns with shared memory:
Layout.
Synchronization.
Partial updates.
Versioning.
File permissions.
Do not use memory mapping merely because it avoids explicit read and write calls.
It changes the programming model but does not remove consistency requirements.
Files themselves can be IPC.
One process writes a file.
Another reads it.
This can be perfectly appropriate.
Batch processing.
Drop directories.
Configuration generation.
Job handoff.
Export/import.
Do not dismiss file-based IPC as primitive.
It can be simple, inspectable, durable, and easy to debug.
But define ownership and atomicity.
A writer should not expose a partially written file as complete data.
A common pattern is:
Write temporary file.
Flush as required.
Close it.
Atomically rename into final location.
Reader only consumes final names.
This reduces partial-read races.
The exact atomicity guarantees depend on filesystem and platform.
Know them.
File-based IPC needs a way to detect new work.
Options include:
Polling.
Filesystem notifications.
Directory scanning.
Explicit notification through another IPC mechanism.
Polling can be sufficient for low-frequency work.
Do not introduce complex notification infrastructure if a five-second directory scan satisfies requirements.
Small and deterministic can beat clever.
If multiple processes consume files, define claiming semantics.
Atomic rename from pending to processing.
This can establish ownership.
Do not let two workers process the same file because both observed it before either marked it claimed.
IPC can be synchronous.
A synchronous request waits for a response.
Client sends request.
Server processes it.
Server returns response.
Client continues.
This is simple when operations are short and bounded.
Do not use unbounded synchronous waits.
Define timeouts or cancellation where required.
IPC can be asynchronous.
A sender submits a message and continues.
The result can arrive later.
This can improve decoupling.
It also introduces:
Correlation.
Queueing.
Retry.
Lifecycle.
Cancellation.
Do not choose asynchronous communication merely because it sounds scalable.
It adds state.
Use it when the problem requires it.
Request-response protocols need correlation when multiple requests can be outstanding.
request_id=42
Response:
Do not assume responses arrive in request order unless the protocol guarantees it.
Correlation identifiers should be unique within the required scope.
They do not need to be globally unique unless the protocol requires it.
A monotonically increasing local request number can be sufficient for one connection.
Do not introduce globally unique identifiers without need.
If identifiers can wrap, define behavior.
IPC messages should have explicit types.
STATUS_REQUEST
STATUS_RESPONSE
START_REQUEST
START_RESPONSE
ERROR_RESPONSE
Do not infer message type from vague payload contents if a type field can make the protocol explicit.
A message type does not authorize the operation.
The receiver still validates:
Connection state.
Sender identity where required.
Sender authority where required.
Message structure.
Message values.
Current application state.
A START_REQUEST received from an unauthorized process remains unauthorized.
IPC transports requests.
It does not grant authority.
IPC messages should be validated at the receiving boundary.
Never assume another local process always sends correct data.
Processes can have bugs.
Versions can differ.
Data can be corrupted.
A local process can be compromised.
Validate.
For every message validate:
Type.
Length.
Required fields.
Ranges.
Encoding.
Current protocol state.
Do not pass malformed IPC data deeper into the application.
Message size limits are essential.
Define maximum payload size.
Reject oversized messages before allocating excessive resources.
MAX_MESSAGE_SIZE = 1 MiB
If header says:
length = 4 GiB
reject it.
Do not attempt allocation first.
Length arithmetic must be checked for overflow.
total = header_size + payload_size
can overflow fixed-width integers.
Validate before arithmetic or use checked arithmetic.
IPC protocols need encoding rules.
Possible encodings include:
Binary.
JSON.
TSV.
Line-oriented text.
Length-prefixed text.
Protocol-specific structures.
Choose based on requirements.
Text protocols are often easier to inspect.
Binary protocols can be smaller and faster.
Neither is automatically better.
For small local control protocols, simple text can be entirely adequate.
Do not build a binary serialization framework to transmit three commands unless there is a reason.
TSV can be useful for simple deterministic records.
STATUS 42 RUNNING
Column count.
Column meaning.
Escaping.
Maximum field length.
Do not assume fields will never contain tabs unless the protocol prohibits them.
If tabs are prohibited, validate and reject them.
JSON can be useful for structured messages.
Validate JSON structure after parsing.
Valid JSON is not necessarily a valid protocol message.
{"type":"START","port":-1}
is valid JSON.
It can still be semantically invalid.
Parsing is not validation.
Binary protocols need byte order.
Multi-byte integers must have defined representation.
Network byte order is commonly big-endian for network protocols.
Local IPC can use another representation if explicitly defined.
Do not use native host byte order in an interoperable protocol unless all participants are guaranteed to share it and that dependency is intentional.
The protocol defines byte order.
A network does not independently invent byte order at runtime.
Protocol designers define representation.
Version IPC protocols when incompatible changes are possible.
A header can include:
magic.
version.
type.
length.
request identifier.
Do not add fields merely for decoration.
Each field should serve a purpose.
Magic values can help identify protocol data.
They do not provide security.
A matching magic number does not authenticate the sender.
Version negotiation can be useful when processes can run different software versions.
Client supports versions 1 and 2.
Server supports version 2.
They select version 2.
If no common version exists:
Reject the connection.
Do not guess.
For tightly coupled processes deployed together, explicit negotiation can be unnecessary.
A fixed protocol version can be simpler.
Know the deployment model.
Backward compatibility has cost.
Do not support old protocol versions forever without need.
When support is removed, fail clearly.
Do not reinterpret old messages as new messages based on guesswork.
IPC state machines define valid message sequences.
CONNECTED
HELLO_SENT
QUALIFIED
READY
CLOSING
A command received before READY can be rejected.
Do not process a valid command in an invalid protocol state.
Message validity includes sequence.
This directly applies the state-machine principle:
An event does not authorize an arbitrary transition.
Only a defined transition does.
IPC peers can disconnect at any time.
Handle:
Clean close.
Crash.
Timeout.
Broken pipe.
Connection reset.
Protocol error.
Local shutdown.
Do not assume a peer will always send a graceful goodbye.
Resources associated with a connection must be cleaned up.
Examples:
Buffers.
Pending requests.
Temporary files.
Shared-memory ownership.
Subscriptions.
Do not leak resources because the peer disappeared unexpectedly.
A broken pipe is normal failure behavior in IPC systems.
Do not crash the entire process merely because one client disconnected unless architecture requires it.
On Unix-like systems, writing to a closed pipe or socket can generate SIGPIPE.
Programs should handle this according to design.
Possible approaches include:
Ignore SIGPIPE and handle the write error.
Use APIs or flags that suppress the signal.
Define another controlled behavior.
Do not let an ordinary client disconnect unexpectedly terminate a long-running server.
Timeouts need clear semantics.
Possible timeouts include:
Connection timeout.
Handshake timeout.
Read timeout.
Write timeout.
Request timeout.
Idle timeout.
Shutdown timeout.
Do not use one vague timeout value for everything unless identical semantics are intentional.
A request timeout means:
The requester stopped waiting.
It does not necessarily mean:
The remote operation did not occur.
This distinction is critical.
Client sends START.
Server performs START.
Response is lost.
Client times out.
Retrying START can duplicate the operation.
Use idempotency or request identifiers where duplication matters.
Timeout is uncertainty.
Do not automatically translate it into operation failure if the remote result is unknown.
IPC retries must consider side effects.
Safe retry:
STATUS request.
Potentially unsafe retry:
TRANSFER_FUNDS.
START_JOB.
DELETE_FILE.
If an operation is not naturally idempotent, use an operation identifier.
The server can remember:
request_id=42 already completed.
Then a duplicate request can return the prior result rather than repeating the action.
Do not rely on transport retries to provide application exactly-once semantics.
Exactly-once effects require application design.
At-most-once, at-least-once, and effectively-once behavior have different tradeoffs.
Define what the system needs.
Do not advertise stronger guarantees than the implementation provides.
Ordering matters.
A stream preserves byte order.
That does not automatically define semantic operation order across multiple connections.
If client A sends operation 1 and client B sends operation 2 concurrently, the server needs a defined ordering mechanism if order matters.
Single event loop.
Queue.
Sequence numbers.
Transactions.
Consensus for distributed systems.
IPC itself does not solve application ordering.
If messages have sequence numbers:
Validate them.
Detect duplicates where required.
Detect stale messages where required.
Do not accept arbitrary sequence jumps if protocol forbids them.
Sequence numbers can wrap.
Define comparison semantics if long-lived communication can reach wraparound.
IPC can cross privilege boundaries.
Unprivileged user process.
Privileged service.
This boundary requires special care.
Never trust a privileged operation request merely because it arrived through a local socket.
Authenticate the caller using an appropriate mechanism.
Authorize the requested operation.
Validate all parameters.
Apply least privilege.
Do not expose generic:
EXECUTE_COMMAND
interfaces from privileged services unless arbitrary execution is explicitly the intended feature.
Prefer narrow operations.
GET_STATUS
RELOAD_CONFIGURATION
START_SERVICE
STOP_SERVICE
Each can have explicit authorization.
Narrow IPC interfaces reduce attack surface.
A privileged service should not accept arbitrary filesystem paths without validation if the operation acts on those paths.
Path traversal and symlink attacks can cross IPC boundaries.
Treat IPC input like any other untrusted input.
Local does not mean safe.
Unix domain socket peer credentials can identify:
User ID.
Group ID.
Process ID.
Availability varies by platform.
Use operating-system-provided peer identity where appropriate rather than trusting a client-supplied field:
{"uid":0}
A client claiming to be root is not evidence.
Obtain identity from the trusted transport or authentication mechanism.
Named-pipe security descriptors on Windows can restrict access.
Unix filesystem permissions can restrict local socket or FIFO access.
These mechanisms can establish part of the access boundary.
Do not duplicate security poorly in application code when the operating system already provides a stronger primitive.
But understand exactly what the OS primitive guarantees.
Authentication answers:
Who is the peer?
Authorization answers:
What may the peer do?
Keep them separate.
IPC confidentiality may matter.
Local IPC can sometimes rely on operating-system isolation.
Network IPC can require encryption such as TLS.
Do not add encryption where it solves no threat in the defined environment merely for decoration.
Do not omit it where data crosses an untrusted network.
Threat model the actual transport.
Integrity matters even when confidentiality does not.
A message altered in transit can change behavior.
Transport and protocol mechanisms should provide the required integrity guarantees.
TCP checksums are not cryptographic integrity protection against an attacker.
Know the distinction.
IPC servers should limit clients.
Possible limits include:
Maximum simultaneous connections.
Maximum requests per connection.
Maximum queue depth.
Maximum pending requests.
Per-client resource limits.
Do not let one client consume unbounded server resources.
Resource exhaustion is an IPC concern.
A client can connect and send nothing.
If each connection consumes memory forever, enough idle clients can exhaust the server.
Use bounded resources and timeouts appropriate to the mission.
Rate limiting can be useful.
Do not add it automatically to tiny trusted local systems if connection limits already solve the problem.
Use the smallest sufficient mechanism.
IPC servers need shutdown behavior.
A graceful shutdown can:
Stop accepting new clients.
Notify existing clients where appropriate.
Finish or cancel active operations according to policy.
Flush required state.
Close IPC endpoints.
Release resources.
Exit.
Do not simply terminate halfway through a persistent state update unless abrupt termination semantics are acceptable.
Shutdown itself can be state-driven.
RUNNING
DRAINING
STOPPING
STOPPED
Do not accept new work in STOPPING unless defined.
Clients need reconnection behavior.
If a server restarts:
Can clients reconnect?
Do they retry automatically?
How often?
Do they resend pending requests?
Are those requests idempotent?
Do not implement reconnect without defining pending-operation behavior.
A reconnect creates a new transport session.
Do not assume it resumes old protocol state automatically.
Perform required handshake again.
Re-authenticate if required.
Re-establish subscriptions.
Do not carry stale connection state into a new connection.
Connection identity and application identity can differ.
A user or agent can reconnect through a new socket while retaining application identity.
Define the relationship.
Do not use ephemeral socket descriptors as durable identities.
File descriptors and handles are process-local resources.
The integer:
5
does not globally identify a connection.
Do not persist file descriptor numbers as durable references.
They can be reused.
IPC endpoint names should be stable where needed.

Temporary runtime endpoints should live in appropriate runtime directories.
Do not place mutable sockets in configuration directories merely because the path is convenient.
Separate configuration from runtime state.
Runtime socket directories need correct permissions.
Do not create privileged sockets in world-writable locations without protections against substitution.
Temporary directories can introduce race conditions.
Use secure creation mechanisms.
If an IPC server creates a filesystem socket:
Handle stale socket files from prior crashes.
Do not blindly delete any file at that path.
Verify what it is and whether removal is safe.
An attacker could place a symlink or unrelated file there.
Filesystem security applies.
PID files are not IPC by themselves.
They can help locate or identify a process.
Do not trust a PID file as proof that the intended process is alive.
PIDs are reused.
If identity matters, verify the process through stronger evidence.

Use process handles or additional identity checks where available.
IPC and process supervision often interact.
A supervisor can:
Start child.
Capture stdout/stderr.
Monitor exit.
Restart according to policy.
Send termination.
This is a controlled parent-child relationship.
Do not create a separate network service if inherited pipes satisfy the requirement.
Simple process trees can be robust.
Subprocess IPC should avoid deadlocks.
A classic deadlock occurs when:
Parent writes large data to child stdin.
Child writes large data to stdout.
Both pipe buffers fill.
Each process waits for the other to read.
If bidirectional communication can be concurrent, design reads and writes accordingly.
Possible solutions include:
Separate threads.
Nonblocking I/O.
Event loops.
Bounded request-response sequencing.
Do not assume pipe buffers are infinite.
Pipe buffer sizes are implementation details.
Do not build correctness around a particular capacity.
A process can block while writing when the reader is slow.
That is backpressure.
Decide whether blocking is acceptable.
Nonblocking IPC returns when an operation cannot proceed immediately.
The program must then wait for readiness through mechanisms such as:
select.
poll.
epoll.
kqueue.
IOCP.
Other platform facilities.
Do not busy-loop:

try again
That wastes CPU.
Wait for readiness or use blocking I/O where appropriate.
Blocking I/O is not inferior.
For simple single-purpose processes, blocking operations can be easiest to reason about.
Use nonblocking complexity when concurrency requirements justify it.
Event-driven IPC can handle many connections efficiently.
It also introduces state management.
Each connection can have:
Read buffer.
Write buffer.
Protocol state.
Authentication state.

Partial messages must remain buffered until complete.

IPC buffers should have bounds.

Maximum header size.
Maximum buffered incomplete data.
Define limits.
Malformed peers should be disconnected according to protocol.
Do not attempt infinite recovery from arbitrary garbage.
Protocol resynchronization is difficult.

Often the safest behavior is:

Require a new handshake.
Do not scan arbitrary bytes looking for something that resembles a header unless the protocol explicitly defines resynchronization.

Process boundaries are real boundaries.

Security engineering protects systems, data, operations, and authority from unauthorized or unintended actions.
Security is a system property.
Security is not a single feature.
Security is not provided by one programming language.
Security is not provided by one firewall.
Security is not provided by encryption alone.
Security depends on architecture, implementation, configuration, operation, and human authority.
A trust boundary separates components or contexts with different levels of trust.
Data crossing a trust boundary should be treated according to the receiving system's validation requirements.
External input is untrusted unless an established mechanism proves otherwise.
Network input is untrusted.
HTTP request input is untrusted.
Command-line input can be untrusted.
Environment variables can be untrusted.
Configuration files can be untrusted when unauthorized parties can modify them.
Database content can be untrusted.
File content can be untrusted.
Module input can be untrusted.
Plugin input can be untrusted.
Inter-process messages can be untrusted.
Data becoming internal does not automatically make it trustworthy.
Trust should be established through defined mechanisms.
Trust should not be inferred merely from location.
localhost does not automatically mean trusted.
A private network does not automatically mean trusted.
An internal service does not automatically mean trusted.
A file under an application directory does not automatically mean trusted.
A module being present does not automatically mean trusted.
A successful network connection does not automatically mean trusted.
A valid JSON document does not automatically mean trusted.
A syntactically valid request does not automatically mean authorized.
Authentication establishes identity according to an authentication mechanism.
Authorization determines what an authenticated or identified actor is permitted to do.
Authentication and authorization are different.
An authenticated user can still be unauthorized for an operation.
An authenticated service can still be unauthorized for an operation.
Authorization should be checked where protected actions occur.
A username alone does not prove identity.
A claimed identifier alone does not prove identity.
A request field saying admin does not grant administrative authority.
Client-controlled data should not define its own authority.
Least privilege means granting only the authority required for a task.
A process should not run as root merely because root avoids permission errors.
A web service should not receive filesystem write access everywhere merely because it needs one writable directory.
A module should receive only the capabilities required for its mission.
A user should receive only the permissions required for their role.
A service account should have only the resources required by that service.
Reducing privilege reduces the consequences of compromise.

This is one strategy, not universal requirement.
Filesystem design should remain small when requirements are small.
One atomic JSON file can be sufficient.
Do not introduce complex multi-file transaction schemes without need.
Complexity creates more recovery states.
Prefer the smallest mechanism satisfying correctness.

The original identifier can be stored in file contents or metadata.
Do not treat a hash as authorization.

This can improve filesystem performance where directories become very large.
Sharding should be deterministic.
The mapping should be stable.
Sharding is an optimization.
Do not add it before scale requires it unless architecture already expects that scale.
A filesystem hierarchy should remain understandable.
Deep unnecessary directory structures complicate operation.

Balance according to actual requirements.

It is not automatically evidence that the content is valid.
A successful write is evidence that the write API accepted the operation according to its contract.
It is not automatically evidence of durable persistence.

It is not automatically evidence that the file is trustworthy.
Evidence should match the claim.

Filesystems provide names and structure for stored data.

DNS stands for Domain Name System.
DNS is a distributed naming system.
DNS maps names to information according to DNS records and protocol rules.
DNS is commonly used to map domain names to IP addresses.
DNS can also publish mail-routing information.
DNS can publish service information.
DNS can publish verification information.
DNS can delegate authority.
DNS can publish cryptographic information.
DNS is not merely a hostname-to-IP lookup table.
A domain name is a hierarchical name in the DNS namespace.
DNS names are composed of labels.
Labels are separated by dots in textual representation.
The hierarchy is interpreted from right to left.
In example.com, com is above example.com in the DNS hierarchy.
The DNS namespace has a root.
The root is conventionally represented by a trailing dot in a fully qualified domain name.
example.com. is an absolute DNS name.
The trailing root dot is commonly omitted in ordinary presentation.
A fully qualified domain name is commonly abbreviated FQDN.
An FQDN identifies a name from the DNS root.
A relative DNS name can be completed using local resolver search rules.
Relative-name expansion can produce different results in different environments.
Do not rely on search-domain behavior for security-sensitive or deterministic naming.
Use the intended absolute name when ambiguity matters.
DNS names are not URLs.
example.com is a DNS name.
https://example.com/path is a URL.
DNS does not resolve the URL path.
DNS does not determine the HTTP resource.
DNS can help locate the network address associated with the hostname portion.
Keep naming layers separate.
DNS names are not IP addresses.
An IP address identifies a network-layer address.
A DNS name can resolve to an IP address.
One DNS name can resolve to multiple IP addresses.
Multiple DNS names can resolve to the same IP address.
A DNS name can exist without an address record.
An IP address can exist without a DNS name.
Name identity and address identity are different.
A hostname is a name assigned to a host according to a system or network naming scheme.
A DNS name can identify a host.
A DNS name can also identify a service or other namespace object.
Do not assume every DNS name represents one physical computer.
A name can represent a load balancer.
A name can represent a cluster.
A name can represent a CDN.
A name can represent a virtual host.
A name can represent a service endpoint.
A name can change addresses over time.
DNS separates naming from network addressing.
This indirection allows an address to change while the name remains stable.
It also means knowing the name does not prove the current address.
Resolve according to current DNS state when current resolution matters.
DNS data is stored in resource records.
A resource record is commonly abbreviated RR.
A resource-record set is commonly abbreviated RRset.
An RRset contains records with the same owner name, class, and type according to DNS semantics.
DNS record types have defined meanings.
An A record maps a DNS name to an IPv4 address.
An AAAA record maps a DNS name to an IPv6 address.
A CNAME record establishes a canonical-name alias according to DNS rules.
An MX record identifies mail exchangers.
A TXT record stores textual data according to applications using TXT records.
An NS record identifies authoritative name servers for a DNS zone or delegation.
An SOA record contains administrative and control information for a DNS zone.
A PTR record is commonly used for reverse DNS mapping.
An SRV record can publish service location information.
CAA records can express certificate-authority authorization policy.
Other DNS record types exist.
Do not infer a record's meaning from its textual appearance alone.
Interpret it according to its DNS type and application protocol.
An A record contains an IPv4 address.
An AAAA record contains an IPv6 address.
A host can have both.
A client can receive multiple A records.
A client can receive multiple AAAA records.
The existence of multiple addresses does not automatically identify one as primary.
Address-selection behavior belongs to the client and network stack according to applicable rules.
Do not assume the first DNS answer is permanently preferred.
Record ordering can vary.
Resolvers can reorder responses.
Authoritative servers can vary response order.
Applications requiring deterministic behavior should not assign unsupported meaning to DNS answer order.
A CNAME record aliases one DNS name to another DNS name.
The CNAME target is another name.
It is not directly an IP address.
Resolution can continue using the target name.
CNAME chains can exist.
Chains should be bounded.
A CNAME loop is invalid for useful resolution.
Resolvers should detect or eventually terminate cyclic resolution according to protocol limits.
Do not recursively follow aliases without bounds.
A CNAME alias does not mean the alias and target are interchangeable in every application context.
Application identity can still depend on the originally requested hostname.
TLS hostname validation commonly uses the requested hostname rather than blindly replacing application identity with DNS canonical names.
DNS aliasing and application identity are separate.
MX records identify mail exchangers for a domain.
MX records include preference values.
Lower preference values are conventionally preferred according to MX semantics.
An MX target is a hostname.
It is not a URL.
It is not an email address.
Mail delivery software resolves the target according to mail and DNS rules.
Do not treat MX records as generic service discovery unless the application protocol defines that behavior.
TXT records contain textual strings.
TXT records are used by many application protocols.
TXT itself does not define the semantic meaning of the text.
SPF-related information can appear in TXT records.
Domain verification tokens can appear in TXT records.
DKIM-related information can appear under selected DNS names.
Other applications can use TXT.
Do not assume every TXT record has the same purpose.
TXT data is application-defined.
An NS record identifies a name server responsible according to zone or delegation semantics.
A delegation directs resolution from a parent zone toward authoritative servers for a child zone.
Delegation is fundamental to DNS hierarchy.
The root delegates top-level domains.
Top-level domains delegate child domains.
Child domains can delegate further subdomains.
No single ordinary DNS server needs to contain the entire DNS namespace.
Authority is distributed.
A zone is an administrative portion of the DNS namespace served authoritatively.
A zone is not necessarily the same thing as a domain.
A domain is a node and descendants in the namespace according to DNS terminology.
A zone contains the portion for which one administrative authority maintains authoritative data, excluding delegated child zones.
A domain can contain multiple zones because subdomains can be delegated.
Do not confuse domain with zone.
A zone apex is the top name of a DNS zone.
For a zone example.com, example.com is the zone apex.
The apex commonly contains SOA and NS records.
Certain aliasing rules at the zone apex differ from ordinary names because required records must coexist there.
Do not assume every provider's proprietary alias feature is a standard CNAME.
Providers can implement ALIAS, ANAME, flattening, or similar features.
These can produce CNAME-like operational behavior without publishing a standard CNAME at the apex.
Distinguish provider features from DNS protocol record types.
The SOA record is the Start of Authority record.
It contains zone control information.
It identifies a primary server name according to SOA semantics.
It contains administrative information.
It contains a serial value.
It contains timing values used by DNS mechanisms.
Exact interpretation follows DNS standards and server implementation.
The SOA serial can be used to determine whether zone data has changed for zone-transfer purposes.
Serial-number handling has defined arithmetic semantics.
Do not treat it as an ordinary unlimited integer without considering DNS serial arithmetic.
Authoritative DNS servers answer using authoritative zone data for names under their authority.
A recursive resolver answers clients by performing or using recursive resolution and caching results.
Authoritative server and recursive resolver are different roles.
One software package can technically provide both roles.
Operationally, the functions remain distinct.
Do not expose unrestricted recursion merely because a server is authoritative.
Open recursive resolvers can be abused.
A stub resolver is the client-side resolver interface commonly used by applications and operating systems.
An application often asks the operating system resolver for an address.
The stub resolver sends queries to configured recursive resolvers.
The application does not necessarily contact authoritative DNS servers directly.
Therefore application-visible DNS behavior can include operating-system and resolver caching.
A recursive resolver accepts a client's recursive query and attempts to obtain the answer.
It can answer from cache.
It can query authoritative hierarchy.
It can return errors.
It can return negative results.
Recursive resolution commonly begins from known root-server information when no useful cached delegation exists.
The resolver can query a root server.
The root can refer it to authoritative servers for a top-level domain.
The resolver can query the top-level-domain servers.
They can refer it to authoritative servers for the requested child zone.
The resolver can query the authoritative server.
The resolver can return the resulting answer to the client.
This process is simplified by caching.
Most lookups do not necessarily begin from the root because useful data can already be cached.
DNS referrals direct a resolver toward another authoritative server.
A referral is not the final answer to the original application question.
It provides information needed to continue resolution.
Resolvers must distinguish answers from referrals.
Glue records provide address information needed to reach delegated name servers in selected delegation situations.
Glue is especially important when a delegated name server's name lies inside the delegated namespace.
Without necessary glue, resolution could become circular.
Glue records are supplied by the parent zone according to delegation requirements.
Glue is not ordinary authoritative child-zone address data merely because it contains an address.
Its role is to make delegation reachable.
Do not confuse glue with the authoritative A or AAAA RRset for the name.
Caching is fundamental to DNS.
DNS responses contain time-to-live values.
TTL stands for Time To Live.
TTL tells caches how long a DNS record can be retained according to DNS semantics.
TTL is commonly expressed in seconds.
A resolver can cache an answer until its TTL expires.
Changing authoritative DNS does not instantly change every cached answer.
Resolvers can continue returning previously cached data until its caching lifetime expires.
DNS propagation is therefore not one global event traveling across the Internet.
What is commonly called propagation is usually the expiration and replacement of cached DNS information across independent resolvers.
Different resolvers can hold different cached states at the same time.
One resolver can show the new address.
Another can still show the old address.
Both can be operating correctly within their cache state.
Do not declare DNS globally updated based on one resolver.
Do not declare DNS globally broken because two resolvers temporarily disagree during a legitimate transition.
Examine TTL and authoritative state.
TTL begins with the authoritative value but observed remaining TTL can decrease in caches.
A resolver returning a lower TTL can indicate cached data nearing expiration.
Do not assume the returned TTL always equals the zone-file TTL.
Caching layers can exist.
Operating systems can cache DNS.
Browsers can cache selected DNS information.
Applications can cache results.
Recursive resolvers cache results.
Network infrastructure can provide additional resolver behavior.
Clearing one cache does not clear every cache.
A local DNS cache flush cannot force remote recursive resolvers to discard valid cached data.
Authority boundaries matter.
Negative DNS answers can also be cached.
A negative answer can state that a name does not exist.
A negative answer can state that the requested record type does not exist for an existing name.
These conditions differ.
NXDOMAIN indicates that the queried domain name does not exist according to the authoritative DNS result.
A NOERROR response with no requested records can indicate that the name exists but has no records of the requested type.
Do not confuse NXDOMAIN with an empty answer.
Negative caching can cause a recently created name to remain unresolved through some caches until the negative cache expires.
Creating the missing record does not instantly remove every cached negative answer.
Account for negative caching during deployment.
SERVFAIL indicates the resolver could not complete resolution successfully.
SERVFAIL does not mean the requested name definitely does not exist.
It can result from upstream failure.
It can result from DNSSEC validation failure.
It can result from authoritative server problems.
It can result from resolver failure.
It can result from delegation problems.
Do not translate SERVFAIL into NXDOMAIN.
REFUSED indicates the server refused the query according to its policy or capability.
REFUSED does not prove the name is absent.
Different DNS response codes represent different states.
Preserve them when diagnosing.
Timeout is not NXDOMAIN.
Timeout is not SERVFAIL unless a resolver returns SERVFAIL as its resulting response.
A client receiving no DNS response knows only that the required response was not received within its waiting behavior.
The server can be unreachable.
The packet can be lost.
A firewall can block traffic.
The resolver can be overloaded.
The network can be unavailable.
Do not invent a DNS content answer from transport failure.
DNS commonly uses UDP port 53.
DNS can use TCP port 53.
Do not assume DNS is UDP-only.
Traditional DNS clients commonly use UDP for ordinary queries when possible.
TCP is used in circumstances defined by DNS protocols.
Large responses can require TCP fallback.
Zone transfers commonly use TCP.
DNSSEC can increase response sizes.
Modern DNS transports also exist.
DNS over TLS is commonly abbreviated DoT.
DNS over HTTPS is commonly abbreviated DoH.
These transports carry DNS using different secure transport mechanisms.
DoT and DoH do not change the underlying meaning of DNS records.
They change transport and privacy/security properties between selected participants.
Do not confuse encrypted DNS transport with DNSSEC.
DNSSEC stands for Domain Name System Security Extensions.
DNSSEC provides mechanisms for authenticating DNS data according to a chain of trust.
DNSSEC can provide origin authentication of DNS data.
DNSSEC can provide integrity protection for signed DNS data.
DNSSEC can provide authenticated denial of existence.
DNSSEC does not encrypt ordinary DNS queries or responses.
DNSSEC does not provide confidentiality.
DoT and DoH can encrypt DNS transport between a client and resolver.
That does not automatically provide end-to-end DNS data authenticity equivalent to DNSSEC.
Transport security and DNS data authentication are different.
DNSSEC uses cryptographic signatures associated with DNS RRsets.
RRSIG records contain DNSSEC signatures.
DNSKEY records publish public keys for a zone.
DS records in a parent zone establish selected trust linkage to a child zone.
NSEC and NSEC3 records support authenticated denial of existence according to DNSSEC mechanisms.
Exact DNSSEC validation follows DNSSEC protocol rules.
Do not implement DNSSEC by merely checking that an RRSIG record exists.
A signature must validate.
The relevant key must be valid.
The chain of trust must be established.
The signed data must match.
Time validity must be considered.
Algorithm support must be considered.
Presence is not validation.
A validating resolver performs DNSSEC validation when configured and supported.
A signed zone with broken DNSSEC can become unreachable to validating resolvers while appearing to work through nonvalidating paths.
This can create apparently inconsistent DNS behavior.
Check DNSSEC status when signed domains produce SERVFAIL unexpectedly.
A DNSSEC chain of trust commonly begins from a configured trust anchor.
The DNS root trust anchor allows validation to proceed through signed delegations.
Trust does not arise merely because a DNS record says it is trusted.
Cryptographic validation and configured trust establish it.
DNSSEC does not establish application authorization.
A correctly signed A record establishes selected authenticity of DNS data.
It does not prove the server at that address is authorized for every application operation.
Application protocols still require their own authentication and authorization where needed.
DNS resolution and service availability are separate.
A name can resolve correctly while the service is down.
A name can resolve correctly while the server refuses connections.
A name can resolve correctly while the application returns errors.
A name can resolve correctly while TLS validation fails.
A name can resolve correctly while a firewall blocks the service port.
A name can resolve correctly while routing fails.
DNS success proves only the DNS result established by the lookup.
It does not prove end-to-end service health.
Likewise, DNS failure does not necessarily prove the underlying server is down.
A server can remain reachable directly by IP while its DNS name fails to resolve.
Do not confuse naming failure with host failure.
A DNS lookup is one stage in network connection establishment.
Application requests can involve:
Interpret application target.
Resolve hostname.
Select an address.
Establish network route.
Establish transport connection.
Perform TLS where applicable.
Perform application protocol exchange.
Authenticate or authorize as required.
Each stage can fail independently.
Report the failed stage.
Do not report "server down" merely because DNS resolution failed.
DNS can support load distribution by returning multiple addresses.
DNS can vary answers.
DNS can use geographically informed responses.
DNS can use health-informed authoritative systems.
DNS can use weighted policies through provider-specific systems.
The DNS protocol itself does not guarantee that every returned address is healthy.
Clients should handle connection failure according to application rules.
DNS is not a substitute for application health checking.
Round-robin DNS commonly refers to returning multiple address records with varying order.
Record order alone does not guarantee balanced traffic.
Clients can cache.
Clients can choose one address.
Resolvers can reorder.
Connection behavior can differ.
Do not infer exact load distribution from DNS record order.
Low TTL values can allow address changes to become visible sooner to compliant caches.
Low TTL does not create instantaneous failover.
Clients can cache beyond expected boundaries.
Existing connections remain established to old addresses.
Applications can maintain their own caches.
DNS changes do not terminate existing TCP connections.
DNS is consulted during resolution, not continuously for every established connection.
A client already connected to an old address can remain connected after DNS changes.
Do not expect a DNS update to move existing connections.
DNS-based failover therefore has timing limits.
If rapid failover is required, design at the appropriate application, transport, load-balancing, or service-discovery layer.
DNS can contribute but should not be assigned guarantees it does not provide.
A DNS record can have a long TTL.
Changing it shortly before migration can leave old data cached for the previous TTL duration.
Operational migrations commonly lower TTL before a planned address change.
The lower TTL itself must first become visible after older cached records expire.
Changing TTL at the same moment as changing the address does not retroactively shorten TTLs already cached.
Plan transitions.
After migration stabilizes, TTL can be increased according to operational needs.
High TTL reduces query load and can improve cache efficiency.
Low TTL allows faster cache turnover.
Neither is universally correct.
Choose according to change frequency and operational requirements.
DNS resolvers can cache failures.
DNS clients should not retry aggressively without bounds.
Repeated immediate retries can increase load during resolver or authoritative failure.
Use appropriate retry behavior.
Multiple configured resolvers can provide resilience.
Do not assume querying many public resolvers simultaneously is always appropriate.
Respect system resolver policy unless architecture requires otherwise.
Applications normally benefit from using the operating system resolver.
Direct DNS implementations require more protocol responsibility.
Do not implement a DNS client from scratch merely to resolve ordinary hostnames unless requirements justify it.
System resolver APIs can provide address resolution.
On POSIX-like systems, getaddrinfo is commonly used.

It can apply system resolver configuration.
It can apply local host mappings.

Name resolution and DNS querying are related but not always identical.
A local hosts file can map names to addresses.

Diagnostic testing should distinguish:

Authoritative DNS result.

Tools such as dig can query DNS directly.
Tools such as nslookup can query DNS through their supported behavior.
Host-resolution tools can use system resolver facilities.

A successful ping by hostname demonstrates some form of name resolution plus selected network behavior.

Reverse DNS maps IP addresses toward names using the DNS reverse namespace.
IPv4 reverse DNS commonly uses in-addr.arpa.
IPv6 reverse DNS commonly uses ip6.arpa.

Reverse DNS is not the automatic inverse of forward DNS.
An A record does not automatically create a PTR record.
A PTR record does not automatically create an A record.
Forward and reverse DNS are managed separately.
A reverse name can differ from the original forward name.
Multiple forward names can point to one IP while reverse DNS returns one selected name.
Do not require mathematical one-to-one symmetry unless the application policy requires matching forward and reverse resolution.
Forward-confirmed reverse DNS is a validation technique used by selected applications.
It involves resolving an address to a name and resolving that name forward to check whether the address is represented.
This provides selected evidence.
It is not general authentication.
DNS names can be internationalized.
Internationalized Domain Names allow non-ASCII user-facing domain labels through defined mechanisms.
DNS wire representation historically operates on an ASCII-compatible representation for these names.
Punycode is used within the IDNA framework to represent selected Unicode domain labels in ASCII-compatible form.

Do not implement IDNA conversion by manually adding or removing xn--.

Unicode domain names create security considerations.
Different characters can look similar.
Display and network forms can differ.
A browser can choose to display an ASCII-compatible form in suspicious situations.

Inspect signatures.
Inspect validity times.
Inspect algorithms.
Inspect parent-child coordination.
Repair the broken trust chain.
Do not disable DNSSEC merely to make the error disappear unless the authorized operational decision is to remove DNSSEC correctly through its defined process.
When building software that accepts a hostname, validate the hostname syntax required by the application.
Resolve it through the intended resolver mechanism.
Treat returned addresses as current resolution results.
Do not treat them as permanent.
If network policy restricts destinations, validate the actual destination addresses.
Establish application identity separately.
Handle multiple addresses.
Handle IPv4 and IPv6 according to requirements.
Handle resolution failure explicitly.
Do not convert resolution failure into a fabricated address.
When building deterministic systems, keep DNS outside consensus semantics unless DNS input is explicitly captured and agreed through the protocol.
DNS can discover candidate endpoints.
The protocol can then validate candidate identity.
Do not let two nodes independently resolving a dynamic DNS name create different authoritative state.
Discovery can vary.
Consensus cannot.
DNS answers the question:
What DNS information is currently available for this name according to the resolver, authority, cache state, query type, and DNS policy involved?
It does not answer:
Is the application running?
Is the destination trustworthy?
Is the destination authorized?
Is the service healthy?
Will every resolver return the same answer right now?
Will this address remain the same?
Those are different questions.
Use DNS for naming.
Use network tests for connectivity.
Use application protocols for service behavior.
Use cryptographic identity where trust requires it.
Use authorization policy for permission.
And when DNS evidence is incomplete, do not turn a resolver's uncertainty into a fabricated answer.
The DNS result is unknown until the required evidence establishes it.
C is a general-purpose programming language.
C is a compiled programming language.
C was designed for efficient systems programming.
C provides relatively direct access to memory and machine-level resources.
C source files commonly use the .c filename extension.
C header files commonly use the .h filename extension.
C source code is translated into executable machine code by a compiler and related build tools.
A C implementation consists of a compiler and supporting implementation facilities.
ISO C refers to standardized versions of the C programming language.
Portable C code avoids unnecessary dependence on implementation-specific behavior.
A C program begins execution through the main function in a hosted environment.
The main function returns an int.
Returning zero from main conventionally indicates successful program termination.
A nonzero program exit status conventionally indicates some form of failure.
C is case-sensitive.
Uppercase and lowercase identifiers are distinct in C.
Statements in C commonly end with a semicolon.
A block of C statements is enclosed by braces.
Whitespace generally separates tokens but is otherwise flexible in many contexts.

Modern C also supports // line comments.
An identifier names an object, function, type, label, macro, or other program entity.
C identifiers can contain letters, digits, and underscores subject to language rules.
An identifier cannot begin with a digit.
C has reserved keywords that cannot be used as ordinary identifiers.
A variable is a named object whose stored value can change during its lifetime.

The short type is an integer type.
The int type is an integer type.
The long type is an integer type.
The long long type is an integer type.

A pointer stores an address or pointer value referring to an object, function, or permitted special location.

Encoding is the representation of information according to defined rules.
An encoding maps information from one representation into another representation.
Encoding does not inherently provide secrecy.
Encoding does not inherently provide authenticity.
Encoding does not inherently provide integrity.
Encoding is not encryption.
Encoding is not hashing.
Encoding is not compression.
These operations can be combined, but they solve different problems.
Text encoding defines how textual information is represented as bytes.
Computers store and transmit bytes.
Human-readable text consists of characters interpreted according to a character model.
A sequence of bytes does not identify its text encoding by itself.
The same bytes can be interpreted differently under different encodings.
The encoding must be known, defined, detected through a reliable mechanism, or otherwise established by the surrounding format or protocol.
Do not guess an encoding when correctness requires certainty.
ASCII is a character encoding.
ASCII defines numeric values for a limited set of characters.
ASCII includes English letters.
ASCII includes digits.
ASCII includes punctuation.
ASCII includes control characters.
ASCII does not represent the full range of human writing systems.
Unicode is a character standard.
Unicode assigns code points to characters and other textual elements.
Unicode is not itself one single byte encoding.
UTF-8 is a Unicode encoding.
UTF-16 is a Unicode encoding.
UTF-32 is a Unicode encoding.
Do not confuse Unicode with UTF-8.
Do not confuse a Unicode code point with its UTF-8 bytes.
A Unicode code point is an abstract numeric value assigned by Unicode.
Code points are commonly written using notation such as U+0041.
U+0041 represents the character LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A.
The UTF-8 representation of a code point can contain one or more bytes.
The UTF-16 representation of a code point can contain one or more 16-bit code units.
The UTF-32 representation commonly uses one 32-bit code unit for each Unicode code point.
Code point and code unit are different concepts.
A code unit is the basic storage unit used by an encoding.
UTF-8 uses 8-bit code units.
UTF-16 uses 16-bit code units.
UTF-32 uses 32-bit code units.
One character is not necessarily one code unit.
One character is not necessarily one byte.
One visible symbol is not necessarily one Unicode code point.
These distinctions matter.
UTF-8 represents Unicode code points using sequences of one to four bytes.
ASCII characters use the same byte values in UTF-8 as they do in ASCII.
This makes UTF-8 compatible with ASCII for the ASCII range.
Characters outside the ASCII range require multiple bytes in UTF-8.
Therefore string byte length and character count can differ.
Do not allocate UTF-8 storage based solely on character count without accounting for byte representation.
Do not truncate UTF-8 arbitrarily at a byte boundary if valid text must be preserved.
A truncation point can fall inside a multi-byte sequence.
Invalid UTF-8 can result.
UTF-8 has defined valid byte sequences.
Not every arbitrary byte sequence is valid UTF-8.
A UTF-8 decoder should reject or explicitly handle malformed sequences according to application policy.
Do not silently interpret malformed UTF-8 as valid text.
UTF-16 represents Unicode using 16-bit code units.
Some Unicode code points require one UTF-16 code unit.
Others require a surrogate pair consisting of two code units.
Therefore one UTF-16 code unit does not always represent one code point.
Splitting a surrogate pair creates invalid Unicode representation.
UTF-16 has byte-order considerations when represented as bytes.
UTF-16LE uses little-endian byte order.
UTF-16BE uses big-endian byte order.
If a protocol uses UTF-16, byte order must be established.
UTF-32 represents Unicode code points using fixed-width 32-bit code units.
Fixed-width code units do not mean user-visible characters have fixed width.
A visible grapheme can still contain multiple code points.
Text rendering and Unicode encoding are separate concerns.
A byte order mark is commonly abbreviated BOM.
A BOM is a Unicode character that can be used at the beginning of selected encoded text to indicate encoding or byte order.
UTF-16 and UTF-32 can use a BOM to indicate byte order.
UTF-8 can contain the byte sequence representing U+FEFF as a signature at the beginning of a file.
UTF-8 does not require a BOM.
Some software expects a UTF-8 BOM.
Some software does not.
Some formats discourage or prohibit it.
The surrounding format determines acceptable behavior.
Do not automatically add a BOM to every UTF-8 file.
Do not automatically remove a BOM when exact bytes matter.
A BOM can become significant if software does not expect it.
For example, a parser expecting the first bytes to contain a particular marker can fail if unexpected BOM bytes precede it.
Encoding rules belong to the format.
Unicode characters can have multiple equivalent representations.
A character with an accent can sometimes be represented as one precomposed code point.
It can sometimes be represented as a base character followed by a combining mark.
These representations can look identical.
Their bytes can differ.
Their code-point sequences can differ.
Unicode normalization defines standardized transformations between selected equivalent representations.
Common normalization forms include NFC.
Common normalization forms include NFD.
Common normalization forms include NFKC.
Common normalization forms include NFKD.

Math.random is not intended for cryptographic security.
Passwords should not be generated or protected using Math.random when cryptographic randomness is required.
Password hashing should be performed with algorithms designed for password storage.
A general cryptographic hash is not automatically an appropriate password-storage algorithm.
Private keys require controlled storage.
A private key delivered to browser JavaScript cannot remain secret from the user controlling that browser.
TLS protects transport between endpoints when correctly configured.
TLS does not prevent application-level XSS.
TLS does not enforce authorization.
TLS does not validate application data semantics.
JavaScript can use WebSocket APIs in supported browsers.
WebSocket provides bidirectional communication over a persistent connection after its opening handshake.
WebSocket messages have message boundaries.
WebSocket and raw TCP are different abstractions.
Browser JavaScript does not ordinarily expose arbitrary raw TCP sockets.
Server-side JavaScript runtimes can provide TCP APIs.
Network capabilities depend on the runtime environment.
A WebSocket connection can close unexpectedly.
WebSocket applications require reconnection policy when reconnection is desired.
Automatic reconnection should use bounded retry behavior.
Immediate infinite retry loops can overload a service.
Exponential backoff can reduce repeated retry load.
Retry behavior should distinguish transient failures from permanent failures.
An operation should not be retried automatically when repeating it can produce unsafe duplicate effects unless the operation is idempotent or otherwise protected.
Idempotency means repeating an operation has the same intended effect as performing it once according to the operation's contract.
GET, PUT, and DELETE have idempotent semantics under HTTP definitions even though repeated requests can produce different response representations.
POST is not inherently idempotent.
Application-level idempotency keys can protect some retried creation operations.
JavaScript can execute in server environments.

Node.js is not the JavaScript language itself.

Runtime-specific APIs should not be mistaken for universal ECMAScript APIs.
process is a Node.js global API rather than a browser JavaScript global.
window is a browser global object in traditional browser contexts.
document is a browser API and is not normally available in a basic Node.js process.
A JavaScript program should know which runtime environment it targets.
Package ecosystems provide third-party JavaScript libraries.
npm is a package manager commonly associated with JavaScript and Node.js.
A package.json file describes package metadata and dependencies in common JavaScript tooling.
package.json is not part of ECMAScript syntax.
Third-party packages introduce dependencies and supply-chain considerations.
A dependency should not be added merely because a small operation can be delegated to a package.

Installing a package can execute lifecycle behavior depending on package manager configuration and package metadata.
Untrusted dependencies can execute code with developer or build-system privileges.
Dependency provenance matters.
Unused dependencies should be removed when practical.

Using JavaScript does not require React.
Using JavaScript does not require Node.js.

Using JavaScript does not require a framework.

Frameworks also introduce dependencies and complexity.
The simplest adequate implementation is often easier to maintain.

TypeScript and JavaScript are distinct languages.
JavaScript runtimes execute JavaScript rather than TypeScript source unless tooling or runtime-specific support transforms it.

External JSON remains untrusted even when a TypeScript type says what shape the programmer expects.
Runtime validation and compile-time typing solve different problems.

An end-to-end test exercises a larger application path.

JavaScript supports destructuring.

A shallow copy does not recursively clone nested objects.

Pure functions produce results without observable side effects according to their defined inputs.

Pure functions can be easier to test and reason about.

ECMAScript modules provide module-scoped bindings.

An API is a source or service interface contract.

API and ABI are different concepts.
Browser JavaScript normally interacts through APIs and protocols rather than native ABIs.

A JavaScript package version is not an ABI version.

Current configuration describes current state.
Evidence about a previous version does not establish that the previous version remains active.
