Add regression tests.
Improve detection where necessary.
Improve containment where necessary.
Improve recovery where necessary.
Reliability engineering turns failure into evidence and evidence into better system behavior.
Reliable systems do not depend on everything always working.
Reliable systems define what happens when things do not work.
They preserve correctness where possible.
They contain failure.
They recover through controlled mechanisms.
They report their actual state.
They preserve evidence.
They do not guess.
They do not claim success without verification.
Reliability is demonstrated through continued correct behavior, controlled failure, and verified recovery.
TLS stands for Transport Layer Security.
TLS is a cryptographic protocol used to protect communication between networked applications.
TLS can provide confidentiality.
TLS can provide integrity.
TLS can provide authentication.
The exact properties established depend on the protocol version, configuration, authentication method, certificate validation, cryptographic algorithms, and application behavior.
TLS is not an application protocol.
TLS can protect application protocols.
HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS.
TLS can protect other protocols.
Do not confuse TLS with HTTPS.
Do not confuse TLS with HTTP.
Do not confuse TLS with TCP.
Do not confuse TLS with DNS.
These are separate layers.
A common connection sequence is:
Resolve a hostname.
Establish a network connection.
Establish a transport connection.
Perform the TLS handshake.
Validate the peer identity.
Establish TLS session keys.
Exchange protected application data.
Each stage can fail independently.
A DNS lookup succeeding does not prove TLS will succeed.
A TCP connection succeeding does not prove TLS will succeed.
A TLS handshake succeeding does not automatically prove the application request will succeed.
Identify the failing layer.
TLS commonly operates over TCP.
TLS is not part of TCP.
TCP provides an ordered byte stream.
TLS protects data carried over that stream.
TLS records are transported through TCP.
TCP does not understand TLS certificates.
TCP does not perform TLS authentication.
TCP does not encrypt application data by itself.
TLS 1.3 is a modern TLS protocol version.
TLS 1.2 remains widely deployed.
Older protocol versions have weaker or obsolete properties and can be disabled according to security requirements.
Protocol version support should be deliberate.
Do not enable obsolete protocol versions merely because an old client requests them unless compatibility requirements explicitly authorize that risk.
TLS protocol negotiation determines which mutually supported TLS version is used according to protocol rules.
The client offers supported capabilities.
The server selects according to the protocol and its configuration.
The selected version must be acceptable to both participants.
Do not assume the highest version supported by the server is always the version used.
The client also matters.
A TLS handshake establishes cryptographic parameters before protected application communication proceeds.
The handshake can negotiate protocol version.
The handshake can negotiate cryptographic algorithms.
The handshake can establish shared key material.
The handshake can authenticate the server.
The handshake can optionally authenticate the client.
The handshake binds selected negotiation state cryptographically.
Do not treat the handshake as merely an exchange of certificates.
Certificates are one part of common TLS authentication.
A TLS certificate commonly uses the X.509 certificate format.
A certificate binds selected identity information to a public key according to a signature and trust model.
A certificate contains a public key or information associated with one.
A certificate contains validity information.
A certificate contains issuer information.
A certificate contains subject-related information.
A certificate can contain Subject Alternative Name information.
A certificate contains a digital signature from its issuer or is otherwise part of a defined trust structure.
A certificate is not a private key.
The public certificate can be distributed.
The private key must remain protected.
Possession of a certificate file does not prove possession of its private key.
A TLS server commonly needs access to the private key corresponding to its certificate.
The server proves possession of appropriate private key material during the TLS handshake according to the selected protocol and authentication method.
Do not send a server's private key to clients.
Clients do not need the server private key to verify the server.
Public-key cryptography allows verification using public information.
Private keys are secrets.
Protect them accordingly.
A certificate authority is commonly abbreviated CA.
A CA can issue certificates according to a public-key infrastructure.
A root CA certificate can serve as a trust anchor.
Intermediate CAs can issue certificates beneath a root or another intermediate.
A server certificate is commonly an end-entity certificate.
A certificate chain connects the end-entity certificate through issuer relationships toward a trusted root according to validation rules.
A server commonly sends its end-entity certificate and required intermediate certificates.
The trusted root is commonly already present in the client's trust store.
The server generally does not need to send the root certificate.
Certificate-chain validation is more than checking that certificate files exist.
The client validates cryptographic signatures.
The client validates issuer relationships.
The client validates certificate validity periods.
The client validates constraints.
The client validates intended usage.
The client validates hostname or application identity where required.
The client determines whether the chain reaches an accepted trust anchor.
If required validation fails, the peer is not authenticated according to that validation policy.
Do not continue as though authentication succeeded.
A certificate can be cryptographically valid but inappropriate for the requested hostname.
Trusting the issuing CA is not sufficient by itself.
Application identity must also be checked.
For HTTPS, hostname verification is essential.
If the client requested example.com, the certificate must be valid for example.com according to certificate identity rules.
A certificate valid for another.example does not become valid for example.com merely because both names resolve to the same IP address.
DNS address equality does not establish TLS identity equality.
The requested hostname matters.
Subject Alternative Name is commonly abbreviated SAN.
Modern certificate hostname identity is represented using SAN entries according to applicable certificate validation rules.
A certificate can contain multiple DNS names.
A certificate can contain IP address identities.
DNS-name identity and IP-address identity are distinct.
A certificate for a DNS name does not automatically validate when connecting by raw IP address.
The certificate must contain the required identity according to the validation rules.
Do not disable hostname validation merely because the server is reachable.
Reachability is not identity.
A wildcard certificate can cover selected subdomains according to certificate matching rules.
A wildcard such as *.example.com does not mean arbitrary recursive matching at every depth.
Wildcard matching has defined semantics.
Do not treat TLS certificate wildcards as shell wildcards.
Do not confuse a wildcard certificate with a wildcard DNS record.
They are independent.
Certificate validity has a start and end.
A certificate can be not yet valid.
A certificate can be expired.
System time therefore matters.
A machine with substantially incorrect time can reject otherwise legitimate certificates.
Do not disable certificate validation to work around a broken clock.
Correct the clock.
Certificate expiration does not mean encryption mathematically stops functioning.
It means the certificate no longer satisfies its validity policy.
The connection should fail validation when expiration is disallowed.
Operational certificate renewal should occur before expiration.
Certificate renewal creates or obtains a certificate with a new validity period.
Renewal can also involve new key material.
Exact behavior depends on certificate management policy.
Automated renewal reduces operational failure risk.
Automation should still be monitored.
A renewal process succeeding does not prove the application loaded the new certificate.
Verify the active service certificate.
A certificate file on disk can be current while the running process still serves an older certificate loaded into memory.
The service can require reload or restart according to implementation.
Verify over the actual network interface.
Do not infer active certificate state solely from filesystem contents.
Certificate revocation provides mechanisms for indicating that a certificate should no longer be trusted before normal expiration.
CRLs are Certificate Revocation Lists.
OCSP is the Online Certificate Status Protocol.
Revocation behavior varies by client, certificate ecosystem, and policy.
Do not assume every TLS client checks revocation identically.
Revocation is not a replacement for protecting private keys.
If a private key is compromised, respond according to certificate and key-compromise procedures.
Replace compromised key material.
Revoke certificates where appropriate.
Do not continue trusting the old key merely because its certificate has not expired.
A private key compromise is different from a certificate expiration.
A private key should have restricted filesystem permissions.
A private key should not be committed to source control.
A private key should not be included in public container images.
A private key should not be printed into ordinary logs.
A private key should not be transmitted through insecure channels.
A private key should not be embedded in client software when it represents server identity.
Treat private keys as security-sensitive material.
A certificate signing request is commonly abbreviated CSR.
A CSR contains information used when requesting a certificate and demonstrates possession of selected key material according to its format.
A CSR is not the resulting certificate.
A CSR is not the private key.
Creating a CSR does not itself create trust.
A CA or other authorized issuance mechanism must issue the certificate according to policy.
Self-signed certificates are signed using their own corresponding private key rather than through an external CA chain.
A self-signed certificate can provide encryption.
It can support authentication if the client explicitly trusts that certificate or key through a secure mechanism.
A self-signed certificate is not automatically insecure.
The problem is trust establishment.
If a client blindly accepts any self-signed certificate, authentication is absent.
If a specific self-signed certificate is securely provisioned as a trust anchor, it can provide authenticated identity within that trust model.
Do not confuse public CA issuance with the only possible trust model.
Private certificate authorities can establish organizational trust.
Pinned certificates or public keys can establish selected trust relationships.
Preconfigured trust anchors can establish selected trust relationships.
The trust mechanism must be defined.
Do not trust a certificate merely because it is syntactically valid.
Certificate validation answers whether the presented identity satisfies the configured trust rules.
It does not answer whether the application operation is authorized.
Authentication and authorization are separate.
A valid TLS client certificate can authenticate a client identity.
The application must still determine what that identity is allowed to do.
Do not grant administrative access merely because mutual TLS succeeded unless policy maps that identity to administrative authority.
Mutual TLS is commonly abbreviated mTLS.
Ordinary public HTTPS commonly authenticates the server to the client.
mTLS additionally authenticates the client using TLS certificate mechanisms.
Both participants can therefore present cryptographic identity.
mTLS does not automatically define application roles.
It establishes identities according to certificate validation.
Authorization remains an application decision.
TLS uses symmetric cryptography for bulk protected communication after key establishment.
Symmetric cryptography is efficient for application data.
Public-key or related asymmetric mechanisms are used during authentication and key establishment according to the selected TLS version and cipher suite.
Do not assume every application byte is encrypted directly using the certificate's public key.
That is not how ordinary TLS data protection works.
Session keys protect the connection.
TLS 1.3 uses modern key-establishment mechanisms according to its protocol.
Ephemeral key exchange can provide forward secrecy.
Forward secrecy means compromise of a long-term authentication key does not automatically reveal past session keys when the protocol and key exchange provide that property and ephemeral secrets are no longer available.
Forward secrecy is not retroactive protection against every form of compromise.
If an attacker captured plaintext at an endpoint, TLS cannot recover confidentiality.
Endpoint security remains necessary.
TLS protects data in transit between TLS endpoints.
TLS does not protect plaintext before encryption at the sending endpoint.
TLS does not protect plaintext after decryption at the receiving endpoint.
If a reverse proxy terminates TLS, traffic beyond that proxy is outside that TLS connection.
It can be protected by another TLS connection.
It can be plaintext.
Architecture determines the protection boundary.
Do not say traffic is end-to-end encrypted merely because the public-facing connection uses TLS if an intermediary terminates TLS.
Identify the actual endpoints.
A load balancer can terminate TLS.
A web server can terminate TLS.
A reverse proxy can terminate TLS.
An application can terminate TLS directly.
TLS termination determines where ciphertext becomes plaintext.
That boundary matters for security.
A proxy can establish another TLS connection to an upstream server.
This is a separate TLS session.
The client-to-proxy session and proxy-to-upstream session have different cryptographic state.
Do not treat them as one continuous TLS session.
TLS confidentiality prevents passive observers between the TLS endpoints from reading protected application data when the protocol is securely configured and uncompromised.
TLS integrity detects unauthorized modification of protected records according to the cryptographic protocol.
TLS authentication establishes selected peer identity according to certificate or other configured authentication mechanisms.
These properties depend on successful validation.
Encryption without authentication can remain vulnerable to active interception.
Do not disable certificate verification and then claim ordinary authenticated TLS security.
A man-in-the-middle attack places an attacker between communicating parties.
Proper certificate validation helps prevent an attacker from impersonating the intended TLS server without appropriate trusted credentials.
If the client accepts any certificate, the attacker can present their own certificate and defeat intended server authentication.
Certificate verification is not optional decoration.
It is central to authenticated TLS.
TLS cipher suites identify combinations of cryptographic mechanisms according to the TLS version.
TLS 1.3 cipher-suite semantics differ from TLS 1.2.
Do not interpret a TLS 1.3 cipher-suite name using TLS 1.2 assumptions.
Protocol version matters.
Modern TLS libraries should generally choose secure defaults unless application requirements require explicit configuration.
Do not construct custom cryptographic algorithm combinations casually.
Cryptographic agility allows protocols and implementations to replace algorithms over time.
Agility does not mean every algorithm should remain enabled.
Weak algorithms should be retired.
Unsupported algorithms should fail negotiation rather than trigger improvised fallback.
TLS negotiation should not silently downgrade below configured security requirements.
Downgrade protection exists in modern TLS mechanisms.
Applications should configure minimum acceptable versions.
Do not enable insecure fallback merely to make a connection succeed.
A failed secure connection is evidence of incompatibility or configuration failure.
Turning off security can hide the problem rather than solve it.
TLS 1.3 simplified and removed selected older cryptographic mechanisms.
TLS 1.3 does not use the same handshake flow as TLS 1.2.
Do not assume packet sequences are identical across versions.
Diagnostic tools must account for protocol version.
TLS records encapsulate protected protocol data.
Applications generally should not manually construct TLS records.
Use a maintained TLS implementation.
TLS is complex.
Correct cryptographic implementation requires precise protocol compliance.
Do not write custom TLS merely to avoid a library dependency.
Use established libraries unless the project specifically requires protocol implementation research.
TLS libraries include implementations such as OpenSSL and platform-provided cryptographic stacks.
Different platforms can expose different APIs.
Protocol behavior should remain standards-compliant even when implementation APIs differ.
Do not bind application semantics to one TLS library unnecessarily.
Platform abstraction can isolate implementation details.
Security requirements should remain consistent across platforms.
A TLS client begins with information about the intended server.
For hostname-based services, this commonly includes the hostname.
The hostname can be used for certificate validation.
The hostname can also be sent through Server Name Indication.
Server Name Indication is commonly abbreviated SNI.
SNI allows a client to indicate the intended hostname during the TLS handshake.
This allows one server address to host multiple TLS identities.
SNI is not DNS.
SNI does not resolve a hostname.
SNI communicates a server-name indication after network connection establishment begins.
The server can use SNI to select a certificate or virtual host.
A missing or incorrect SNI value can cause the server to present an unexpected certificate.
This can lead to hostname-validation failure.
Do not conclude the certificate installation is universally broken until the SNI behavior is checked.
Connecting directly to an IP address while expecting a name-based virtual host can produce a different certificate.
Diagnostic tools should send the intended SNI hostname.
Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation is commonly abbreviated ALPN.
ALPN allows peers to negotiate selected application protocols within the TLS handshake.
HTTP/2 commonly uses ALPN.
HTTP/1.1 can be selected according to negotiation.
ALPN does not replace the application protocol.
It selects or identifies which supported application protocol will be used over the TLS connection.
Do not confuse ALPN with TCP port selection.
Port 443 is conventionally used for HTTPS.
TLS itself is not restricted to port 443.
TLS can operate on other ports.
Other protocols can use TLS on their assigned or configured ports.
Port number does not prove TLS is present.
A service listening on 443 can still be misconfigured.
A TLS handshake test establishes whether TLS actually responds.
Likewise, a TLS service can run on a nonstandard port.
Do not identify protocol solely by port number.
HTTPS commonly uses URI scheme https.
The scheme indicates HTTP over a secure TLS connection according to HTTPS semantics.
The server's certificate identity should correspond to the requested host.
The HTTP Host header and TLS SNI can both involve the requested hostname but operate at different layers.
SNI is used during TLS handshake.
The HTTP Host field is part of the later HTTP request.
Do not confuse them.
TLS must normally be established before encrypted HTTP headers can be exchanged.
Therefore the server can need SNI before it sees the HTTP Host header.
This is why SNI matters for certificate selection.
TLS handshake failure occurs before ordinary protected application exchange.
An HTTP status code is not normally available when TLS itself cannot be established.
If a client reports certificate failure, debugging HTTP routing first can be premature.
Establish TLS success first.
Then inspect HTTP.

Modern secure communication uses TLS.
The term SSL is still used colloquially in phrases such as SSL certificate.

A certificate can be encoded in different representations.

File extensions are conventions.

A password-protected key file is not permission to expose it publicly.
Password protection is one control.
File access control still matters.
A certificate chain file can contain multiple certificates.
Ordering can matter to server configuration.
The server should present the chain required for clients to construct validation toward a trusted root.

The server should provide the required chain.
Trust stores differ.
Operating systems can maintain trust stores.
Browsers can use operating-system trust stores or their own trust mechanisms depending on implementation.
Applications can ship private trust stores.
Containers can have separate CA bundles.
A certificate trusted on one machine can be untrusted on another.

Private CA deployments require clients to trust the appropriate CA.

TLS session resumption can allow returning clients to establish protected sessions with reduced handshake overhead.

They can also indicate interception.
Determine the environment.
TLS interception changes the security boundary.
The inspecting intermediary terminates one TLS connection and establishes another.
It can see plaintext.
Do not call such a connection cryptographically end-to-end between original client and origin server.
It is two protected connections with an intermediary.
A reverse proxy is similar structurally, though intentionally part of the service architecture.
Identify every termination point.
TLS does not authenticate IP routing.
An attacker can redirect traffic toward another address.
Certificate validation should still reject an endpoint unable to authenticate as the intended hostname.
This is one reason DNS compromise does not automatically defeat properly validated HTTPS.
If the attacker also controls or obtains trusted certificate credentials for the hostname, the situation changes.
Security properties depend on multiple systems.
DNSSEC and TLS can complement each other.
DNSSEC authenticates selected DNS data.
TLS authenticates the application endpoint according to its trust model and protects transport.
Neither universally replaces the other.
DANE is a mechanism that can associate TLS information with DNSSEC-authenticated DNS records for supported applications.
DANE depends on DNSSEC validation.
DANE is not ordinary public Web PKI behavior in every client.
Do not assume browser support or application behavior without evidence.
TLSA records are used by DANE.
A TLSA record's meaning depends on its usage, selector, matching type, and DNSSEC-authenticated context.
Do not treat a TLSA record as a generic certificate fingerprint.
Follow DANE rules.
HTTP Strict Transport Security is commonly abbreviated HSTS.
HSTS is an HTTP security policy instructing supporting clients to use HTTPS for a host according to defined rules.
HSTS is not part of the TLS handshake.
It is delivered through HTTP over a secure connection and affects future client behavior.
Do not confuse HSTS with TLS itself.
HSTS can reduce opportunities for downgrade to plaintext HTTP.
HSTS does not repair an invalid TLS certificate.
If HTTPS is broken, HSTS can make the site inaccessible rather than permit insecure fallback.
That is intentional security behavior.
HSTS preload is a browser ecosystem mechanism that can cause HTTPS enforcement before a site is first visited.
Preload has operational consequences.
Do not enable long-lived or preloaded HSTS without ensuring HTTPS can remain reliably available.
Security policy creates obligations.
TLS redirect behavior is an HTTP behavior.
A server can redirect http:// requests to https://.
The initial HTTP request before the redirect is not protected by the later TLS session.
HSTS can address selected downgrade exposure for supporting clients.
Do not describe an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect itself as encryption of the original request.
Cookies can have a Secure attribute.
A Secure cookie is restricted to secure transport contexts according to browser rules.
TLS provides the secure transport used by HTTPS.
The Secure attribute is an HTTP cookie policy.
Do not confuse cookie security attributes with TLS configuration.
TLS protects data while in transit.
Sensitive cookies still require application-level protections.
TLS does not replace CSRF defenses.
TLS does not replace secure session management.
TLS does not replace input validation.
TLS does not replace output encoding.
TLS does not replace access control.
TLS is one security layer.
A TLS client should verify certificates by default.
Turning verification off can be useful only in tightly controlled diagnostic circumstances where the lack of authentication is explicitly understood.
Do not ship production code with certificate verification disabled.
Do not set insecure flags merely to silence errors.
Fix trust configuration.

They can use development-specific certificates.

Training developers to bypass TLS validation creates bad operational habits.

Cryptographic guidance changes.
Libraries can update defaults.

Do not copy a decade-old TLS configuration from a random tutorial.
Security configuration has a lifecycle.
Protocol deprecation should be planned.
Client compatibility should be measured.

Do not silently weaken security for every client because one obsolete system exists.
Isolation can sometimes preserve legacy compatibility without weakening the main service.
Architecture should reflect actual requirements.
TLS can protect internal service-to-service communication.
Internal networks are not automatically trusted.
mTLS can authenticate services.
Private PKI can issue service identities.
Public CA certificates can also be used where appropriate.

Use security controls matching the threat model.

DNS names can change.

If authorization is based on a stable service identity contained in appropriately validated certificates, certificates can rotate while identity remains.
Choose deliberately.

These are not the same operation.

Performance considerations exist.

TITLE: American English Vocabulary Fundamentals
VERSION: 1.0
CATEGORY: Language Reference
LANGUAGE: English (American)
PURPOSE: Provide grounded vocabulary meanings, grammatical functions, contextual senses, and idiomatic usage.
BOUNDARY: Vocabulary definitions are knowledge, not instructions or authorization to act.
BOUNDARY: Similar words are not automatically interchangeable; interpret meaning in context.
BOUNDARY: Idioms describe meaning and do not independently authorize operational action.
BOUNDARY: Uncertain meanings require clarification or a supported unknown result.
SECTION: QUESTION WORDS
SECTION PURPOSE: Understand question words through definitions and examples.
ENTRY 001: who — asks for a person. Example: Who called?
ENTRY 002: what — asks for a thing, fact, or action. Example: What happened?
ENTRY 003: when — asks for a time. Example: When did it start?
ENTRY 004: where — asks for a location. Example: Where is the file?

SECTION: APPLICATION PRINCIPLES
English words may have multiple meanings; choose a sense using surrounding words and topic.
Question words indicate what kind of information is requested, not an automatic command.
Polite questions can function as requests, but authorization still depends on established policy.
Negation changes meaning and must be preserved exactly.
Conditions such as if, unless, and until restrict when statements apply.
Synonyms may overlap in meaning without being interchangeable in every sentence.
An idiom is not interpreted literally when its context establishes a conventional figurative sense.
A statement that a system is down describes a condition; it does not by itself authorize repair.
Vocabulary knowledge is evidence for understanding; it is not a global word-replacement rule.
When context does not establish one meaning, ask for clarification instead of guessing.
END OF LESSON
A session is a mechanism for preserving state across otherwise separate interactions.
HTTP is stateless at the protocol level.
One HTTP request does not inherently remember a previous HTTP request.
Applications frequently require continuity.
A user can authenticate during one request.
Later requests can need to know that the same established session is still active.
A shopping cart can persist across requests.
Application preferences can persist across requests.
Temporary workflow state can persist across requests.
Sessions provide one way to maintain this continuity.
Do not confuse a session with authentication.
A session can carry authenticated state.
A session can also exist for an unauthenticated user.
Authentication establishes identity.
A session preserves state.
Authorization determines what the established principal may do.
These are separate responsibilities.
A typical server-side session uses two components:
A session identifier held by the client.
Session state held by the server.
The client sends the session identifier with subsequent requests.
The server uses that identifier to locate the associated session state.
The session identifier is a reference.
It does not need to contain the complete session state.
A simplified flow is:
Client makes request.
Server creates session.
Server generates session identifier.
Server stores session state associated with that identifier.
Server sends the identifier to the client.
Client returns the identifier on later requests.
Server locates the session.
Server validates the session.
Server uses the session state.
Do not trust a session identifier merely because the client supplied one.
The server must determine whether it corresponds to a valid active session.
A session identifier should be unpredictable.
Use a cryptographically secure random source.
Do not generate session identifiers from sequential numbers.
Do not generate session identifiers from user IDs.
Do not generate session identifiers from timestamps.
Do not generate session identifiers from predictable counters.
Do not create a session identifier by concatenating public values.
An attacker who can predict another session identifier can potentially impersonate that session.
Session identifiers are credentials when possession grants access to session state.
Treat them as secrets.
Do not log full session identifiers.
Do not expose them unnecessarily.
Do not place them in URLs unless a protocol explicitly requires it and the risks are understood.
URLs commonly appear in:
Browser history.
Server logs.
Proxy logs.
Analytics systems.
Referrer information.
Screenshots.
Copied links.
Session identifiers should normally be transmitted using mechanisms intended for credentials.
Web applications commonly use cookies.
A cookie is data associated with HTTP requests according to browser cookie rules.
A session cookie can contain a session identifier.
The browser can automatically send the cookie with matching requests.
The cookie itself does not make the session secure.
Its contents and attributes matter.
A session cookie commonly looks conceptually like:
session=<random identifier>
The identifier maps to server-side state.
Do not put plaintext passwords into session cookies.
Do not put private keys into session cookies.
Do not put unnecessary secrets into session cookies.
A cookie can have a Secure attribute.
Secure instructs compatible browsers to send the cookie only over secure transport according to browser rules.
Use Secure for session credentials when HTTPS is required.
Do not expose an authenticated session over plaintext HTTP.
A cookie can have an HttpOnly attribute.
HttpOnly prevents ordinary client-side JavaScript from reading the cookie according to browser behavior.
This can reduce direct session-cookie theft through some script-based attacks.
HttpOnly does not prevent every consequence of cross-site scripting.
A malicious script can potentially perform requests using the user's existing session even when it cannot read the cookie.
Prevent script injection.
Do not treat HttpOnly as complete XSS protection.
A cookie can have a SameSite attribute.
SameSite controls selected cross-site cookie behavior.
Common values include:
Strict.
Lax.
None.
Their exact behavior depends on browser rules and request context.
SameSite can reduce selected cross-site request attacks.
It does not replace complete CSRF analysis.
When SameSite=None is used, browsers commonly require Secure.
Use cookie settings appropriate to the application's actual cross-site requirements.
Do not weaken cookie policy merely to make an integration work without understanding why.
Cookie Domain controls which hosts can receive a cookie according to browser rules.
Avoid unnecessarily broad cookie domains.
A cookie scoped to an entire parent domain can be exposed to more subdomains than required.
Keep session-cookie scope narrow.
Cookie Path restricts cookie transmission according to URL path matching.
Path can reduce unnecessary exposure.
Path is not a strong security boundary against malicious code within the same origin.
Do not rely on cookie Path as the sole authorization mechanism.
Cookie expiration controls persistence.
A session cookie can expire when the browser session ends according to browser behavior.
A persistent cookie can contain an explicit expiration or maximum age.
Cookie persistence and server-side session lifetime are separate.
Deleting the cookie does not necessarily destroy server-side session state.
Expiring server-side session state does not necessarily immediately remove the cookie from the browser.
The server must validate the session on every request where it is used.
If the server-side session is expired, the request must not regain authority merely because the browser still has the identifier.
Server state is authoritative for server-side sessions.
A session can have a creation time.
A session can have a last-activity time.
A session can have an absolute expiration time.
A session can have an idle expiration time.
These values have different meanings.
Absolute expiration limits total session lifetime.
Idle expiration limits how long the session can remain unused.
A session can use both.
For example:
Absolute lifetime: eight hours.
Idle lifetime: thirty minutes.
The session ends when either applicable limit is reached.
Exact durations depend on application requirements.
Do not invent arbitrary session durations without considering risk and usability.
High-risk administrative sessions can require shorter lifetimes.
Low-risk applications can use different policies.
Session expiration should be enforced by the server.
Do not rely solely on browser cookie expiration.
A copied session identifier can exist outside the original browser.
Server-side expiration limits its validity.
A session can be invalidated before expiration.
Logout is a common reason.
Credential change can be another reason.
Account disabling can be another reason.
Security incident response can be another reason.
Administrative revocation can be another reason.
Session invalidation should make future use of that session fail.
Do not merely hide the application interface after logout.
Destroy or invalidate the authentication state.
A logout operation for a server-side session commonly does the following:
Identify the current session.
Invalidate or delete its server-side state.
Expire the client cookie.
Return the user to an unauthenticated state.
The server-side invalidation is the critical authority change.
Cookie deletion cleans up the client state.
If the cookie is deleted but the server session remains active, a copied identifier can still be usable.
Do not equate client cleanup with server invalidation.
A system can support logging out one session.
A system can support logging out all sessions.
These are different operations.
Logout current session invalidates one session.
Logout all sessions invalidates every applicable session associated with the account.
To support global logout, the system needs enough server-side state or revocation information to identify those sessions.
Do not claim global logout if old tokens remain valid independently.
Session rotation replaces one session identifier with another.
Rotation is important when authentication state changes.
Anonymous session exists.
User logs in successfully.
Application rotates the session identifier.
Authenticated state becomes associated with the new identifier.
The old identifier is invalidated or otherwise prevented from representing the authenticated session.
This helps prevent session fixation.
Session fixation occurs when an attacker establishes or predicts a session identifier and causes a victim to authenticate using that same identifier.
If the application continues using it after login, the attacker can potentially use the known identifier to access the authenticated session.
Rotate session identifiers when privilege state changes.
Login is a common rotation point.
Privilege elevation can be another rotation point.
Sensitive reauthentication can be another rotation point.
Do not retain an externally supplied or previously exposed identifier after authentication without considering fixation.
Session rotation should preserve only state that is intended to survive.
Shopping cart contents may survive login.
Authentication state should be newly established.
Temporary security-sensitive state should be reviewed.
Do not blindly copy every anonymous-session field into an authenticated session.
Untrusted pre-authentication state can become dangerous after privilege elevation.
A session can contain:
Authenticated principal identifier.
Authentication time.
Authentication method.
Session creation time.
Last activity time.
CSRF-related state.
Temporary workflow state.
Selected application preferences.
Other bounded state.
Store only what is required.
Do not turn the session into an uncontrolled dumping ground.
Session state is security-sensitive.
If an attacker can modify server-side session state, they can potentially change identity or authority information.
Protect the session store.
Do not let clients directly modify trusted server-side session fields.
authenticated_user_id
role
authentication_level
must come from trusted application logic.
Do not copy client request parameters directly into trusted session authority fields.
A request containing:
role=administrator
does not become trustworthy because the value is stored in the session.
Untrusted input remains untrusted.
Sessions can be stored in memory.
Sessions can be stored in files.
Sessions can be stored in databases.
Sessions can be stored in distributed caches.
Sessions can be stored using other server-side mechanisms.
Each storage mechanism has operational and security properties.
In-memory sessions are fast.
They can disappear when the process restarts.
They can be difficult to share across multiple application instances without additional architecture.
File-backed sessions are simple.
Filesystem permissions matter.
Concurrent access matters.
Cleanup matters.
Database-backed sessions can persist across processes and servers.
Database availability matters.
Query cost matters.
Distributed cache sessions can support multiple application instances.
Cache availability matters.
Eviction behavior matters.
Replication behavior matters.
Do not select a session store merely because it is fashionable.
Use the smallest mechanism that satisfies requirements.
A single-server application does not automatically need a distributed session cluster.
A multi-server application must ensure a request can access the required session state.
One approach is shared session storage.
Another approach is request affinity.
Another approach is self-contained client tokens.
These are different architectures.
Do not mix their assumptions.
Request affinity is sometimes called sticky sessions.
A load balancer routes a client repeatedly to the same application instance.
This can allow instance-local session state.
If that instance fails, the session can be lost unless state is replicated elsewhere.
Sticky routing is an infrastructure technique.
It is not session security.
Shared session storage allows multiple application instances to access the same session state.
This can simplify failover.
It introduces a shared dependency.
Protect access to the session store.
Only authorized application components should read or modify session state.
Do not expose a session database directly to clients.
Session records should have bounded lifetimes.
Expired records should be removed or marked unusable.
Otherwise the session store can grow indefinitely.
Cleanup can occur:
On access.
Periodically.
Through database expiration.
Through cache TTL.
Through scheduled maintenance.
The exact mechanism depends on storage.
Expiration must still be enforced even if physical cleanup is delayed.
An expired session record remaining in storage must not become valid merely because cleanup has not run yet.
Logical validity and physical deletion are separate.
Session IDs can be stored in a database as hashes rather than plaintext when the design permits.
If an attacker obtains the session database, plaintext active session identifiers can potentially be used directly.
Hashing session tokens can reduce this risk.
The client possesses the random token.
The server hashes the presented token.
The server looks up the hash.
This resembles API-token verification.
Do not confuse session-token hashing with password hashing.
High-entropy random session tokens do not require deliberately slow password hashing.
A normal secure cryptographic hash can be appropriate for random tokens according to design.
Passwords are low-entropy human secrets.
Random session tokens should have high entropy.
Different threat models require different primitives.
Do not apply expensive password hashing blindly to every random session token.
Session identifiers need sufficient entropy.
Entropy makes guessing infeasible.
Length alone is not enough if generation is predictable.
A 128-character sequential identifier is still predictable.
Use cryptographically secure randomness.
Encoding does not create entropy.
Hex.
Base64.
Base64url.
These represent bytes.
They do not make weak random data strong.
Generate strong random bytes first.
Then encode them safely.
Session identifiers should avoid characters that cause transport ambiguity.
Use an established framework's session generation when it provides a secure implementation.
Do not invent a custom token format without need.
Framework session systems should be configured correctly.
Defaults can differ.
Check:
Cookie name.
Secure.
HttpOnly.
SameSite.
Lifetime.
Storage.
Rotation behavior.
Garbage collection.
Domain.
Path.
Do not assume framework defaults match production security requirements.
A framework can manage session lifecycle.
Understand what its session regeneration function actually does.
Some APIs create a new ID while retaining old state.
Some invalidate the old ID.
Some require explicit destruction.
Use documented behavior.
Do not guess.
PHP provides built-in session support.
A PHP application can call session_start() to initialize or resume a session according to configuration.
PHP commonly obtains a session identifier from a cookie.
PHP loads the associated session state.
The application can access session data through $_SESSION.

can hold an authenticated user identifier after successful authentication.
Do not set it before authentication succeeds.
PHP session configuration controls security behavior.
Relevant settings can include cookie security attributes and session identifier behavior.

PHP session IDs should be regenerated after successful login.
session_regenerate_id() participates in that process.
Use it according to PHP's documented semantics.
Do not manually invent replacement IDs when the runtime provides secure session handling.
A PHP logout can require:
Starting the session.
Clearing application session state.
Invalidating the session record.
Expiring the session cookie.
Exact implementation depends on configuration.
Do not merely unset one user variable if other authenticated state remains.
Clear the complete security-relevant session state.
Session destruction should not accidentally destroy unrelated server state outside the intended session.
Understand framework and language behavior.
Do not use global destructive operations casually.
Sessions can exist in non-PHP systems.
The principles remain similar.
Generate secure identifiers.
Protect transport.
Validate server-side state.
Rotate after authentication.
Expire sessions.
Support invalidation.
Keep authority explicit.
Do not make security depend on one programming language.
Client-side storage is different from server-side sessions.
Browsers provide mechanisms such as:
Cookies.
localStorage.
sessionStorage.
These have different access and transmission behavior.
localStorage values are accessible to JavaScript running in the origin.
They are not automatically attached to HTTP requests.
sessionStorage is also script-accessible and is scoped according to browser session rules.
Do not assume sessionStorage is equivalent to a server session because the names are similar.
They are different concepts.
Browser storage containing bearer credentials can be exposed through script execution.
Cookie-based credentials with HttpOnly can reduce direct script access.
Architecture determines the appropriate mechanism.
There is no universal rule that every token must always be stored in one specific browser mechanism.
Analyze the threat model.
Do not store credentials casually.
A server-side session and a JSON Web Token are not the same thing.
A server-side session commonly stores state on the server and gives the client an opaque identifier.
A self-contained JWT can carry claims inside the token.
The server can validate the token cryptographically without loading ordinary session state.
Both can represent authenticated continuity.
Their lifecycle properties differ.
Do not call every authentication token a session ID.
A JWT can be used within a session architecture.
A session can be implemented without JWT.
JWT is a token format.
Session is an application-state concept.
Stateless token authentication is not truly state-free in every operational sense.
Keys must exist.
Accounts have state.
Permissions can change.
Revocation can be required.
Security events can require invalidation.
Do not use "stateless" to pretend lifecycle problems disappeared.
Self-contained tokens can make immediate revocation more difficult.
A token can remain cryptographically valid until expiration.
If immediate revocation is required, the system needs a mechanism such as:
Short token lifetime.
Revocation records.
Token introspection.
Account version checks.
Signing-key changes.
Another defined invalidation strategy.
Do not promise session revocation that the architecture cannot enforce.
Server-side sessions make individual invalidation straightforward because the server controls the session record.
They require session storage.
This is a tradeoff.
Do not choose token architecture solely to avoid one database lookup without measuring whether that lookup is actually a problem.
Simple systems benefit from simple sessions.
Performance optimization should follow evidence.
Session state can become stale.
Suppose the session contains:
role=editor
The administrator changes the user's role to viewer.
If the application trusts the old session role until logout, the user can retain editor authority longer than intended.
This is an authorization freshness issue.
Possible approaches include:
Load current role on each request.
Invalidate sessions when role changes.
Store a permission version and compare it.
Use short session lifetimes.
Refresh session authority periodically.
Choose according to requirements.
Do not assume session-cached authorization is current.
Authentication state can also become stale.
An account can be disabled while sessions remain active.
A password can be changed while sessions remain active.
A credential can be revoked while sessions remain active.
Policy should define whether those events invalidate sessions.
Implement that behavior explicitly.
Do not assume password change automatically invalidates sessions unless the system does it.
A session can store an authentication timestamp.
Sensitive operations can require recent authentication.
User logged in six hours ago.
User requests a high-risk security change.
Application requires reauthentication.
After successful reauthentication, the session records a new authentication time or elevated assurance state according to policy.
Do not infer recent authentication from recent activity.
Clicking pages for six hours is not the same as proving the credential again.
Session activity and authentication age are separate.
A session can have an authentication assurance level.
Password authenticated.
Password plus additional factor authenticated.
Hardware authenticator verified.
Exact levels are application-defined.
Authorization can require a minimum assurance level for sensitive operations.
Do not let the client set the assurance level.
It must derive from completed authentication.
Step-up authentication can temporarily elevate session assurance.
Define how long that elevation lasts.
Do not leave elevated state permanent accidentally.
Privilege elevation should have a lifecycle.
Session state can represent impersonation.
If an administrator intentionally impersonates another user, preserve:
Actual authenticated administrator identity.
Effective user identity.
Impersonation start time.
Applicable authorization.
Do not overwrite the actor identity and lose accountability.
A session can carry both actor and effective principal.
Audit logs should distinguish them.
Do not let ordinary users create impersonation state.
Impersonation is a privileged operation.
Session hijacking occurs when an attacker obtains a valid session credential and uses it.
Possible exposure paths include:

Device information.

Proxies can alter characteristics.

It is not equivalent to a session credential.
A session nonce can be used for particular operations.

A session identifier can be reusable throughout a session.

Different purposes.
CSRF tokens can be associated with sessions.
A CSRF token helps verify that state-changing requests came through an expected interaction according to the application's CSRF model.
It does not authenticate the user independently.
The session establishes the user context.
The CSRF mechanism protects request integrity against selected cross-site attacks.
Do not use the session ID itself as a visible CSRF token.
Exposing the session credential defeats its confidentiality.
Generate separate CSRF state.

They should be validated server-side.
Do not merely include a hidden field and fail to verify it.
A token that is never checked provides no protection.
SameSite cookies can complement CSRF tokens.

Do not assume one mechanism is universally sufficient.
Session management interacts with CSRF but is not the same problem.
Concurrent sessions can be allowed.
A user can be logged in from multiple devices.
Policy should define whether this is permitted.
Possible models include:
Unlimited active sessions.
Limited number of sessions.
One session per device.
One active session total.

Session administration is a protected operation.

Authorization is the process of determining whether an authenticated or otherwise identified principal is permitted to perform a requested action on a resource.
Authorization answers:
What is this principal allowed to do?
Authorization does not establish identity.
Authentication establishes identity.
Authorization evaluates permissions.
Keep them separate.
A user can authenticate successfully and still be unauthorized.
An unauthenticated requester can sometimes be authorized to access a public resource.
Public access is an authorization decision.
Do not require authentication merely to claim that authorization exists.
Authorization requires a decision context.
The context commonly includes:
Principal.
Action.
Resource.
Applicable policy.
Relevant state.
The authorization decision determines whether the requested operation is permitted.
A useful authorization question is:
May principal P perform action A on resource R under policy C?
Every part matters.
Changing the principal can change the result.
Changing the action can change the result.
Changing the resource can change the result.
Changing applicable policy can change the result.
Changing relevant state can change the result.
Do not reduce authorization to a single boolean stored on the user account unless the system is genuinely that simple.
A permission represents authority to perform a defined operation.
Examples include:
Read a document.
Create a record.
Modify a record.
Delete a record.
Publish content.
Manage users.
Change configuration.
Execute an administrative operation.
Permissions should describe actual authority.

A role is a collection or classification of authority according to a system's access-control model.
Examples can include:
User.
Editor.
Administrator.
Operator.
Auditor.
Roles are application-defined.
The name of a role does not inherently define its permissions.
"Administrator" means only what the system's authorization policy says it means.
Do not infer permissions from a role's English name.
Role-Based Access Control is commonly abbreviated RBAC.
RBAC assigns permissions to roles.
Principals are assigned roles.
Authorization can then determine whether one of the principal's roles contains the required permission.
A simplified relationship is:
Principal -> Role -> Permission.
Real systems can include additional constraints.
Do not confuse RBAC with authentication.
RBAC assumes the principal has already been established or otherwise identified.
A role should not be supplied by an untrusted client as authoritative input.
The server determines the principal's roles from trusted authorization state.
Never authorize because a form field says:

Client-side state is not authorization authority.
The server must make the authoritative authorization decision.
Hiding a user-interface element can improve usability.

A user can construct HTTP requests manually.
A user can modify HTML.
A user can modify JavaScript.
A user can call an API directly.
Authorization must be enforced where the protected operation occurs.
Do not rely on the interface to enforce permissions.
Every protected server-side action should enforce the applicable authorization policy.
A page can be protected.
An API endpoint can be protected.
A command can be protected.
A database operation can be protected.
A file operation can be protected.

Do not assume requests only arrive through the expected user interface.
Authorization should normally occur after authentication when the resource requires an authenticated identity.
A common request sequence is:

Authenticate the requester.
Establish the principal.
Determine the target resource.
Evaluate authorization.

If unauthorized, reject the operation.

A permission check should occur before the protected effect.

Do not delete the file and then evaluate the role.

Read access is authority.

Execute access is authority.
Administrative access is authority.
Do not focus only on destructive operations.

Least privilege means a principal receives only the authority required for its legitimate function.

Narrow authority reduces the impact of mistakes and compromise.

Authority should match purpose.
Default deny means access is denied unless policy explicitly permits it.

Unknown permission should not become permission granted.

Do not assume an operation is safe merely because it is not explicitly forbidden.

Access Control Lists are commonly abbreviated ACLs.
An ACL associates resources or objects with access rules.
An ACL can specify which principals or groups may perform which operations.
For example:
User A can read File X.
Group B can read and modify File X.
User C has no access to File X.
ACLs are resource-oriented access-control structures.
Do not confuse ACLs with filesystem permissions specifically.
Filesystems can use ACLs.
Applications can also implement ACLs.
Discretionary Access Control is commonly abbreviated DAC.
DAC commonly allows an object's owner or another authorized principal to control access according to system rules.
Mandatory Access Control is commonly abbreviated MAC.
MAC enforces access according to centrally defined security labels or policy.
Do not confuse Mandatory Access Control with a network interface MAC address.
They share an abbreviation.
They are unrelated concepts.
Attribute-Based Access Control is commonly abbreviated ABAC.
ABAC evaluates attributes associated with subjects, resources, actions, and environment.
Example attributes can include:
Department.
Resource classification.
Employment status.
Device state.
Time.
Operation type.
ABAC can express policies more flexibly than simple roles.
Flexibility also increases policy complexity.
Do not add ABAC when a small role or ownership check solves the requirement.
Authorization architecture should remain as simple as the actual requirements allow.
Policy complexity creates failure opportunities.
Ownership-based authorization allows operations according to a defined ownership relationship.
A user may modify their own profile.
A user may read their own private document.
A user may delete a resource they created if policy permits it.
Ownership must be established from trusted server-side state.
Do not accept:
owner_id=<current user>
from the client as proof of ownership.
The server should load the resource.
The server should determine its recorded owner.
The server should compare that ownership with the authenticated principal according to policy.
Client claims do not establish ownership.
An object identifier identifies a resource.
It does not authorize access to that resource.
Knowing another user's resource ID does not grant permission to read it.
This distinction is critical.
Authorization must be evaluated after identifying the requested object.
Insecure Direct Object Reference is commonly abbreviated IDOR.
IDOR vulnerabilities occur when an application exposes object identifiers and fails to enforce appropriate authorization on access to those objects.
/documents/100
/documents/101
If User A is authorized for document 100 but can change the URL to 101 and receive User B's document without an authorization check, access control is broken.
The problem is not that identifiers are sequential.
Random identifiers can make discovery harder.
They do not replace authorization.
A UUID does not grant security merely because it is difficult to guess.
If an unauthorized user obtains the UUID, the server must still reject access.
Do not use unguessability as the only access-control mechanism for protected resources.
Capability-based systems intentionally use possession of an unforgeable capability as authority.
That is a specific authorization model.
Do not accidentally create a capability system merely by assuming nobody will discover a URL.
If possession is intended to grant authority, define the credential as a capability and protect it accordingly.
If possession is not intended to grant authority, enforce ordinary authorization.
Object-level authorization checks the requester's authority over the specific target object.
Function-level authorization checks whether the principal may perform a type of operation.
Both can be required.
A user can have permission to edit documents generally while lacking permission to edit a particular document.
Do not stop at function-level authorization when object ownership or scope matters.
Permission: edit_document.
Resource: document 123.
Policy can require both:
Principal has edit_document permission.
Principal is authorized for document 123.
One does not imply the other.
Administrative permission can intentionally override ordinary ownership restrictions.
If so, encode that rule explicitly.
Do not scatter undocumented administrator bypasses throughout the code.
Centralize authorization policy where practical.
Explicit policy is easier to review.
An authorization rule should be understandable.
Allow update when the principal owns the record.
Allow update when the principal has records.admin permission.
Otherwise deny.
This is clearer than:
if ($user)
where authentication is accidentally treated as universal authorization.
Authenticated does not mean authorized.
Roles can be hierarchical.
An administrator role can include permissions from an editor role.
An editor can include permissions from a viewer role.
Role inheritance should be explicit.
Do not infer hierarchy from role names.
A role called "senior_editor" does not automatically inherit "editor" unless policy says so.
Role hierarchies can simplify policy.
They can also create hidden privilege expansion.
Review inherited permissions.
A role change can affect many permissions at once.
Treat role assignment as a security-sensitive operation.
Only authorized principals should assign privileged roles.
Do not let users modify their own role fields unless explicitly permitted.
Mass assignment can create authorization vulnerabilities.
Suppose an account update accepts:
name
email
role
If ordinary users should only modify name and email, accepting role from the request can allow privilege escalation.
Use explicit writable-field allowlists.
Do not bind every request field directly into privileged models.
Privilege escalation occurs when a principal gains authority beyond what policy permits.
Vertical privilege escalation moves toward more privileged authority.
Ordinary user becomes administrator.
Horizontal privilege escalation accesses another principal's resources at the same nominal privilege level.
User A accesses User B's private record.
Both are authorization failures.
Do not focus only on administrator escalation.
Horizontal access-control failures are common and serious.
Authorization boundaries should be tested for both.
For every protected operation, test:
Authorized principal succeeds.
Unauthenticated requester behaves according to policy.
Authenticated but unauthorized principal is denied.
Wrong owner is denied.
Wrong role is denied.
Revoked authority is denied.
Malformed or manipulated identifiers do not bypass checks.
Negative authorization testing is essential.
A test suite that verifies only successful authorized operations does not establish access-control enforcement.
Try to violate the policy.
Authorization tests should operate at the actual enforcement boundary.
If the HTTP endpoint performs the check, test the endpoint.
If the service layer performs the check, test the service layer.
If both are expected to enforce independent boundaries, test both.
Do not test only whether a button is hidden.
UI tests are not sufficient evidence of server authorization.
Middleware can enforce broad authorization rules.
Require authentication.
Require administrator role.
Require a named permission.
Middleware is useful for route-level policy.
Resource-specific authorization can still require application logic after loading the target resource.
Do not force every authorization decision into routing middleware if the decision requires resource state unavailable there.
Put checks where sufficient evidence exists.
Authorization logic can be centralized in policy functions.

Central policy reduces inconsistent enforcement.

Keep policies bounded by resource or domain.
Small explicit policy is easier to audit.
Authorization checks should return a deterministic decision for the same relevant state.
Allow.
Deny.
If the policy engine itself fails, protected operations should fail safely.
Do not convert exceptions into allow.
Do not use:

for protected operations.

Authorization can depend on current state.
A user's role can change.
A resource's owner can change.
A contract can expire.
A membership can become inactive.
A permission can be revoked.
Do not assume authority established yesterday remains valid forever.
Evaluate current policy where required.
Cached authorization can improve performance.

If permissions are revoked, cached authorization can continue granting access until expiration unless invalidation exists.
The acceptable delay must be defined.
Do not cache authorization indefinitely merely for speed.
Security state has freshness requirements.
Authorization data can be versioned.
A role or permission update can invalidate relevant caches.

That can be acceptable or unacceptable depending on policy.

A safer design for highly sensitive operations can consult current authorization state.
A lower-risk application can accept bounded session-cached permissions.
Architecture should match requirements.

because it arrived as JSON.

Delegated authority should remain bounded.

A Linux distribution combines the Linux kernel with user-space software, libraries, utilities, configuration, and package management.
Ubuntu is a Linux distribution.
Debian is a Linux distribution.
Fedora is a Linux distribution.
Arch Linux is a Linux distribution.
Linux and Ubuntu are not synonyms.
Ubuntu uses the Linux kernel.
The kernel and user space are different execution environments.
Kernel space contains privileged kernel execution.
User space contains ordinary application processes.
Applications normally request kernel services through system calls.
A system call provides a controlled interface from user space to the kernel.
Programs should not assume that ordinary user-space code can directly access arbitrary kernel memory.
A process is an executing program instance.
A program file and a running process are different things.
Multiple processes can execute the same program.
Each process has a process identifier.
A process identifier is commonly abbreviated PID.
PID 1 has a special role as the initial user-space process within a Linux PID namespace.
On many modern Linux distributions systemd runs as PID 1.
A parent process can create child processes.
A process has a parent process identifier.
A parent process identifier is commonly abbreviated PPID.
Processes have credentials.
Process credentials include user identity information.
Process credentials include group identity information.
Linux users are identified internally by numeric user identifiers.
A user identifier is commonly abbreviated UID.
Linux groups are identified internally by numeric group identifiers.
A group identifier is commonly abbreviated GID.
User names provide human-readable mappings to UIDs.
Group names provide human-readable mappings to GIDs.
The root user conventionally has UID 0.
UID 0 receives special privileges from the kernel.
Running as root grants substantial authority.
Applications should not run as root merely because doing so avoids permission problems.
Least privilege means granting only the authority required for a task.
A service should run under an appropriate dedicated account when practical.
A dedicated service account can limit damage from compromise.
Changing file permissions to make everything writable is not least privilege.
Linux files have ownership.
A file has an owning user.
A file has an owning group.
Traditional Unix file permissions contain read, write, and execute bits.
Permissions are defined separately for owner, group, and other.
The read permission is represented by r.
The write permission is represented by w.
The execute permission is represented by x.
For a regular file, read permission permits reading file contents according to applicable access checks.
For a regular file, write permission permits modifying file contents according to applicable access checks.
For a regular file, execute permission permits execution when other requirements are satisfied.
Directory permissions have different practical meanings from regular-file permissions.
Read permission on a directory permits listing directory entries according to applicable access checks.
Write permission on a directory permits creating, removing, or renaming entries according to applicable access checks.
Execute permission on a directory permits traversing or searching the directory according to applicable access checks.
Writing an existing file and creating a new file involve different permission checks.
Deleting a file primarily depends on permissions on its containing directory rather than the file's own write bit.
A process must be able to traverse parent directories to access a path.
chmod changes traditional file mode permissions.
chown changes file ownership.
chgrp changes group ownership.
chmod does not change the owning user.
chown does not inherently change every permission bit.
Numeric chmod modes encode permission bits.
Permission value 4 represents read.
Permission value 2 represents write.
Permission value 1 represents execute.
Permission values are combined for owner, group, and other.
Mode 755 commonly means owner read-write-execute and group and other read-execute.
Mode 644 commonly means owner read-write and group and other read-only.
Mode 600 commonly means owner read-write with no group or other permissions.
Mode 700 commonly means owner read-write-execute with no group or other permissions.
Mode 777 grants read, write, and execute permissions broadly.
chmod 777 should not be used as a generic solution to permission problems.
World-writable files and directories increase security risk.
Permissions should reflect actual required access.
The setuid permission can cause an executable to run with the file owner's effective UID under applicable conditions.
The setgid permission has special behavior for executable files and directories.
On directories, setgid can cause new entries to inherit the directory's group.
The sticky bit on a shared writable directory restricts removal or renaming of entries according to ownership rules.
The /tmp directory commonly uses the sticky bit.
umask influences permission bits removed from newly created files and directories.
umask is not itself the final file permission.
The creating program's requested mode and the umask together influence resulting traditional permissions.
Access Control Lists can provide permissions beyond traditional owner-group-other mode bits.
Linux ACLs are commonly manipulated with getfacl and setfacl.
Traditional mode bits are not always the entire access-control story.
Linux capabilities can grant selected privileged kernel operations without granting full root authority.
Capabilities divide some traditional root privileges into smaller units.
Granting a process one required capability can be safer than running the entire process as root.
Capabilities should still be treated as privileged authority.
Linux uses a hierarchical filesystem namespace.
The root of the filesystem namespace is /.
Absolute paths begin with /.
Relative paths are interpreted relative to a process's current working directory.
The current directory is represented by .
The parent directory is represented by ..
Path normalization matters for security.
Untrusted paths can contain traversal components.
Applications should not blindly concatenate untrusted strings into privileged filesystem paths.
The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard describes common directory purposes on Linux systems.
Not every Linux system follows every hierarchy convention identically.
/etc commonly contains system configuration.
/var commonly contains variable system data.
/var/log commonly contains logs.
/var/lib commonly contains persistent application state.
/var/cache commonly contains application cache data.
/run commonly contains runtime state.
/tmp commonly contains temporary files.
/usr commonly contains installed user-space programs and data.
/usr/bin commonly contains executable programs.
/usr/lib commonly contains libraries and supporting files.
/usr/local commonly contains locally installed software outside distribution package management conventions.
/opt commonly contains optional or self-contained application software.
/home commonly contains user home directories.
/root is commonly the root user's home directory.
/dev exposes device nodes and related interfaces.
/proc exposes a virtual filesystem containing process and kernel information.
/sys exposes kernel device and subsystem information through sysfs.
/boot commonly contains boot-related files.
Filesystem hierarchy conventions communicate intent.
Application-specific installation layouts can deliberately use /opt.
Persistent application data should not be confused with temporary runtime data.
Configuration and mutable runtime data should be distinguished when practical.
Logs and configuration serve different purposes.
Executable binaries and writable application state should be separated when practical.
A regular file stores byte data.
A directory maps names to filesystem objects.
A symbolic link contains a pathname reference.
A hard link creates another directory entry referring to the same inode where supported.
A symbolic link and a hard link are different mechanisms.
Removing one hard link does not remove file data while other hard links still reference the inode.
A symbolic link can become dangling when its target no longer exists.
Following symbolic links can have security implications.
Privileged programs should handle untrusted symbolic links carefully.
An inode stores filesystem metadata for an object in traditional Unix filesystem designs.
A filename is stored in a directory entry rather than being the inode itself.
Different filesystems implement details differently.
A filesystem can be mounted into the filesystem namespace.
mount attaches a filesystem at a mount point.
umount detaches a mounted filesystem when conditions permit.
A mount point is a directory where another filesystem becomes accessible.
Different mount points can reside on different storage devices or filesystem types.
Renaming a file within one filesystem can have different atomicity properties from moving data between filesystems.
Atomic rename behavior should not be assumed across filesystem boundaries.
Atomic file replacement is useful for durable configuration updates.
A common pattern writes complete new content to a temporary file and renames it over the target.
Durability can require additional synchronization beyond rename.
fsync requests synchronization of file data or metadata according to its contract.
A successful write system call does not necessarily mean data has reached persistent physical storage.
Buffering and caching can delay physical storage.
Durability requirements should be explicit.
A file descriptor is a process-local integer referring to an open resource.
Standard input conventionally uses file descriptor 0.
Standard output conventionally uses file descriptor 1.
Standard error conventionally uses file descriptor 2.
Standard input is commonly abbreviated stdin.
Standard output is commonly abbreviated stdout.
Standard error is commonly abbreviated stderr.
File descriptors can refer to regular files.
File descriptors can refer to pipes.
File descriptors can refer to sockets.
File descriptors can refer to devices.
File descriptors are finite process resources.
A process that leaks file descriptors can eventually fail to open additional resources.
Opening a file and closing a file are distinct lifecycle operations.
close releases a file descriptor reference.
A closed descriptor number can later be reused.
Programs should not assume a descriptor number permanently identifies the same resource.
Shell redirection changes where standard streams are connected.
The > operator commonly redirects standard output to a file and truncates or creates it according to shell semantics.
The >> operator commonly appends standard output.
The < operator commonly redirects standard input.
2> commonly redirects standard error in shells such as Bash.
2>&1 commonly redirects standard error to the current destination of standard output according to shell evaluation order.
A pipe connects the output of one process to the input of another.
The | shell operator commonly creates a pipeline.
A pipeline allows programs to compose through streams.
Pipes carry bytes.
A pipe is not a persistent file.
A pipe has finite buffering.
A writer can block when a pipe buffer is full and no reader drains it.
A reader can observe end-of-file when all writing endpoints are closed.

Anonymous pipes are commonly created between related processes.

Linux IPC mechanisms include pipes.
Linux IPC mechanisms include Unix domain sockets.
Linux IPC mechanisms include network sockets.
Linux IPC mechanisms include shared memory.
Linux IPC mechanisms include signals.

A socket is an endpoint for communication.
An Internet socket can use IPv4.
An Internet socket can use IPv6.

Unix domain sockets can be represented by filesystem paths or abstract namespace addresses on Linux.
A Unix domain socket is not a TCP socket.
TCP provides a reliable ordered byte stream.
UDP provides datagram communication.
TCP does not preserve application message boundaries.
An application protocol over TCP must define framing.
UDP preserves datagram boundaries.
UDP does not provide TCP's reliable ordered delivery semantics.
localhost commonly refers to the local host.
127.0.0.1 is the IPv4 loopback address commonly used for localhost.

Binding a service to 127.0.0.1 restricts ordinary IPv4 network access to the local host.
Binding to 0.0.0.0 generally means listening on all available IPv4 interfaces.

Listening on all interfaces exposes a service more broadly than listening on loopback.

A port identifies a transport endpoint in combination with address and protocol.
TCP port numbers and UDP port numbers are separate namespaces.
A process must bind a listening socket before accepting applicable incoming connections.
A successful bind does not prove the service protocol works correctly.
A successful TCP connection does not prove application qualification.

DNS resolves names according to DNS configuration.
A hostname and an IP address are different identifiers.

Processes have an environment.

Do not authenticate because the username exists.
Do not authenticate because a password field is nonempty.
Do not authenticate because the submitted hash resembles the stored format.
Perform actual verification.

Use established authentication functions.
Do not write custom comparison logic when the cryptographic library provides an appropriate constant-time comparison primitive.
Constant-time comparison is relevant for selected secret comparisons.
It does not make an otherwise insecure authentication design secure.
Use the correct primitive for the correct data.

Multi-factor authentication is commonly abbreviated MFA.
MFA requires authentication evidence from more than one factor category according to the system's design.
Common factor categories include:
Something the user knows.
Something the user has.
Something the user is.
A password is something the user knows.
A hardware authenticator can be something the user has.
A biometric characteristic can be something the user is.

TOTP stands for Time-based One-Time Password.
TOTP generates short-lived codes from a shared secret and time according to its algorithm.
The server and authenticator share secret material.

HOTP is counter-based rather than time-based.
