Do not erase actor identity.
Auditability matters.
Impersonation features should be explicit.
An administrator acting as another user should remain attributable to the administrator.
Do not replace audit identity with the impersonated account and lose the original actor.
Authentication and audit identity can carry multiple principals.
A secure system records who authenticated and under what mechanism.
Credential rotation replaces authentication credentials.
Password rotation changes the password.
Key rotation changes key material.
Token rotation changes token material.
Certificate rotation can change certificate and possibly key material.
Do not call every lifecycle event password reset.
Use precise terminology.
Forced periodic password changes are not automatically beneficial if they cause predictable password patterns or unnecessary user behavior.
Password-change policy should follow the system's security requirements.
Require change when compromise is known or suspected.
Do not invent arbitrary credential policy without a reason.
Password length matters.
Password entropy depends on selection behavior.
Longer user-chosen passwords or passphrases can provide strong resistance when selected well.
Arbitrary composition rules can encourage predictable substitutions.
Authentication policy should be designed for actual security properties.
Do not measure password strength solely by whether it contains one uppercase letter and one symbol.
Password managers can generate and store unique passwords.
Supporting password managers improves practical credential hygiene.
Do not block paste into password fields merely to force manual typing.
Manual typing is not an authentication factor.
Password fields should use appropriate input types in HTML.
The browser can obscure display.
Obscuring a password on screen is not encryption.
The server still requires protected transport.
Do not confuse masked characters with cryptographic protection.
Credential autocomplete behavior should be configured according to the form's purpose and platform standards.
Password managers are security tools.
Do not deliberately break them without a defined requirement.
Authentication forms should protect against cross-site request attacks where authentication state changes or account operations make such protection relevant.
Login CSRF can matter in selected applications.
Logout requests can require deliberate state-changing request semantics.
Authentication endpoints are still web application endpoints.
Normal web security principles apply.
Authentication responses should avoid open redirects.
An attacker can abuse a login return URL to send users to a malicious destination after successful authentication.
Validate redirect targets.
Do not trust arbitrary return URLs.
Authentication pages should not embed untrusted third-party scripts unnecessarily.
Scripts running in the authentication origin can potentially access submitted data according to browser security rules.
Minimize attack surface around credentials.
Content security controls can help reduce script injection risk.
TLS cannot protect credentials from malicious script executing inside the legitimate page.
Endpoint integrity matters.
Cross-site scripting can steal session credentials or perform authenticated actions depending on browser protections.
HttpOnly can prevent direct JavaScript reading of selected cookies.
It does not prevent all actions using the authenticated session.
Prevent XSS.
Do not rely solely on cookie flags.
CSRF abuses a browser's existing authentication state to submit unwanted requests.
The attacker does not necessarily know the session credential.
Authentication can be completely valid while the request is unauthorized by the user's intent.
CSRF defenses are therefore separate from authentication.
Do not treat authenticated request as proof the human intentionally initiated it.
Authentication establishes principal identity.
Request integrity and intent can require additional controls.
Sensitive operations can require confirmation or reauthentication.
Context matters.
Authentication endpoints themselves require availability protection.
An attacker can flood login attempts.
Expensive password hashing intentionally consumes resources.
This can create denial-of-service pressure.
Rate limiting and resource controls should account for hashing cost.
Do not weaken password hashing solely because attackers can send requests.
Control request volume.
Authentication databases are high-value targets.
Protect password hashes.
Protect MFA secrets.
Protect recovery credentials.
Protect signing keys.
Protect session state.
Restrict administrative access.
Audit changes.
Backups contain authentication data too.
Protect backups according to the sensitivity of the original data.
Deleting credentials from the active database while leaving unprotected backups can preserve exposure.
Credential lifecycle includes backup retention.
Authentication data should have defined retention.
Do not retain expired reset tokens indefinitely without reason.
Do not retain obsolete MFA secrets after replacement unless required for controlled rollback.
Do not retain revoked API keys as usable credentials.
Historical audit records can retain identifiers without retaining usable secrets.
Separate history from active credential material.
Authentication systems need recovery procedures.
Loss of the authentication database can prevent login.
Loss of signing keys can invalidate tokens.
Loss of private CA keys can affect certificate issuance.
Loss of MFA seed data can prevent verification.
Back up what must be recoverable.
Do not back up what should never leave protected hardware without explicit policy.
Recovery planning is part of authentication architecture.
High availability can require multiple authentication servers.
Replicated authentication state must remain consistent enough for security requirements.
A revoked credential should not remain accepted indefinitely by a stale replica.
Distributed authentication systems must define consistency behavior.
Do not assume replication delay has no security consequence.
Authentication decisions should be deterministic for the same relevant validated state where system design requires determinism.
If credential verification succeeds under the defined rules, the authentication result follows those rules.
If required evidence is absent, authentication fails.
Do not replace missing evidence with probability.
Machine-learning risk signals can supplement authentication policy.
They should not silently redefine identity.
A model prediction that a login "looks normal" is not possession of the user's credential.
Keep evidence and inference separate.
Authentication should be explainable at the mechanism level.
For example:
Password verifier matched.
TOTP verified.
Client certificate chain validated.
WebAuthn signature verified.
Token signature and claims validated.
Session identifier mapped to active authenticated session.
These are concrete authentication facts.
"User seemed legitimate" is not equivalent.
Authentication failures should be classified.
Unknown account.
Invalid credential.
Expired credential.
Revoked credential.
Invalid token signature.
Expired token.
Wrong audience.
Wrong issuer.
MFA required.
MFA failed.
Session expired.
Session invalidated.
Certificate validation failed.
Protocol error.
Rate limit applied.
Internal authentication service failure.
These are different states.
User-facing responses can intentionally generalize them.
Internal systems should preserve enough distinction for diagnosis.
Do not convert authentication-service failure into invalid password unless that behavior is explicitly required.
If the password database is unavailable, the system does not know that the password was wrong.
The correct internal state is authentication unavailable or failed due to system error.
Absence of verification is not verification failure caused by incorrect credentials.
This distinction matters.
Fail closed for protected operations when authentication authority is unavailable unless architecture explicitly defines another trusted mechanism.
Do not authenticate everyone because the authentication database is offline.
Availability failure must not become authorization bypass.
Cached authentication can exist in selected systems.
Offline authentication can exist in selected systems.
Such behavior must be explicitly designed.
The cache itself becomes authentication authority for its validity period.
Protect it.
Define expiration.
Do not invent offline trust automatically.
An account can have multiple credentials.
A user can have a password.
A user can have multiple WebAuthn authenticators.
A user can have recovery codes.
A user can have API tokens.
Revoking one credential does not necessarily disable the account.
Credential identity and account identity are separate.
Track which credential authenticated the session when useful.
This enables selective revocation and auditing.
A stolen hardware credential can be revoked without changing unrelated credentials.
A compromised API key can be revoked without changing the user's password.
Credential granularity improves incident response.
Do not make every credential share one irreversible global state unless simplicity requirements justify it.
API keys should have identifiers distinct from secret material.
The system can display an identifier safely while storing a protected verifier for the secret.
This allows operators to identify which key was used without logging the secret itself.
Do not use the complete secret as the key's display name.
API keys can have creation dates.
They can have expiration dates.
They can have last-used information.
They can have scopes.
They can have revocation state.
These improve lifecycle management.
Do not create permanent anonymous secrets with no ownership metadata.
Secret comparison for API keys should use appropriate secure verification.
If API keys have sufficient random entropy, storing a cryptographic hash of the secret can reduce direct disclosure risk.
Exact design depends on lookup requirements and threat model.
Do not assume API secrets must always be stored plaintext.
Authentication keys should be generated using cryptographically secure randomness.
Human-generated API keys are likely to be weaker.
Generate them automatically.
Provide them once where appropriate.
Store only what the server requires for verification.
Authentication tokens should have enough entropy to resist guessing.
Do not use incremental token values.
Do not use account ID plus timestamp.
Do not use predictable database row IDs.
Random credential generation must use a cryptographically secure random-number generator.
UUIDs have different versions and properties.
Do not assume every UUID is an authentication secret.
Some UUIDs contain predictable or structured information.
Use purpose-built random tokens for credentials.
Credential format can include a nonsecret prefix.
A prefix can identify token type.
A prefix can help secret-scanning systems.
A prefix does not reduce security if the remaining secret has sufficient entropy.
Do not treat the visible prefix as secret.
Secret scanners can detect credential patterns in source repositories.
Use them as a defensive control.
They do not replace credential management.
If a credential is committed publicly, assume exposure according to incident policy.
Deleting the commit later may not remove every copy.
Rotate the credential.
Do not merely hide the repository and continue using the exposed secret.
Version-control history can retain deleted secrets.
Credential removal requires history handling where appropriate and credential rotation.
Rotation is the critical security action.
A secret already exposed cannot become secret again by deleting one copy.
Environment variables can provide credentials to processes.
Environment variables are not automatically secure.
Other processes, debugging tools, crash reports, or configuration dumps can expose them depending on platform.
Use the credential mechanism appropriate to the environment.
Do not print environment variables containing secrets.
Secret-management systems can provide credentials dynamically.
They can centralize rotation.
They can control access.
They add infrastructure dependencies.
Use them when requirements justify them.
Do not add a secret manager merely as decoration.
The authentication system itself becomes critical infrastructure.
Administrative authentication should be stronger where risk requires it.
Administrative accounts should not share credentials.
Administrative actions should be attributable.
Default passwords should be changed or eliminated.
Factory credentials should not remain active in production.
Do not ship universal administrative passwords.
Bootstrap authentication requires special care.
A system's first administrator must be established through a controlled process.
Bootstrap credentials should be temporary where possible.
They should be invalidated after initial setup.
Do not leave installation credentials active indefinitely.
Account provisioning establishes an identity record.
Provisioning is not authentication.
An administrator creating an account does not prove the future user is currently present.
Credential enrollment establishes how that user will authenticate.
Keep provisioning and authentication separate.
Credential enrollment should occur through an authenticated or otherwise controlled process.
Adding a new MFA device changes future authentication authority.
Treat it as a security-sensitive operation.
Do not allow a session with insufficient assurance to silently enroll a new authenticator if policy requires stronger verification.
Removing MFA similarly changes authentication strength.
Require appropriate verification.
Log the change.
Notify the account owner where policy requires it.
Do not allow an attacker with a temporary session to permanently weaken authentication without controls.
Authentication notifications can alert users to new logins or credential changes.
Notifications are detection mechanisms.
They are not authentication proof.
An email saying a login occurred does not prevent the login.
Use notification as an additional control, not the primary verifier.
Account enumeration can occur through:
Login error differences.
Password-reset responses.
Registration responses.
Timing differences.
API status codes.
Authentication design should consider information disclosure across all related endpoints.
Do not fix the login message while leaving reset endpoints revealing the same account information.
Authentication endpoints should return appropriate HTTP status behavior according to application design.
HTTP status codes communicate protocol state.
They do not themselves perform authentication.
A 401 response commonly indicates authentication is required or has failed according to HTTP authentication semantics.
A 403 response commonly indicates the server understood the request but refuses it according to authorization semantics.
Exact application behavior can vary.
Do not use status codes as substitutes for internal security logic.
Authorize second.
Then construct the appropriate response.
HTTP Basic authentication transmits a username and password-like credential encoded for HTTP.
Base64 encoding is not encryption.
Basic authentication should use TLS when confidentiality is required.
Do not describe Basic authentication as encrypted because the header is Base64 encoded.
The Authorization header can carry credentials.
Do not log it by default.
Proxies should not expose it unnecessarily.
Application debugging should redact it.
Bearer authentication commonly uses:
Authorization: Bearer <token>
The token is a credential.
The word Bearer is not the secret.
Do not expose the token.
Do not put bearer tokens in public examples using real credentials.
Use placeholders.
Authentication headers can traverse reverse proxies.
Proxy configuration must preserve or deliberately remove them according to architecture.
Do not accidentally forward external credentials to unrelated upstream services.
Credential boundaries matter.
A reverse proxy can perform authentication before forwarding a request.
The upstream application can trust authentication metadata only if the proxy boundary is controlled.
The proxy must remove client-supplied copies of trusted identity headers.
Then it can set its own authenticated identity headers.
Do not trust X-User or similar headers directly from the Internet.
A client can forge them.
Trusted authentication headers require a trusted intermediary.
The upstream should only accept requests from that intermediary or otherwise authenticate the intermediary.
Transport and network controls can establish the boundary.
Do not create header-based authentication without defining who is allowed to set the header.
Authentication middleware can centralize credential validation.
Authorization middleware can then evaluate permissions.
Keep their responsibilities distinct.
Authentication middleware should establish principal identity.
It should not silently grant every authenticated user every route.
Authorization remains necessary.
Public routes intentionally require no authentication.
Protected routes require authenticated identity.
Privileged routes require authenticated identity plus authorization.
Do not add authentication to a route and assume privilege separation now exists.
Authentication state should have one authoritative representation within the request context.
Avoid multiple components independently parsing credentials and reaching conflicting identities.
Authenticate once through a controlled mechanism where practical.
Propagate the established principal.
Do not let downstream code replace it using untrusted parameters.
An authenticated user ID should come from authentication context.
It should not come from request parameters for operations acting as the current user.
For example, changing the current user's password should use the authenticated principal.
Do not accept user_id=123 as proof that the requester is user 123.
For administrative operations targeting another account, the target account can come from the request.
The actor identity must still come from authenticated context.
Keep actor and target distinct.
Audit both.
Authentication should not be bypassed because a request originates from localhost unless architecture explicitly defines localhost as a trusted boundary.
Local processes can be compromised.
Containers can share hosts.
Proxy configurations can make remote traffic appear local.
Use explicit authentication where required.
Unix domain sockets or local IPC can provide different trust boundaries.
Filesystem permissions can restrict access.
Peer credentials can provide process identity on supported platforms.
These can participate in authentication architecture.
Do not pretend they are password authentication.
State the actual mechanism.
Peer credential APIs can identify local process user IDs according to operating-system semantics.
That identity can be sufficient for selected local services.
The trust root is then the operating system.
Authorization still determines permitted operations.
Authentication chains can involve multiple authorities.
A hardware module can authenticate a key.
The operating system can authenticate a user.
The application can authenticate a session.
The service can authenticate another service.
Do not lose track of which authority established which identity.
Authentication evidence should have provenance.
Who asserted the identity?
What credential was verified?
Which trust anchor was used?
When was authentication performed?
What assurance level resulted?
These questions support secure decisions.
Do not accept unauthenticated identity metadata simply because it looks structured.
JSON claims are still claims.
Headers are still claims.
Form fields are still claims.
Cookies are still claims until validated.
Tokens are still claims until validated.
Certificates are still data until validated.
Validation establishes trusted meaning.
Authentication libraries can fail.
Database connections can fail.
Identity providers can be unavailable.
Certificate validation can fail.
Time services can fail.
Random-number generation can fail.
Do not convert infrastructure failure into successful authentication.
Fail safely.
Authentication errors should not leak secrets.
An exception message should not include passwords.
Database errors should not expose password hashes.
Token-validation errors should not dump complete tokens.
Certificate errors should not dump private keys.
Debugging output must remain bounded.
Security-sensitive values should be redacted.
Redaction should preserve enough identifiers for diagnosis.
For example, log a token identifier or fingerprint rather than the token itself where appropriate.
Do not destroy all diagnostic value merely by writing "[SECRET]" for everything.
Design observability intentionally.
Authentication metrics can include:
Success count.
Failure count.
Failure categories.
MFA challenge rate.
Password-reset rate.
Credential-revocation rate.
Session creation rate.
Identity-provider latency.
Authentication-service availability.
Do not put secret values into metric labels.
Metrics systems can have broad access.
Authentication rate anomalies can indicate attacks.
They can also indicate software bugs.
Evidence is required before assigning cause.
A spike in failed logins does not prove a malicious attack by itself.
Investigate source patterns and context.
Do not turn correlation into certainty.
Authentication should support incident containment.
Disable an account.
Revoke a credential.
Invalidate sessions.
Rotate signing keys.
Disable an authentication mechanism.
Block compromised identity-provider trust.
Exact controls depend on architecture.
Plan them before incidents.
Emergency access accounts can provide recovery when normal identity infrastructure fails.
They are highly sensitive.
Protect them strongly.
Monitor their use.
Do not use them for ordinary administration.
A recovery mechanism that is routinely used becomes an ordinary authentication mechanism and should be governed accordingly.
Authentication systems should minimize shared secrets.
Shared administrator passwords make attribution difficult.
Shared API keys make selective revocation difficult.
Distinct credentials improve control.
Do not trade away identity clarity merely for convenience.
Authentication is not ownership.
Authenticating an account proves control according to the authentication mechanism at that moment.
It does not establish legal ownership of data, devices, domains, or other property.
Keep technical identity separate from external ownership concepts.
Authentication is not permanent.
A session can expire.
A credential can be revoked.
A key can be rotated.
An account can be disabled.
Identity evidence has context and lifetime.
Do not assume authentication performed months ago is sufficient for every present operation.
Authentication is not trust in every statement made by the authenticated principal.
An authenticated user can provide false data.
An authenticated service can malfunction.
Authentication establishes identity.
It does not establish correctness.
Authentication is not authorization.
Authentication is not encryption.
Authentication is not hashing.
Authentication is not identification alone.
Authentication is not account creation.
Authentication is not session storage.
Authentication is not permission.
Authentication is not auditing.
Authentication interacts with all of these systems but remains distinct.
Do not confuse username with authenticated identity.
Do not confuse email address with authenticated identity.
Do not confuse account existence with authentication.
Do not confuse password presence with password verification.
Do not confuse password hashing with encryption.
Do not confuse salt with pepper.
Do not confuse Base64 with encryption.
Do not confuse a session ID with harmless metadata.
Do not confuse a cookie with authentication merely because it exists.
Do not confuse MFA with asking for two passwords.
Do not confuse TOTP with a permanent password.
Do not confuse a recovery code with ordinary account metadata.
Do not confuse password reset with password recovery.
A secure system should not need to reveal the old password.
Do not confuse a public key with a private key.
Do not confuse possession of a certificate with possession of its private key.
Do not confuse a valid certificate with application authorization.
Do not confuse mTLS with role assignment.
Do not confuse a bearer token with encryption.
Do not confuse JWT decoding with JWT validation.
Do not confuse a JWT signature with confidentiality.
Do not confuse token validity with token authorization.
Do not confuse OAuth with authentication generally.
Do not confuse OpenID Connect with OAuth authorization alone.
Do not confuse SSO with identical permissions across applications.
Do not confuse a service account with a human account.
Do not confuse a device identity with a user identity.
Do not confuse IP address with identity.
Do not confuse DNS name with identity proof.
Do not confuse reverse DNS with authentication.
Do not confuse risk score with identity proof.
Do not confuse familiar behavior with authentication.
Do not confuse successful TLS transport with application login.
Do not confuse an HTTP status code with an authentication decision.
Do not confuse account provisioning with authentication.
Do not confuse authentication with authorization.
When implementing password login:
Receive the identifier and password over protected transport.
Locate the candidate account according to the identifier rules.
Perform password verification using the established password-hashing function.
Do not expose whether the account exists when policy requires nondisclosure.
If verification fails, remain unauthenticated.
If additional authentication factors are required, complete them.
Only after all required evidence succeeds should authenticated state be established.
Create or rotate the session credential securely.
Bind the session to the authenticated internal principal.
Return the session credential through the intended secure mechanism.
Record the authentication event according to logging policy.
Do not set authenticated state before verification completes.
When validating a session:
Receive the session credential.
Validate its format.
Locate or verify the session according to the session design.
Confirm it exists.
Confirm it is active.
Confirm it is not expired.
Confirm the associated account remains eligible for authentication according to policy.
Establish the request principal.
Do not trust a user ID supplied separately by the client.
When validating a signed token:
Parse it using a protocol-aware library.
Determine the expected issuer and validation policy from trusted configuration.
Select trusted verification keys according to controlled rules.
Verify the signature.
Verify the allowed algorithm.
Verify issuer where required.
Verify audience where required.
Verify expiration.
Verify not-before conditions where required.
Verify application-specific claims.
Only then establish authenticated identity.
Do not trust claims before validation.
When authenticating a service with a private key:
Provision the service with the intended private key.
Provision the verifier with appropriate public trust information.
Generate a fresh challenge or use a protocol providing equivalent freshness.
Have the service prove possession of the private key according to the protocol.
Verify the proof.
Map the validated key identity to the service principal.
Then apply authorization.
Do not transmit the private key.
When adding MFA:
Define which factor categories are required.
Enroll the additional authenticator through a controlled process.
Verify enrollment before relying on it.
Provide controlled recovery mechanisms.
Protect enrollment secrets.
Log authenticator changes.
Require the factors according to policy.
Do not call the system MFA merely because it displays two screens.
When resetting a password:
Establish the account being recovered.
Issue a cryptographically unpredictable, limited-lifetime recovery credential through the defined recovery channel.
Verify that credential.
Invalidate it after successful use.
Accept the new password.
Hash it using the current password-hashing policy.
Replace the old verifier.
Invalidate other authentication state where policy requires.
Record the security event.
Do not reveal or email the previous password.
When revoking an API credential:
Identify the exact credential.
Mark it revoked or remove its verifier according to design.
Ensure future validation rejects it.
Invalidate derived sessions or tokens where policy requires.
Record the revocation.
Do not disable unrelated credentials unless the incident requires it.
When authentication infrastructure fails:
Determine whether credential verification can still be performed according to an explicitly trusted mechanism.
If not, fail protected authentication attempts safely.
Report authentication infrastructure failure.
Do not report invalid credentials unless they were actually tested and found invalid.
Do not grant anonymous access to protected operations.
Preserve evidence for diagnosis.
When investigating suspicious authentication:
Identify the account.
Identify the credential or mechanism used.
Identify whether authentication actually succeeded.
Identify the session created.
Identify source information available.
Identify subsequent authorized actions separately.
Identify credential changes.
Identify session invalidations.
Do not infer compromise merely from one unusual login.
Do not dismiss compromise merely because a valid credential was used.
A stolen credential can authenticate successfully.
Authentication proves credential possession according to the mechanism.
It does not prove benevolent intent.
When designing an authentication system, define:
What identities exist?
What identifies each principal?
What evidence authenticates each principal?
Where are credentials stored?
How are credentials protected?
How are credentials enrolled?
How are credentials rotated?
How are credentials revoked?
How are sessions created?
How do sessions expire?
How are sessions invalidated?
Is MFA required?
How does recovery work?
How are authentication events audited?
How does the system behave when authentication infrastructure fails?
How are machine identities handled?
How are administrative identities handled?
How is trust bootstrapped?
Only then implement the mechanism.
Keep authentication small.
Keep authentication deterministic.
Keep credential ownership explicit.
Keep trust anchors explicit.
Keep failure explicit.
Keep authentication separate from authorization.
A reliable authentication system does not guess identity.
A reliable authentication system validates evidence.
A reliable authentication system protects credentials.
A reliable authentication system does not store plaintext passwords.
A reliable authentication system does not trust client claims without validation.
A reliable authentication system uses secure randomness for authentication secrets.
A reliable authentication system limits credential lifetime where appropriate.
A reliable authentication system supports revocation.
A reliable authentication system preserves auditability.
A reliable authentication system fails safely.
A reliable authentication system does not turn infrastructure failure into successful login.
A reliable authentication system distinguishes account identity from credential identity.
A reliable authentication system distinguishes human identity from machine identity.
A reliable authentication system distinguishes authentication from authorization.
Which principal has been established by the evidence accepted under this authentication policy?
If the evidence validates, authenticate according to policy.
If the evidence does not validate, do not authenticate.
If the evidence is missing, do not authenticate.
If the authentication authority is unavailable, do not fabricate an identity.
If the evidence establishes only possession of a credential, do not claim it establishes anything beyond what that credential represents.
Identity is established by evidence.
Permission comes afterward.
TITLE: General Language Fundamentals
VERSION: 1.0
CATEGORY: Language Reference
LANGUAGE: English
SECTION 1: LANGUAGE AND COMMUNICATION
Language is a system of words, symbols, and grammatical
relationships used to communicate information, intentions,
questions, instructions, and social meaning.
The meaning of an expression depends on its vocabulary,
grammar, context, and intended use.
The same word may have different meanings in different
contexts.
Example:
"The server is running" describes an operational state.
"She is running" describes physical movement.
Language understanding requires distinguishing the meaning
of an expression from its individual words.
SECTION 2: WORDS AND VOCABULARY
A word is a meaningful unit of language.
A noun names a person, place, object, idea, or concept.
Examples: operator, computer, server, language, trust.
A verb expresses an action, occurrence, or state.
Examples: run, explain, compare, know, exist.
An adjective describes or qualifies a noun.
Examples: active, reliable, deterministic, small.
An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb.
Examples: quickly, carefully, usually, clearly.
A pronoun may refer to a person, object, or previously
identified subject.
Examples: I, you, she, he, it, we, they.
A preposition expresses a relationship.
Examples: in, on, under, before, after, between.
A conjunction connects words, phrases, or clauses.
Examples: and, but, or, because, although.
An interjection expresses a reaction or emotion.
Examples: oh, wow, hey, ouch.
SECTION 3: SENTENCE STRUCTURE
A sentence is a grammatical expression that communicates
a statement, question, instruction, or exclamation.
A common English sentence pattern is:
Subject + Verb + Object.
"The operator starts Digit."
Subject: the operator
Verb: starts
Object: Digit
Not every English sentence follows this pattern.
"Stop."
This is an imperative sentence with an implied subject.
Word order may change the meaning of a sentence.
"The operator instructed Digit."
"Digit instructed the operator."
These sentences describe different relationships.
SECTION 4: SENTENCE PURPOSE
A declarative sentence communicates a statement.
Example: "The server is online."
An interrogative sentence asks a question.
Example: "Is the server online?"
An imperative sentence communicates an instruction,
request, or command.
Example: "Check the server."
An exclamatory sentence expresses emphasis or reaction.
Example: "That was unexpected!"
A sentence's grammatical form and intended purpose
may differ.
"Could you check the server?"
This is grammatically a question but ordinarily functions
as a polite request.
SECTION 5: QUESTIONS
Questions seek information, confirmation, explanation,
or clarification.
Who asks about identity.
What asks about identity, definition, or information.
When asks about time.
Where asks about location.
Why asks about cause or reason.
How asks about method, process, or condition.
Which asks for selection among alternatives.
Examples:
"What is a compiler?"
"How does compilation work?"
"Why did the program stop?"
"Which language is appropriate?"
A yes-or-no question requests confirmation or denial.
"Is the module active?"
A question may contain assumptions that are not established.
"Why did the server fail again?"
This question assumes a previous failure.
An unsupported assumption is not established evidence.
SECTION 6: REQUESTS AND INSTRUCTIONS
A request asks for an action or information.
"Explain the difference."
"Please summarize the report."
"Can you show the results?"
A command directly instructs an action.
"Restart the service."
"Read the file."
Courtesy expressions may modify the tone of a request
without changing its underlying purpose.
"Explain this."
"Please explain this."
"Could you explain this, please?"
All three may express the same informational request.
A request is not evidence that an action has occurred.
An instruction is not evidence of authorization.
SECTION 7: GREETINGS AND SOCIAL EXPRESSIONS
A greeting begins or acknowledges an interaction.
Common greetings:
hello
hi
hey
good morning
good afternoon
good evening
"Hi" and "hello" are commonly interchangeable greetings.
A farewell indicates the end of an interaction.
Common farewells:
goodbye
bye
see you later
take care
An acknowledgment indicates receipt or recognition.
okay
understood
got it
all right
An expression of gratitude communicates appreciation.
thank you
thanks
thank you very much
A response to gratitude may acknowledge the appreciation.
you're welcome
glad to help
no problem
Social expressions do not necessarily request technical
information.
SECTION 8: SYNONYMS AND ANTONYMS
Synonyms are words with similar meanings.
begin / start
finish / complete
quick / fast
assist / help
Synonyms are not always interchangeable in every context.
Antonyms express contrasting meanings.
active / inactive
open / closed
start / stop
present / absent
Opposite words may describe a contrast without establishing
that only two possible states exist.
A service may be active, inactive, failed, or activating.
SECTION 9: INFORMAL ENGLISH
Informal language may use contractions, shortened words,
colloquial expressions, and nonstandard spelling.
Common contractions:
I'm = I am
you're = you are
it's = it is or it has, depending on context
don't = do not
can't = cannot
won't = will not
we're = we are
Common informal expressions:
gonna = going to, in informal speech
wanna = want to, in informal speech
kinda = kind of
gotta = got to or have to, depending on context
Informal spelling may represent ordinary expressions.
"thx" may mean "thanks."
"pls" may mean "please."
"u" may mean "you."
These meanings depend on context.
An unfamiliar abbreviation must not automatically be
assigned an unsupported meaning.
SECTION 10: CONTEXT
Context is the information surrounding an expression that
helps determine its meaning.
Context may include:
The current sentence.
Earlier statements.
The subject under discussion.
The requested action.
Previously established facts.
"The module failed."
"Why?"
The second expression may refer to the previously
mentioned module failure.
Without the earlier statement, "Why?" has an incomplete
referent.
Context does not establish facts that were never supplied.
A missing referent remains unresolved until sufficient
information is available.
SECTION 11: COMPARISONS
A comparison examines similarities, differences, or
relationships between two or more subjects.
Common comparison expressions:
compare
contrast
difference between
similarities between
better than
less than
more than
"Compare PHP and C."
This expression identifies two subjects:
PHP
C
A comparison may examine attributes such as:
purpose
type system
execution model
capabilities
limitations
common applications
A meaningful comparison requires information about the
subjects being compared.
A comparison must distinguish factual attributes from
subjective preferences.
"Better" requires an evaluation criterion.
"Which language is better?"
This question does not identify the criterion for better.
SECTION 12: EXPLANATIONS AND REASONS
An explanation describes a concept, relationship,
mechanism, or cause.
"Explain how a compiler works."
"Why is validation necessary?"
A definition identifies the meaning of a term.
A procedural explanation describes steps or operations.
A causal explanation identifies a supported relationship
between an event and its cause.
An explanation should not invent a cause merely because
a cause was requested.
"The service stopped" does not establish why it stopped.
SECTION 13: AMBIGUITY
An ambiguous expression has more than one plausible
interpretation.
"Check the port."
This may refer to a network port or a physical connector.
"Open the file."
The intended file may be unknown.
Ambiguity may be resolved through context or clarification.
When context is insufficient, the intended meaning remains
unknown.
Uncertainty is different from contradiction.
Uncertainty means sufficient information is unavailable.
Contradiction means available statements conflict.
SECTION 14: NEGATION
Negation reverses or denies a proposition.
Common negation expressions:
not
no
never
none
without
"The service is active."
"The service is not active."
Negation may apply to only part of a sentence.
"Not every module failed."
This does not mean that no modules failed.
"No modules failed."
This means the number of failed modules is zero.
The scope of negation affects meaning.
SECTION 15: TIME AND TENSE
English uses tense and other grammatical structures to
describe time.
Past:
"The module started."
Present:
"The module is active."
Future:
"The module will start."
An intention concerning the future is not evidence of
completed action.
"I will upload the lesson."
This does not establish that the lesson was uploaded.
"I uploaded the lesson."
This asserts a completed past action.
The accuracy of a statement is separate from its tense.
SECTION 16: CONVERSATIONAL CONTINUITY
A conversation consists of related exchanges.
A follow-up expression may depend on information from
an earlier exchange.
Operator: "Explain PHP."
Operator: "Now compare it with C."
The word "it" may refer to PHP when the context clearly
establishes that referent.
A later instruction may revise an earlier request.
"Explain PHP."
"Actually, compare PHP and C."
The second request changes the requested operation.
Conversational continuity requires reliable context.
Missing context must not be reconstructed through guessing.
SECTION 17: COMMUNICATION AND EVIDENCE
A statement may express:
A fact.
An opinion.
A question.
An instruction.
A prediction.
A hypothesis.
A preference.
These categories have different evidentiary meanings.
"PHP is a programming language."
This is a factual claim.
"I prefer PHP."
This expresses a preference.
"PHP might be appropriate."
This expresses possibility.
"Use PHP."
This expresses an instruction.
A preference is not universal evidence.
A prediction is not a completed event.
A hypothesis is not a verified conclusion.
SECTION 18: CLEAR COMMUNICATION
Clear communication expresses relevant meaning with
sufficient precision.
An effective explanation identifies its subject.
A concise response avoids unnecessary repetition.
A technical response preserves important distinctions.
An acknowledgment does not need to repeat an entire request.
When information is insufficient, a clarification may be
more appropriate than an unsupported conclusion.
Accuracy and clarity are complementary communication goals.
SECTION 19: LANGUAGE VARIATION
English varies by region, community, profession, and
individual speaker.
The same concept may have multiple ordinary expressions.
"Hello."
"Hi."
"Hey."
Technical language may assign specialized meanings to
ordinary words.
A computer process and a manufacturing process are
different uses of the word "process."
Regional and informal variations do not automatically
indicate an error.
Meaning must be evaluated in context.
SECTION 20: REFERENCE BOUNDARIES
This lesson describes English language concepts.
It does not establish the truth of unrelated factual claims.
It does not grant permission to perform actions.
It does not replace module contracts or system policies.
It does not establish that every described language
operation is implemented by the current software.
Language reference knowledge may support interpretation
when an authorized module can apply it deterministically.
Unknown meanings remain unknown until sufficient
authorized information is available.
END OF LESSON
Input validation is the process of determining whether supplied data satisfies the requirements defined for that input.
Applications receive input from many sources.
Examples include:
HTML forms.
URLs.
Query parameters.
HTTP headers.
Cookies.
JSON requests.
XML requests.
API clients.
Command-line arguments.
Configuration files.
Environment variables.
Uploaded files.
Databases.
Message queues.
Network protocols.
Other applications.
Hardware devices.
Users.
Do not assume input is trustworthy because it came from a familiar source.
Input crossing a trust boundary must be treated according to the receiving system's requirements.
A trust boundary is a point where data moves between components or contexts with different trust assumptions.
Browser to server.
Client application to API.
Internet to application.
Application to database.
Plugin to host application.
External service to internal service.
Configuration file to privileged process.
Message queue to worker.
User-controlled file to parser.
Do not trust data merely because it is inside the application now.
Its origin still matters.
Input validation answers:
Does this input satisfy the requirements for this field or operation?
Validation does not answer:
Is this user authorized?
Is this input safe in every possible output context?
Is this data true?
Is this data trustworthy?
Is this request legitimate?
Keep these questions separate.
Valid input can still be unauthorized.
Valid input can still be malicious in another context.
Valid input can still be factually false.
Valid input can still violate a business rule.
Validation establishes conformance to defined input requirements.
A useful validation process is:
Identify the expected input.
Define its type.
Define its format.
Define its allowed values.
Define its length or size constraints.
Define its range where applicable.
Define whether it is required.
Define any structural relationships.
Parse it.
Validate it.
Reject it if the requirements are not satisfied.
Do not begin with arbitrary transformations intended to make unknown input acceptable.
Know what valid input means first.
Validation should be explicit.
For example:
Expected:
Integer from 1 through 100.
Valid:
1
42
100
Invalid:
0
101
-5
hello
12.5
The validation rule is clear.
Do not write:
if value looks roughly numeric, accept it.
Define the accepted domain.
Types matter.
Common input types include:
Boolean.
Integer.
Floating-point number.
String.
Enumeration.
Date.
Time.
Timestamp.
Identifier.
Array.
Object.
Binary data.
File.
Do not treat every input as an arbitrary string forever.
Parse into the intended type when appropriate.
If an API requires an integer, validate an integer.
Do not accept:
"twelve"
because application code might later convert it unpredictably.
Type conversion can hide invalid input.
"12abc"
might be partially interpreted as 12 by permissive conversion routines.
Do not rely on implicit conversion.
Use strict parsing where possible.
Parsing and validation are related but distinct.
Parsing determines whether input can be interpreted according to a grammar or representation.
Validation determines whether the parsed value satisfies application requirements.
"2026-10-01"
can parse as a date.
The application can still reject it if only future dates are permitted.
Syntactically valid does not mean semantically acceptable.
Syntax describes structure.
Semantics describe meaning.
Validate both where required.
A syntactically valid email-shaped string does not prove the mailbox exists.
A syntactically valid IP address does not prove the address belongs to a trusted system.
A syntactically valid user ID does not prove the requester may access that user.
A syntactically valid URL does not prove the destination is permitted.
Do not infer more than validation establishes.
Allowlist validation defines what is accepted.
status must be one of:
pending
active
disabled
Anything else is rejected.
This is preferable when the valid set is known.
Do not attempt to enumerate every possible invalid status.
Define the valid domain.
A denylist identifies known prohibited values or patterns.
Denylisting can be useful in selected contexts.
It is generally weaker than defining the valid input when the valid domain is known.
A denylist can miss new or unexpected forms.
Rejecting:
<script>
does not define valid HTML.
Many other representations can exist.
Do not build general input safety from a small list of bad strings.
Prefer positive validation when possible.
A field with a fixed vocabulary should use an enumeration.
method:
GET
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE
if those are the only accepted values for the application context.
Reject unknown values.
Do not silently interpret:
POTS
as:
Validation should not guess intent.
A boolean should have a defined representation.
For example, an API can define:
true
false
Do not accept arbitrary values such as:
yes
on
enabled
unless the interface explicitly defines them.
Different languages interpret truthiness differently.
Explicit representation prevents ambiguity.
An integer field should define range.
port:
1 through 65535.
Do not merely validate that it contains digits.
999999 is digits.
It is not a valid TCP or UDP port number.
Type validation and range validation are separate.
A quantity can require:
minimum.
maximum.
Both.
Neither.
Define the actual domain.
Do not use arbitrary limits without a requirement.
Length validation constrains strings, arrays, files, or other collections.
username:
1 through 64 characters.
Do not allow unlimited input when the application has a finite requirement.
Unbounded input can create:
Memory pressure.
Storage growth.
Processing cost.
Log flooding.
Rendering problems.
Protocol failures.
Denial-of-service conditions.
Set meaningful limits.
Do not choose tiny limits that reject legitimate data merely for convenience.
Validation should reflect the actual system.
Character count and byte count are different.
A Unicode string can contain characters represented by multiple bytes.
If a protocol limits bytes, validate bytes.
If an application limits characters, validate characters.
Do not confuse the two.
A database column size can be measured according to database semantics.
Understand the storage model.
Do not assume a 255-character application limit matches every database type automatically.
Unicode requires deliberate handling.
Input can contain:
ASCII.
Accented characters.
CJK characters.
Emoji.
Combining characters.
Other Unicode sequences.
Do not reject non-ASCII input unless the specification requires ASCII.
Do not assume one byte equals one character.
Normalization can matter when equivalent-looking Unicode sequences have different binary representations.
Unicode normalization can convert defined equivalent representations into a canonical form.
Use normalization only when the application's semantics require it.
Do not normalize blindly if exact byte preservation matters.
Identifiers can have stricter rules than human-readable text.
For example, a module slug can require:
lowercase ASCII letters.
digits.
hyphen.
Maximum length.
That is valid if the identifier specification defines it.
Do not apply identifier restrictions to ordinary prose fields without reason.
Different fields require different validation.
Do not create one universal string validator.
A username is not an email address.
An email address is not a filesystem path.
A filesystem path is not a URL.
A URL is not a shell argument.
A shell argument is not SQL.
Context matters.
Validation should be field-specific.
Regular expressions can validate some formats.
They are not automatically the best tool for every input.
Use a regular expression when the accepted language is appropriately expressed by one.
Do not create enormous fragile expressions for formats that already have reliable parsers.
A parser can be clearer.
Regular expressions can also have performance risks.
Certain expressions can exhibit excessive backtracking on crafted input.
Keep expressions bounded and understandable.
Do not accept a complex regular expression merely because it passes ordinary examples.
Test adversarial lengths and patterns.
A regular expression matching format does not establish meaning.
^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$
can match:
2026-99-99
The string has the expected shape.
It is not a valid calendar date.
Use semantic validation after format validation.
Dates should use defined formats.
YYYY-MM-DD
If that is the interface contract, reject ambiguous alternatives unless explicitly supported.
Do not guess whether:
01/02/03
means:
January 2, 2003.
February 1, 2003.
January 2, 1903.
Ambiguous date formats create errors.
Use explicit formats.
Validate actual calendar rules.
February 30 is not valid.
Leap years matter.
Use reliable date libraries where appropriate.
Time zones matter for timestamps.
Define whether timestamps are:
UTC.
Offset-aware.
Local to a specified zone.
Do not accept ambiguous local times where the protocol requires a global instant.
Daylight-saving transitions can create nonexistent or repeated local times.
Use appropriate time representations.
Do not invent timezone assumptions silently.
Numeric validation should consider overflow.
A value can contain valid digits and still exceed the receiving type.
999999999999999999999999999999999999
may exceed a fixed-width integer.
Check conversion errors.
Check range.
Do not allow overflow to wrap into another value.
Signed and unsigned ranges differ.
A negative value can be invalid for an unsigned quantity.
Do not cast negative input to unsigned and accept the resulting large number.
Validate before unsafe conversion.
Floating-point values require care.
NaN.
Infinity.
Negative infinity.
Signed zero.
Very large exponents.
These can be accepted by some parsers.
If the application requires ordinary finite numbers, explicitly require finite values.
Do not assume every parsed floating-point value is suitable.
Money should not casually use binary floating-point when exact decimal behavior is required.
This is a representation issue beyond validation.
Input validation should still enforce permitted monetary format and range.
Amount must be nonnegative.
Amount must have no more than two decimal places if policy requires cents.
Do not silently round arbitrary user input unless the interface defines rounding.
Identifiers should be validated according to their actual format.
A UUID should be parsed as a UUID if the system requires UUIDs.
A hexadecimal digest should have the expected length and allowed characters.
A database integer ID should be validated as the correct integer domain.
Do not accept arbitrary strings as identifiers and hope downstream code rejects them.
An identifier being valid does not establish that the resource exists.
Existence is another check.
Existence does not establish authorization.
Authorization is another check.
Input: document_id=42.
Validation:
42 is a valid identifier.
Lookup:
Document 42 exists.
Authorization:
Requester may or may not access document 42.
Keep the sequence clear.
Validation is not authorization.
Ownership is not established by input.
A request can contain:
user_id=42
That does not prove the requester is user 42.
Authentication establishes the principal.
Do not trust identity fields supplied by the client as requester identity.
The client can identify a target.
The server identifies the actor from trusted authentication state.
Input validation cannot repair a broken trust model.
If a client is allowed to submit:
role=administrator
validation can confirm that administrator is a recognized role.
That does not mean the client is authorized to assign it.
A perfectly valid unauthorized value must still be rejected by authorization.
Valid is not permitted.
This distinction is critical.
Business-rule validation determines whether input makes sense within application state.
Requested quantity is 10.
The field permits integers from 1 through 100.
Input validation succeeds.
Inventory contains only 3 units.
Business rule rejects the transaction.
Do not overload syntax validation with every domain rule.
Keep layers understandable.
Cross-field validation evaluates relationships between inputs.
start_date must not be after end_date.
password_confirmation must equal password.
minimum must not exceed maximum.
If fields are individually valid but collectively inconsistent, reject the request.
Do not validate fields only in isolation when relationships matter.
Conditional fields can depend on other fields.
If shipping_method is delivery, delivery_address is required.
If authentication_method is certificate, certificate identifier is required.
Define these dependencies.
Do not accept incomplete combinations.
Structured input requires structural validation.
JSON can contain:
Objects.
Arrays.
Strings.
Numbers.
Booleans.
Null.
A valid JSON document can still violate the API schema.
{"age":"twenty"}
is valid JSON.
If age must be an integer, the request is invalid for that API.
JSON syntax validation is not application validation.
Define the expected JSON structure.
Reject missing required fields.
Reject wrong types.
Reject invalid values.
Decide how unknown fields are handled.
Do not ignore unexpected security-sensitive fields casually.
An API can reject unknown fields.
This makes contracts strict and catches client errors.
Another API can permit unknown fields for compatibility.
That is a deliberate protocol decision.
Do not accidentally accept unknown fields because the parser happens to preserve them.
Mass assignment is dangerous when arbitrary input fields map directly to object properties.
Suppose an API expects:
display_name
email
but receives:
is_admin
If the model blindly assigns all fields, a client can modify protected state.
Use explicit field allowlists.
Validation should define which fields are accepted.
Do not expose internal model structure directly as an input contract.
An object can contain fields the client may read but not write.
Readability and writability are separate.
id
created_at
owner_id
role
can be returned in responses.
They do not necessarily belong in update requests.
Define writable fields explicitly.
Missing and null are different.
In JSON:
field absent
is different from:
"field": null
An update API can interpret these differently.
Absent means unchanged.
Null means clear the value.
Define semantics.
Do not collapse them accidentally.
Empty string can also be distinct from null.
""
may mean intentionally blank.
null may mean no value.
Field absent may mean no update.
Know the application's model.
Whitespace handling should be deliberate.
For human-entered names, trimming leading and trailing whitespace can be reasonable.
For passwords, automatically trimming whitespace can change the credential.
For cryptographic material, whitespace can be meaningful depending on format.
Do not apply global trim() to every field.
Normalization is field-specific.
Sanitization is not the same as validation.
Validation asks whether input meets requirements.
Sanitization transforms data.
Removing characters.
Replacing characters.
Normalizing whitespace.
Stripping markup.
A transformation can change the user's input.
Do not silently sanitize malformed input into something different unless the interface defines that behavior.
Rejecting invalid input is often clearer.
For example, username specification allows:
a-z
0-9
_
Input:
alice<script>
Do not automatically transform it into:
alicescript
That may create an unintended username.
Reject it.
Let the requester provide valid input.
Sanitization can be appropriate for specific transformations.
Canonical line endings.
Defined Unicode normalization.
Removing formatting from a field explicitly defined as plain text.
But transformation rules should be known.
Do not use sanitization as a vague security ritual.
Escaping is not validation.
Escaping prepares data for a specific output or interpreter context.
HTML escaping.
SQL parameter binding.
Shell argument handling.
URL encoding.
JSON encoding.
Each context has different rules.
Validating input does not eliminate the need for safe output handling.
A valid name can contain:
O'Connor
The apostrophe is valid data.
SQL must still handle it safely.
Do not reject apostrophes merely to avoid SQL injection.
Use parameterized queries.
Input validation and SQL injection prevention are complementary.
Validation limits accepted input according to business requirements.
Parameterized SQL separates data from SQL syntax.
Do not construct SQL by concatenating validated strings and assume validation makes it safe.
Use the database interface correctly.
A numeric ID validated as an integer can reduce injection risk.
Still use parameter binding.
Defense should follow the interpreter boundary.
HTML output requires context-appropriate encoding.
A comment field can legitimately contain:
<
>
&
quotes.
If arbitrary plain text is allowed, these characters are valid.
When rendering the text into HTML, escape it.
Do not permanently replace characters during input merely because they are special in HTML.
Store data according to application requirements.
Encode for output context.
Output encoding should happen as close as practical to the output boundary.
Do not HTML-escape a value before storing it unless storage semantics explicitly require escaped HTML.
Otherwise the value can become double-encoded or unsuitable for other output formats.
Store canonical data.
Encode for the destination.
JavaScript contexts require different escaping than HTML text contexts.
HTML attributes have different concerns.
URLs have different encoding.
CSS contexts differ again.
Do not create one universal escape() function and use it everywhere.
Context determines safe encoding.
Shell commands are interpreter boundaries.
Input validation can constrain expected values.
Do not build shell commands through untrusted string concatenation.
Use APIs that pass arguments separately where possible.
If a field represents a known operation, use an allowlist.
operation must be:
start
stop
status
Do not allow arbitrary command text.
Validation should reduce the input language to what the application actually needs.
Filesystem paths require special care.
A filename is not necessarily a safe path.
Input such as:
../../etc/passwd
can be syntactically valid text.
If the application expects a simple filename, define a simple filename grammar.
If the application accepts paths, canonicalize and constrain them according to the intended root.
Do not merely search for "../".
Alternate separators and encodings can exist.
Use platform-aware path handling.
Path canonicalization resolves representations into a consistent path form according to filesystem rules.
Validation can then verify the resolved path remains within the permitted root.
Do not authorize based solely on the raw path string.
Requested path.
Join with permitted root.
Resolve canonical path.
Verify canonical path remains inside permitted root.
Then apply authorization.
Do not allow canonicalization to escape the intended directory.
Symbolic links can complicate filesystem containment.
A path can appear inside an allowed directory while a symbolic link points elsewhere.
If the threat model includes this, resolve according to filesystem semantics and policy.
Do not claim string prefix checking alone provides filesystem confinement.
Filename extensions are not reliable file-type evidence.
A file named:
photo.jpg
can contain non-image data.
Validate uploaded files according to actual requirements.
Possible checks include:
Size.
Filename.
Extension if relevant.
MIME information.
Magic bytes or file signature.
Parser success.
Image dimensions.
Archive structure.
Other format-specific properties.
No single check proves universal safety.
Define what the application requires.
Do not trust the browser-supplied Content-Type header as definitive file type.
It is client input.
It can be useful metadata.
Validate content where required.
Uploaded filenames are client-controlled.
Do not use them directly as trusted filesystem paths.
Generate server-side storage names where appropriate.
Preserve original filenames only as metadata if needed.
Validate them before display.
Do not let an uploaded filename overwrite arbitrary server files.
Upload size should be limited.
Limits can exist at multiple layers:
Reverse proxy.
Web server.
Application runtime.
Application code.
Storage system.
Know which limit is authoritative.
Do not accept unlimited uploads and attempt validation only after storing enormous data in memory.
Reject oversized input as early as practical.
Streaming validation can help for large inputs.
Do not load a multi-gigabyte body into memory merely to determine it exceeds the permitted size.
Enforce transport and application limits.
Archives require special care.
A small compressed archive can expand into enormous data.
Validate:
Compressed size.
Uncompressed size.
Entry count.
Entry paths.
Compression ratio where relevant.
Do not extract arbitrary archives blindly.
Archive entries can contain path traversal.
Validate extraction paths.
Do not allow:
../../target
to escape the extraction directory.
Parsers should have bounded resource use.
Complex input can consume CPU or memory even when structurally valid.
Deeply nested JSON.
Huge arrays.
Pathological XML.
Complex regular-expression input.
Large multipart requests.
Malformed compressed data.
Define structural limits.
Maximum nesting depth.
Maximum collection size.
Maximum body size.
Maximum field count.
Do not assume valid syntax means safe resource consumption.
XML parsers can have features that are unnecessary or dangerous in some contexts.
Configure parsers according to application requirements.
Do not enable external entity processing unless required and safely designed.
Use secure parser settings.
Do not parse more language than necessary.
General rule:
Reduce accepted complexity.
If the application needs simple JSON, do not accept arbitrary serialized objects.
If it needs plain text, do not accept executable markup.
If it needs an integer, do not accept expressions.
Smaller input languages are easier to validate.
Protocol messages should be validated before processing.
Check:
Message length.
Version.
Message type.
Required fields.
Field types.
Ranges.
Checksums or integrity fields where protocol-defined.
Sequence or state where protocol-defined.
Do not execute actions based on partially parsed malformed messages.
A parser should distinguish:
Incomplete input.
Malformed input.
Unsupported input.
Valid input.
These states can require different handling.
Do not convert malformed input into defaults silently.
Defaults can be appropriate for omitted optional values.
They should not conceal invalid supplied values.
Optional limit absent -> default 20.
limit=garbage -> reject.
Do not interpret invalid as absent.
This distinction catches errors and attacks.
Unknown protocol versions should be handled according to protocol policy.
Do not assume an unknown version is compatible.
Reject unsupported versions or negotiate according to specification.
Do not guess.
Version fields should be validated before version-specific parsing where practical.
Network length fields require bounds checking.
If a message claims:
payload_length = 4,000,000,000
do not allocate memory blindly.
Validate the declared length against protocol limits and available data.
Integer overflow can occur when calculating buffer sizes.
Check arithmetic.
Do not trust length fields simply because they are part of a binary protocol.
Binary input is still input.
Validate magic values.
Validate header sizes.
Validate offsets.
Validate counts.
Validate indexes.
Validate boundaries.
Do not read beyond available data.
Memory-safe languages reduce some consequences.
They do not remove logical validation requirements.
An invalid index can still crash or produce wrong behavior.
C and C++ require especially careful bounds handling.
Before copying input into a fixed-size buffer, establish the permitted size.
Do not use unbounded copy operations on untrusted input.
Validate lengths before arithmetic and allocation.
Check return values from parsing functions.
Do not assume parsing succeeded.
For example, in C:
strtol()
can provide more controlled parsing than casual atoi() usage because errors and range can be examined.
Use appropriate APIs.
Do not rely on functions that provide no useful error detection when correctness matters.
A successful parse should consume the intended input.
123abc
A parser can parse prefix 123 and stop at a.
If the field requires a complete integer, reject remaining characters.
Do not accept partial parsing accidentally.
C string input can contain termination and length issues depending on source.
Know whether data is NUL-terminated.
Do not call string functions on arbitrary binary buffers without establishing termination.
Input length and representation are part of validation.
C++ streams and conversion functions also require error checking.
Exceptions or fail states should be handled.
Do not assume conversion succeeded because a value variable exists.
C# parsing APIs commonly provide TryParse-style operations.
Use explicit success results where appropriate.
Do not catch every parsing exception and substitute zero.
Zero can be a valid value and can hide malformed input.
Go conversion functions return errors.
Check them.
Do not discard errors with blank identifiers when the input matters.
JavaScript can perform surprising coercions.
Number("")
can produce a numeric value.
Loose equality can coerce types.
Use explicit validation.
Do not rely on JavaScript truthiness for security-sensitive input.
PHP also performs type juggling.
Values such as:
"0"
null
can behave differently depending on comparison.
Use strict comparisons where required.
Validate types explicitly.
Do not use loose comparison as a substitute for input validation.
SQL types can coerce values too.
Do not depend on database coercion to validate application input.
Validate before persistence.
Database constraints should provide an additional integrity layer.
NOT NULL.
CHECK.
FOREIGN KEY.
UNIQUE.
Data type constraints.
Application validation improves user-facing errors.
Database constraints protect structural integrity.
Use both where appropriate.
Do not assume application validation can never be bypassed.
Other code paths can write to the database.
Database invariants can provide defense in depth.
Validation rules should align with database constraints.
If application allows 100 characters but database permits only 50, requests can fail unexpectedly.
If database allows more than application, that can be intentional.
Know the relationship.
Do not let mismatched limits arise accidentally.
Configuration input needs validation.
Configuration files are often treated as trusted.
They can still contain mistakes.
Required keys.
Types.
Paths.
Ports.
Modes.
Unknown options.
Do not let malformed configuration produce unpredictable runtime behavior.
Fail clearly.
A configuration error should not silently disable security.
auth_required = "flase"
should not be interpreted as false because it resembles the word.
Reject invalid configuration.
Configuration should be deterministic.
Environment variables are strings at the environment boundary.
Parse them into required types.
PORT=18473
can become an integer after validation.
Do not assume:
PORT=banana
