Security provides authority boundaries.
Networking provides communication when the database is remote.
The operating system provides the execution environment.
Each layer has a defined responsibility.
Correct systems preserve those boundaries.
Configuration is the process of supplying a system with values that select or adjust behavior without requiring the program itself to be rewritten.
Configuration can determine:
Network addresses.
Ports.
Filesystem locations.
Logging levels.
Feature enablement.
Resource limits.
Timeouts.
Retry limits.
Module selection.
Runtime modes.
Service endpoints.
Database connections.
Protocol options.
Operational parameters.
Configuration should select among behavior the software is designed and authorized to perform.
Configuration should not secretly redefine the architecture of the system.
Code defines capability.
Policy defines permitted behavior where policy applies.
Configuration selects permitted operating parameters.
Keep these concepts separate.
A configuration value is input.
Treat configuration as input.
Do not assume configuration is valid merely because it came from a local file.
Configuration can be:
Malformed.
Incomplete.
Outdated.
Mistyped.
Corrupted.
Generated incorrectly.
Modified manually.
Copied from another environment.
Incompatible with the running software.
Validate configuration before using it.
A useful configuration lifecycle is:
Discover configuration source.
Read configuration.
Parse configuration.
Validate structure.
Validate values.
Resolve precedence.
Apply defaults where defined.
Construct the effective configuration.
Validate cross-field relationships.
Freeze or publish the effective configuration.
Use it.
Do not begin operating on partially validated configuration.
Configuration formats can include:
Plain text.
TSV.
CSV.
INI.
JSON.
YAML.
TOML.
XML.
Environment variables.
Command-line arguments.
Database records.
Operating-system configuration stores.
Remote configuration services.
Compiled defaults.
The format is not the configuration architecture.
Choose a format appropriate to the system.
Do not adopt a complex format merely because it is popular.
Small systems often benefit from simple configuration.
A configuration schema defines what configuration is accepted.
The schema can specify:
Known keys.
Required keys.
Optional keys.
Types.
Ranges.
Allowed values.
Defaults.
Relationships.
Deprecations.
Version.
For example:
host = string
port = integer from 1 through 65535
timeout_seconds = integer from 1 through 300
log_level = one of debug, info, warning, error
enabled = boolean
Do not accept arbitrary values and hope downstream code handles them.
Configuration validation should fail clearly.
Invalid:
port=banana
Do not silently convert it to:
port=0
Reject it.
port=70000
Do not clamp it to:
65535
log_level=verboseish
Do not guess:
debug
Configuration should be deterministic.
The same configuration sources under the same precedence rules should produce the same effective configuration.
Do not make configuration resolution depend on arbitrary iteration order.
Do not randomly choose between duplicate settings.
Define precedence.
A common precedence model can be:
System configuration file.
Application configuration file.
The exact order is application-specific.
There is no universal precedence hierarchy.
Define one.
Document it.
Implement it consistently.
Do not let different modules invent different precedence rules.
For example, if command-line options override environment variables, that rule should apply consistently unless an option explicitly defines otherwise.
Precedence answers:
When multiple sources provide the same setting, which one wins?
It does not answer:
Is the winning value valid?
Validate the resulting value.
A higher-precedence source should not be allowed to bypass validation.
File:
port=8080
Environment:
PORT=banana
If environment has higher precedence, the effective input is invalid.
Do not fall back silently to 8080 unless fallback-on-invalid is explicitly defined.
Invalid override is not the same as absent override.
This distinction matters.
Absent means:
No value was supplied by this source.
Invalid means:
A value was supplied but violates the contract.
Do not treat malformed configuration as missing configuration.
Defaults apply to absent optional configuration according to defined rules.
Defaults should not normally conceal malformed supplied values.
Default port = 8080.
PORT absent:
Use 8080.
PORT=abc:
Reject configuration.
Do not use 8080 merely because parsing abc failed.
Otherwise configuration mistakes become invisible.
Defaults should be explicit.
Do not scatter hidden defaults throughout the program.
network.c assumes timeout=10.
worker.c assumes timeout=30.
api.c assumes timeout=60.
This creates inconsistent behavior.
Define the authoritative default once where practical.
Defaults are part of system behavior.
Document important defaults.
A default should be safe and meaningful.
Do not choose insecure defaults merely because they make setup easier.
authentication_required = false
can be a dangerous default if authentication is required by the product's security model.
Security-sensitive defaults should follow policy.
Do not let missing configuration silently disable required protections.
Required configuration should be required.
If the system cannot operate correctly without a value, do not invent one unless a defined default exists.
Required cryptographic identity file missing.
Do not silently generate or select an unrelated identity unless the system explicitly defines that behavior.
Fail clearly or enter the defined initialization workflow.
Do not guess.
Configuration keys should have stable names.
rpc_host
rpc_port
data_path
log_level
Avoid ambiguous names such as:
address
value
mode2
thing
Configuration is an interface.
Treat key names as interface design.
Names should describe semantics.
Namespaces can group related settings.
network.host
network.port
network.timeout
logging.level
logging.path
storage.path
storage.max_size
Grouping can improve clarity.
Do not create unnecessary hierarchy for a tiny configuration.
Keep it proportional.
Configuration types should remain explicit.
A boolean is not an arbitrary string.
Define accepted forms.
true
false
Do not accept:
yes
y
1
on
enabled
unless the configuration specification explicitly allows them.
Permissive parsing can create ambiguity.
If multiple forms are accepted, define them exactly.
Integer configuration should be parsed strictly.
Check:
Complete parse.
Range.
Overflow.
Sign.
Do not use permissive conversion that accepts prefixes and ignores trailing garbage.
18473abc
should not become:
18473
if the configuration requires an integer.
Floating-point configuration requires defined semantics.
If only finite values are permitted, reject:
NaN
Infinity
-Infinity
Define range and precision requirements.
Do not use floating point for values requiring exact integer or decimal semantics merely because parsing is convenient.
Durations should have clear units.
Bad:
timeout=30
Thirty what?
Seconds?
Milliseconds?
Minutes?
Prefer either a documented universal unit:
timeout_seconds=30
or a defined duration grammar:
timeout=30s
Do not make units depend on which module reads the value.
Storage sizes should also have defined units.
cache_bytes=1048576
or:
cache_size=1MiB
if the parser explicitly supports that grammar.
Do not interpret:
1M
differently on different platforms or modules.
Configuration paths should have defined semantics.
Questions include:
Absolute or relative?
If relative, relative to what?
Working directory?
Executable directory?
Configuration file directory?
Data directory?
Define it.
Do not let path interpretation depend accidentally on where the process was launched.
A service started by systemd can have a different working directory than the same binary launched manually.
Relative-path ambiguity creates deployment defects.
Canonicalize paths where appropriate.
Do not canonicalize away meaningful semantics blindly.
Validate path existence only when existence is required at configuration time.
Input file must exist.
Output directory might be created later.
Know the requirement.
Do not require every configured path to exist merely because path validation exists.
Permissions matter.
A path can exist while the process cannot read or write it.
Configuration validation can check required access where practical.
Do not claim a path is usable merely because stat() succeeded.
The actual operation can still fail.
Runtime error handling remains required.
Configuration validation reduces predictable failures.
It cannot prove future operations will succeed.
Hostnames and addresses should use appropriate parsers.
Do not parse network endpoints through casual string splitting when IPv6 or other valid formats can contain colons.
Define endpoint representation.
host and port as separate fields.
This can be clearer than one overloaded string.
If a URL is expected, parse it as a URL.
If a hostname is expected, do not accept an arbitrary URL unless explicitly supported.
Keep types distinct.
Ports must be validated according to the application's permitted range.
The general transport range can be 1 through 65535.
An application can impose a narrower allowed range.
Do not assume any numerically valid port is permitted by application policy.
Configuration relationships require cross-field validation.
tls_enabled=true
can require:
certificate_path
private_key_path
Another example:
mode=client
server_host
server_port
Another:
mode=standalone
can prohibit:
cluster_peer
Validate combinations.
Individually valid values can form an invalid configuration.
Configuration modes should have defined behavior.
development
test
production
Do not let a mode become a vague switch that changes dozens of undocumented behaviors.
If a mode affects behavior, document what it selects.
Security behavior should not be hidden behind surprising mode semantics.
production=true
should not be the only thing preventing debug authentication bypass unless that architecture is explicitly designed and controlled.
Prefer explicit security settings where clarity matters.
Feature flags are configuration.
A feature flag selects whether an existing feature is active.
It should not introduce code paths that have never been validated.
Feature flags can be:
Boolean.
Enumerated.
Percentage-based.
Identity-based.
Time-based.
Simple systems should prefer simple flags.
Do not build an experimentation platform when a boolean is sufficient.
A feature disabled by configuration still exists in the code.
Do not confuse disabled with absent.
Security analysis should consider dormant code if it can be re-enabled.
Configuration can select modules.
modules=network,storage,monitoring
Validate module names.
Reject unknown modules unless forward-compatible behavior explicitly allows them.
Do not dynamically load arbitrary paths merely because a configuration key says:
module=/tmp/whatever
unless arbitrary module loading is intentionally authorized.
Module selection and module trust are separate.
Configuration can select among approved components.
It does not automatically authorize arbitrary executable code.
Plugin paths are security boundaries.
Treat them accordingly.
A configuration file can be human-editable.
Human-editable configuration should produce useful errors.
config.ini:12: invalid value for rpc_port: expected integer 1..65535
This is more useful than:
configuration failed
Include enough context to correct the error.
Do not expose secrets in error messages.
Invalid API token format.
Do not print the entire token.
Configuration diagnostics should identify source.
rpc_port = 18473
source = /etc/example/config.ini
source = command line
Knowing provenance helps debugging.
Do not make operators guess which layer supplied the effective value.
An effective configuration is the fully resolved configuration after precedence, defaults, parsing, and validation.
Effective configuration:
host = 127.0.0.1
port = 8080
timeout_seconds = 30
log_level = info
Each value can optionally retain provenance.

value = 127.0.0.1
source = default
port:
value = 8081
source = environment
This can greatly improve observability.
Do not expose sensitive provenance or values where access is unauthorized.
Configuration introspection can support:
Debugging.
Support.
Auditing.
Testing.
Deployment verification.
A command such as:
program --show-config
can display effective non-secret configuration.
This can eliminate uncertainty.
Do not require operators to mentally merge five configuration sources.
Show what the process actually loaded.
The effective configuration is more important than what one file contains.
A file can say:
while environment says:
PORT=8081
The running process uses 8081.
Debug runtime state, not assumptions.
Configuration loading should identify which files were actually read.
Do not assume the file you edited is the file the process loaded.
Possible causes include:
Different working directory.
Different service user.
Different --config argument.
Different environment.
Container filesystem.
Stale deployment.
Symlink.
Multiple installations.
Log or expose the loaded configuration source where appropriate.
Configuration discovery should be deterministic.
Search arbitrary directories until a file named config is found.
Better:
Use a documented search order.
Explicit --config path.
Application-specific environment path.
System default path.
Built-in defaults.
Again, exact rules are application-specific.
Define them.
Do not let configuration discovery depend on filesystem enumeration order.
Explicit configuration paths are useful for services.
program --config /etc/program/config.ini
This reduces ambiguity.
A default path can still exist.
Command-line override can make testing easier.
Do not create so many discovery mechanisms that operators cannot predict which file wins.
Configuration files can include other files.
Includes can be useful for:
Shared settings.
Environment separation.
Secret separation.
Large configurations.
Includes also add complexity.
If includes are supported, define:
Path resolution.
Maximum nesting.
Cycle handling.
Precedence.
Duplicate keys.
Missing includes.
Optional includes.
Do not allow infinite include recursion.
Detect cycles.
a.conf includes b.conf
b.conf includes a.conf
Do not recurse forever.
Include order must be deterministic.
If later files override earlier files, define that.
Do not depend on directory ordering unless explicitly sorted and specified.
Wildcard includes should have deterministic ordering.
conf.d/*.conf
Sort filenames according to a defined rule before applying them.
Do not trust filesystem enumeration order.
Duplicate keys require defined semantics.
Possible policies:
Reject duplicates.
First value wins.
Last value wins.
Collect into list.
Different formats have different conventions.
Choose intentionally.
For security-sensitive configuration, rejecting ambiguous duplicates can be safer.
Do not let one parser use first-value semantics while another uses last-value semantics.
Parser differentials create defects.
Unknown keys require policy.
A strict configuration system can reject unknown keys.
This catches:
Typos.
Removed settings.
Unsupported features.
Wrong-version configuration.
log_levle=debug
should not silently do nothing.
Rejecting it immediately reveals the mistake.
Some systems need forward compatibility and can preserve or ignore unknown fields.
If so, define that behavior.
Do not silently ignore unknown security-sensitive settings.
Warnings can be appropriate for deprecated keys.
warning: network_timeout is deprecated; use network.timeout_seconds
Deprecation should have a migration path.
Do not remove configuration keys without considering deployed installations.
Configuration is an external interface.
Version configuration formats when incompatible changes occur.
config_version=2
Versioning can determine:
Accepted keys.
Value grammar.
Migration behavior.
Do not infer incompatible versions from random key presence if an explicit version would be clearer.
A configuration migration can transform old known configuration into a new known representation.
Migration should be deterministic.
Do not guess ambiguous mappings.
If an old value has no safe equivalent, require operator intervention.
Do not fabricate intent.
Preserve a backup when modifying operator-owned configuration where appropriate.
Automatic migration should not destroy evidence of prior state.
A migration should be testable.
Configuration parsers should not execute arbitrary code.
A configuration file should normally describe data.
Do not use a general programming language as configuration merely for convenience unless executable configuration is an intentional architectural choice.
Executable configuration increases:
Attack surface.
Complexity.
Nondeterminism.
Debugging difficulty.
Portability problems.
Data configuration is easier to validate.
Keep configuration declarative where practical.
Declarative configuration describes desired parameters.
Imperative scripts perform operations.
Do not confuse them.
Configuration:
data_path=/var/lib/program
Imperative behavior:
mkdir /var/lib/program
The application can perform the operation according to defined initialization logic.
The configuration should not need arbitrary shell commands.
Do not put:
on_start=rm -rf ...
into a generic configuration language unless executing arbitrary commands is explicitly the feature.
Configuration should not become an accidental command interpreter.
Secrets can appear in configuration.
Examples include:
Passwords.
API keys.
Private keys.
Tokens.
Database credentials.
Do not print secrets in configuration dumps.
Do not include secrets in ordinary logs.
Do not expose secrets through diagnostics.
Redact them.
database_password = <redacted>
Do not redact whether the value exists if existence is useful and safe.
database_password = configured
can aid diagnostics.
Secret storage should follow system security requirements.
Possible sources include:
Protected files.
Operating-system secret stores.
Dedicated secret systems.
The correct method depends on deployment.
Do not claim environment variables are universally secure.
Do not claim configuration files are universally insecure.
Evaluate actual access controls and threat model.
File permissions matter.
A secret configuration file readable by every user can expose credentials.
Use least privilege.
Do not make a configuration file world-writable.
Configuration integrity matters.
If an attacker can alter privileged configuration, they can often alter system behavior.
Protect configuration according to its authority.
A service running as an unprivileged user should not normally be able to rewrite root-controlled security policy configuration unless that behavior is explicitly required.
Separate operator-controlled configuration from application-generated state.
/etc/program/config
can be operator-owned configuration.
/var/lib/program/state
can be application state.
Do not mix them casually.
Configuration is not state.
This distinction is important.
Configuration describes selected operating parameters.
State records what the system currently knows or has done.
peer=chain01.example
State:
last_connected_peer=chain02.example
retry_limit=5
retry_count=3
Do not store changing runtime state in static configuration merely because a file already exists.
Likewise, do not treat configuration as historical evidence.
Configuration can change.
If historical configuration matters, record snapshots or revision history separately.
A current configuration file does not prove what configuration was active yesterday.
Configuration and policy are different.
Policy can establish:
Authentication is required.
Configuration can select:
authentication_backend=local
if multiple approved backends exist.
Configuration should not be able to set:
authentication_required=false
if policy forbids disabling authentication.
Do not let configuration override higher-level authority.
Configuration operates within the boundaries established by the system and its governing rules.
Configuration does not create authority.
A configurable value is not automatically a permitted value.
The schema and policy define permitted values.
role=administrator
can be syntactically valid.
That does not mean arbitrary configuration sources are authorized to assign administrator authority.
Know who controls the configuration source.
Configuration source authority matters.
A user-specific configuration file can control user-level preferences.
It should not necessarily control system-wide security policy.
Separate scopes.
Possible scopes include:
Built-in.
System.
Organization.
User.
Project.
Session.
Command.
Higher-precedence does not always mean higher authority.
A command-line argument supplied by an unprivileged user should not override root-controlled policy merely because CLI normally has highest precedence.
Precedence operates only among settings that the source is authorized to control.
Authority comes first.
This can be modeled as:
Determine source.
Determine which settings the source may control.
Parse.
Validate.
Apply precedence among authorized sources.
Do not let precedence become privilege escalation.
System policy:
sandbox_required=true
User configuration:
sandbox_required=false
If users are not authorized to disable the sandbox, the user value must not override policy.
This is not a precedence question.
It is an authority question.
Configuration layers should have explicit ownership.
System policy layer.
Application defaults.
Operator configuration.
User preferences.
Runtime overrides.
Do not merge everything into one undifferentiated map if authority differs.
Configuration can be immutable after startup.
This is often the simplest model.
Process starts.
Configuration loads.
Configuration validates.
Effective configuration is created.
Runtime uses it until restart.
This reduces synchronization complexity.
If runtime reload is unnecessary, do not implement it.
Restart-based configuration changes are predictable.
Dynamic reload can be useful where restarts are expensive.
If reload is supported, define exactly which settings are reloadable.
Some settings can change safely.
Examples might include:
Log level.
Polling interval.
Some timeouts.
Other settings can require restart.
Data directory.
Process identity.
Network architecture.
Loaded cryptographic identity.
The exact distinction depends on application.
Do not pretend every setting can be hot-reloaded.
Reload behavior is part of configuration semantics.
A reload should:
Read new configuration.
Parse it.
Validate it completely.
Construct candidate effective configuration.
Apply allowed changes atomically where practical.
If validation fails, preserve the previous valid configuration.
Do not partially apply a malformed reload.
Old:
New:
port=8081
timeout=banana
Do not change port to 8081 and then fail on timeout unless partial reload is explicitly designed.
Prefer:
Validate candidate.
Reject entire candidate.
Continue using previous valid configuration.
This preserves known-good state.
Log the rejection.
Do not terminate a healthy service merely because an optional runtime reload file is malformed unless policy requires termination.
Startup and reload can have different failure semantics.
At startup:
No valid configuration can mean the process cannot safely start.
At reload:
A previously valid configuration already exists.
The system can often continue using it.
Define behavior.
Do not confuse reload failure with runtime failure.
Configuration reload should not create races.
If multiple threads read configuration, publish a consistent configuration snapshot.
Do not let one thread observe half old and half new settings.
Possible techniques include:
Immutable configuration object replacement.
Read-write locks.
Atomic pointer swap.
Language-specific synchronization.
Choose according to implementation.
A snapshot model is often simple:
Build complete new configuration.
Validate it.
Atomically replace the current configuration reference.
Readers use either old or new snapshot.
Never partial.
Dynamic configuration can affect active operations.
timeout changes from 60 to 10 seconds.
Does an existing operation use 60 or 10?
Define semantics.
A common rule is:
Existing operations retain the configuration snapshot they started with.
New operations use new configuration.
Another design can update active operations.
Either can be valid.
Do not leave it accidental.
Configuration should have lifecycle boundaries.
Some settings apply:
At process start.
At module initialization.
At connection creation.
Per request.
At operation start.
Define when a setting is read.
Do not repeatedly read environment variables throughout the program if startup configuration is supposed to be fixed.
Load once.
Validate once.
Use the validated representation.
Environment variables are process input.
They are strings.
Parse them.

becomes validated integer 8080.

Typed effective configuration reduces ambiguity.
Environment variable names should be namespaced where appropriate.

Do not depend on generic names such as:

if the environment contains many applications and ambiguity matters.
Case sensitivity of environment variables can differ across operating systems.
Platform-independent systems should define canonical configuration semantics.
Do not create behavior that works only because one operating system treats environment variable names case-insensitively.
Configuration files can have encoding requirements.
UTF-8 is a common choice.
Do not rely on platform-default text encoding.
The same configuration should parse consistently across supported platforms.
Line endings can differ.
Parsers should handle defined line-ending forms where appropriate.
Do not make configuration invalid merely because it moved between Windows and Linux if the format is intended to be portable.
Path values can still be platform-specific.
Separate platform-neutral configuration from platform-specific implementation details.

is inherently deployment-specific.
But protocol behavior selected by configuration should remain consistent.
Platform-independent software can have platform-specific defaults.
Default data directory differs by operating system.
That can be valid if the path is not consensus-visible or protocol-visible.
Do not let platform-specific defaults alter shared protocol semantics.
Consensus-visible configuration requires exceptional care.
If configuration affects consensus decisions, every participating node must apply compatible values according to protocol.
Local operator configuration should not arbitrarily redefine consensus rules.
Protocol constants and consensus rules are generally not ordinary local preferences.
Do not expose consensus-critical behavior as casual configuration unless the protocol explicitly defines it.

would be disastrous if nodes could independently select validation rules.
Shared rules belong to the protocol.
Network.
Peer.
Local storage.
Logging.
Resource use.
Other non-consensus behavior.
Know the boundary.
Configuration can select a network identifier if the software supports multiple networks.
Once selected, protocol validation should enforce that network.
Do not dynamically reinterpret incoming data according to whichever network makes it valid.
Configuration selects context.
Validation operates within that context.
Configuration changes can require state compatibility checks.
Changing network while reusing the same data directory can mix incompatible data.
Validate relationships between configuration and persistent state.
Do not blindly start.
A marker file or database metadata can identify the state format or network.

Do not silently rewrite state identity.

Do not assume a syntactically valid database connection means the intended database was selected.
Deployment verification can check identity.
Configuration can include instance identifiers.

Configuration.
Identity.

Secret.

An installer can write configuration.
A deployment system can render configuration.
A module can generate defaults.

Reproducibility.

Suppose:

Environment port = 8082.
CLI port = 8083.

Configuration fuzzing can expose parser failures.

Configuration errors should fail early.

Likewise:

Unknown mode.

Some validation requires runtime resources.
DNS resolution.
Remote database availability.
Network connectivity.

Configuration validation.
Dependency readiness.

This distinction improves diagnosis.
A useful startup sequence can be:
Validate configuration.
Initialize local resources.
Validate required identities.
Connect dependencies.
Qualify dependencies.
Enter operational state.

Error categories should preserve cause.
Configuration parsing errors are different from:

Missing files.
Network failures.

These can aid diagnostics.

Use enough structure to identify the failure class.
A configuration file missing can have different semantics depending on whether the file is required.
Optional file absent:
Continue.
Required file absent:
Fail.
Do not treat all missing files identically.
An unreadable file is not the same as an absent file.
File exists but permission denied.
Do not silently treat it as absent and use defaults.
That can bypass intended configuration.
Report the permission failure.
Likewise, a malformed file is not absent.
This principle is important:
Missing optional configuration can fall back.
Present but invalid configuration should normally fail.
Do not reward corruption by silently ignoring it.
Configuration should support reproducibility.
If two deployments are intended to behave identically, their effective configuration should be comparable.
A normalized effective configuration can help.

network.port=8080
network.timeout_seconds=30
logging.level=info
Stable ordering makes diffs useful.
Do not include secrets in ordinary configuration comparisons.
Hashing configuration can provide an identifier for a specific effective configuration.
config_hash = SHA-256(normalized_nonsecret_or_complete_internal_representation)
The exact representation must be defined if the hash has operational meaning.
Do not hash arbitrary serializer output and assume stability across versions.
Canonicalization matters.
A configuration hash can help answer:
Are these two processes running equivalent configuration?
It does not prove the configuration is correct.
It does not prove authorization.
It is an identity for bytes or canonical data.
Do not overstate it.
Configuration revisions can be useful.
revision=17
The process can report:

This improves auditability.
Do not use revision numbers as substitutes for content validation.
A revision can contain malformed data.

Authentication can fail.
Network partitions can occur.
Updates can arrive out of order.

If remote configuration is used, define:

Integrity.
Caching.
Startup behavior when unavailable.
Update ordering.
Rollback.
Versioning.
Staleness limits.
Authority.

Configuration updates can carry versions.

revision 43

Do not roll configuration backward accidentally.
Intentional rollback should be explicit.
A rollback is not the same as receiving stale data.

Software testing evaluates whether software behaves according to defined expectations.
A test provides evidence about behavior under tested conditions.
A passing test does not prove that software has no defects.
A failing test provides evidence that an expected condition was not satisfied.
Testing and debugging are different activities.
Testing discovers or demonstrates behavior.
Debugging investigates the cause of incorrect behavior.
Verification asks whether a system satisfies specified requirements.
Validation asks whether the resulting system satisfies its intended use and requirements.
Testing can contribute evidence to verification and validation.
A test should have a defined purpose.
A test should have defined inputs.
A test should have defined expected results.
A test should have observable results.
A test without a meaningful expected result provides weak evidence.
A test should distinguish success from failure.
A test should not silently convert failure into success.
A test should not report success merely because execution completed.
Execution completion and correctness are different.
A program compiling successfully does not prove that it works correctly.
A program linking successfully does not prove that it works correctly.
A program starting successfully does not prove that it works correctly.
A module loading successfully does not prove that the module works correctly.
A network connection succeeding does not prove that the protocol works correctly.
An HTTP response being received does not prove that the requested operation succeeded.
A database connection succeeding does not prove that a query is correct.
A query executing successfully does not prove that its result is correct.
A function returning a value does not prove that the value is correct.
Each claim requires evidence appropriate to that claim.
A test case is a defined set of conditions used to evaluate behavior.
A test suite is a collection of test cases.
A test runner executes tests and reports results.
A test fixture establishes state required by a test.
A test oracle determines the expected result against which observed behavior is compared.
A deterministic test produces the same expected result when executed under the same defined conditions.
Nondeterministic tests are harder to diagnose.
A flaky test passes and fails inconsistently without an intentional change to the tested behavior.
Flaky tests reduce confidence in test results.
A flaky test should be investigated.
Repeatedly rerunning a flaky test until it passes does not repair the underlying problem.
A test should fail for the behavior it is intended to test.
A test failing because of unrelated infrastructure provides weaker evidence about the target behavior.
Test environments should control relevant dependencies where practical.
Tests should minimize irrelevant dependencies.
A unit test evaluates a small unit of software behavior.
A unit is commonly a function, method, class, module component, or similarly bounded piece of behavior.
A unit test should isolate the behavior being evaluated where practical.
A unit test does not necessarily require complete system startup.
A unit test can test valid input.
A unit test can test invalid input.
A unit test can test boundary conditions.
A unit test can test error handling.
A unit test can test state transitions.
A unit test can test deterministic transformations.
Unit tests are useful for fast local feedback.
Unit tests do not replace integration tests.
An integration test evaluates interactions between components.
An integration test can test an application and database together.
An integration test can test a host and module together.
An integration test can test a client and server together.
An integration test can test a parser and storage layer together.
Integration testing can discover problems that isolated unit tests cannot.
Correct components can interact incorrectly.
Interface assumptions can disagree.
Serialization can disagree.
Version expectations can disagree.
Error propagation can disagree.
Integration tests evaluate these boundaries.
A system test evaluates a complete or substantially complete system.
A system test can exercise behavior through public interfaces.
A system test can include multiple services.
A system test can include networking.
A system test can include persistent storage.
A system test can include platform-specific behavior.
System tests provide broader behavioral evidence.
System tests can be slower and harder to diagnose than unit tests.
Different test levels answer different questions.
An end-to-end test evaluates a complete operational path.
An end-to-end test begins from an external or high-level entry point and verifies the resulting system behavior.
An end-to-end test can verify a request from client through server to persistence and back.
An end-to-end test can verify a module from discovery through activation and behavior.
An end-to-end test can verify a transaction from submission through final acceptance.
An end-to-end test should verify the actual result rather than only intermediate logs.
An intermediate success message is not proof of final success.
A smoke test checks a small set of essential functionality.
A smoke test determines whether a build is sufficiently functional for deeper testing.
A smoke test is intentionally limited.
Passing a smoke test does not mean every feature works.
A sanity test checks focused behavior after a change or repair.
Terminology around smoke and sanity testing can vary.
The important property is the defined scope of the test.
A regression test checks that previously working behavior remains correct after changes.
A regression occurs when a change breaks behavior that previously worked.
A defect repair should often receive a regression test.
A regression test preserves evidence of the expected repaired behavior.
Without a regression test, the same defect can return unnoticed.
A regression suite should include important historical failures.
Historical defects can become future test cases.
Testing can preserve lessons learned from failures.
Positive testing verifies accepted or expected behavior.
Negative testing verifies rejection of invalid, prohibited, unsupported, or unauthorized behavior.
Both positive and negative tests are important.
A parser should be tested with valid input.
A parser should be tested with malformed input.
Authentication should be tested with valid credentials.
Authentication should be tested with invalid credentials.

Authorization should be tested with insufficient authority.

The Chaos Foundation is intended to preserve the long-term continuity of Chaos MVC so that stewardship of the framework does not depend permanently on a single developer
The Chaos Foundation is intended to operate independently from STN-Labz while supporting the long-term development and stewardship of Chaos MVC.
STN-Labz is the organization that currently develops and maintains Chaos MVC. The proposed Chaos Foundation does not currently replace STN-Labz in that role.
Establishing the Chaos Foundation will not automatically transfer ownership, authority, intellectual property, or control of Chaos MVC from STN-Labz to the Chaos Foundation. Any such transfer must be explicitly established
The Chaos Foundation is intended to provide organizational stewardship for Chaos MVC without exercising authority over independent developers merely because they develop software for Chaos MVC.
Developers and organizations may participate in the Chaos MVC ecosystem without becoming organizationally subordinate to the Chaos Foundation.
Technical standards, certification requirements, compatibility requirements, and project governance established for Chaos MVC are distinct from organizational control over independent developers.
The Chaos Foundation is intended to protect the continuity and integrity of Chaos MVC while allowing the framework and its development community to grow beyond dependence on STN-Labz alone.
The mission of the Chaos Foundation is intended to be the long-term stewardship, stability, accessibility, and responsible development of Chaos MVC and its ecosystem.
The Chaos Foundation is intended to support the maintenance of Chaos MVC standards, technical documentation, developer documentation, and compatibility guidance.
The Chaos Foundation is intended to support a developer community in which individuals and organizations can contribute to the Chaos MVC ecosystem while remaining independent.
The Chaos Foundation is intended to support Chaos MVC developer education, qualification, and certification programs while keeping certification distinct from employment or organizational membership.
Governance of the Chaos Foundation is intended to protect the continuity and integrity of Chaos MVC rather than provide personal control of the framework to any individual Foundation participant.
Technical decisions concerning Chaos MVC are intended to be based on engineering requirements, security, compatibility, maintainability, and the long-term interests of the framework.
The Chaos Foundation is intended to preserve documented standards and development practices so that Chaos MVC remains maintainable as its developer community grows.
The Chaos Foundation is intended to support security research, vulnerability reporting, responsible remediation, and coordinated security practices concerning Chaos MVC.
The Chaos Foundation is intended to support publication and preservation of Chaos MVC releases, documentation, specifications, and historical project information.
The Chaos MVC developer certification structure includes Theme Developer, Module Developer, and Chaos Certified Developer.
A Theme Developer certification represents qualification to develop themes for Chaos MVC according to established Chaos MVC development requirements and standards.
A Module Developer certification represents qualification to develop modules for Chaos MVC according to established Chaos MVC development requirements and standards.
A Chaos Certified Developer represents broader demonstrated qualification in Chaos MVC development beyond a single theme or module specialization.
Chaos MVC developer certification represents demonstrated technical qualification. Certification does not by itself establish employment, organizational membership, project ownership, or unrestricted authority over Chaos MVC.
Independent developers may create software for the Chaos MVC ecosystem without becoming employees of STN-Labz or members of the proposed Chaos Foundation.
Chaos MVC modules and themes are expected to follow the technical, security, compatibility, packaging, and development requirements applicable to their type.
Chaos MVC uses developer identity and signing to establish the origin of signed software. A developer signing key identifies the developer responsible for the signed software rather than creating a separate identity for every product.
Chaos MVC module signing uses RSA-3072 with SHA-256. A module record can associate a module with the public key of its developer so that the module's origin can be verified.
Certification and software signing serve different purposes in the Chaos MVC ecosystem. Certification demonstrates developer qualification, while signing provides cryptographic evidence of software origin.
Chaos MVC is a web application framework developed and maintained by STN-Labz. It uses the Model-View-Controller architectural pattern to organize web applications.
Chaos MVC is designed around small, understandable components and predictable behavior. Its architecture favors straightforward operation and maintainability over unnecessary complexity.
Chaos MVC separates framework Core functionality from extensible functionality provided by modules and themes.
The Chaos MVC Core provides the fundamental framework behavior required for a Chaos MVC installation to operate. Core functionality is distinct from optional functionality supplied by modules and themes.
A Chaos MVC module extends an installation with functionality without requiring that functionality to become part of the framework Core.
A Chaos MVC theme controls the presentation and visual design of a Chaos MVC installation while remaining separate from the application's underlying functional behavior.
Chaos MVC modules are accessed through the module architecture, and user-facing module routes use the form /user/modules/{slug}.
Chaos MVC themes are managed separately from modules, and user-facing theme routes use the form /user/themes/{slug}.
Chaos MVC follows a lowercase naming convention for controllers, models, views, classes, and other framework components where the applicable Chaos MVC standard requires lowercase naming.
Chaos MVC models are owned and named by their module. For example, the developers module uses developers_model rather than a generic model name.
Chaos MVC supports filesystem-backed Pages using Markdown, JSON, HTML, and PHP content.
Chaos MVC supports GitHub Flavored Markdown for Markdown content.
Chaos MVC provides web discovery resources including RSS, sitemap.xml, ror.xml, and site.json
Chaos MVC provides a Site Resource Declaration through site.json so a site can expose structured information about itself according to the applicable STN-Labz site schema.
Chaos MVC treats security-sensitive operations as explicit operations. For example, logout is performed as a CSRF-protected POST rather than an unprotected GET request.
Chaos MVC security follows the principle that trust must be supported by predictable behavior, validation, and evidence rather than assumption.
Chaos MVC follows the engineering principle Determinism ? Probably. Security behavior should be deterministic where deterministic behavior is required rather than relying on an assumption that something will probably behave correctly.
Chaos MVC treats the framework Core as a protected architectural boundary. Changes to Core require deliberate authorization and should not be used when functionality can properly remain outside Core.
Chaos MVC separates optional functionality into modules so additional capabilities can be introduced without unnecessarily expanding the framework Core
Chaos MVC uses CSRF protection for security-sensitive state-changing requests. A valid CSRF token demonstrates that a protected request originated through an authorized application interaction.
Chaos MVC logout is a state-changing security operation and therefore uses a CSRF-protected POST request rather than an unprotected GET request.
Chaos MVC software signing provides cryptographic evidence of software origin. Signing does not by itself prove that software is secure, correct, compatible, or trustworthy.
Chaos MVC module signing uses RSA-3072 with SHA-256 and associates signed modules with the public key of the responsible developer.
Chaos MVC distinguishes developer identity from individual software artifacts. A developer uses their developer signing identity rather than requiring a separate signing identity for every module.
Chaos MVC compatibility and security requirements are separate from developer certification. A qualified developer must still produce software that satisfies the applicable technical and security requirements.
Chaos MVC security defects may justify a framework patch or release when remediation requires a distributed change to supported installations.
Chaos MVC Patch Day is Saturday when a qualifying patch is ready. Qualifying reasons for a patch include security issues, major enhancements, and major Core features.
A scheduled Patch Day does not require a Chaos MVC release every Saturday. A release occurs when a qualifying patch is ready.
Chaos MVC security decisions should preserve clear boundaries between authorization, qualification, identity, and technical capability. Possessing one does not automatically grant the others.
Permission to execute an operation in Chaos MVC does not mean permission to act outside the boundaries established for that operation.
Chaos MVC uses versioned releases so installations, developers, and administrators can identify the framework version they are using.
Chaos MVC distinguishes ordinary development from release-worthy changes. Not every development change requires an immediate public release.
Chaos MVC Patch Day is Saturday when a qualifying patch is ready. Qualifying reasons include security issues, major enhancements, and major Core features.
Patch Day does not mean Chaos MVC must release a new version every Saturday. A release occurs when qualifying work is ready for distribution.
A Chaos MVC security issue may justify a release when supported installations require a distributed change to correct the issue.
A major enhancement may justify a Chaos MVC release when the enhancement materially improves framework functionality and is ready for supported use.
A major Core feature may justify a Chaos MVC release when the feature belongs within the framework Core and is ready for supported use.
Chaos MVC release documentation should distinguish security changes, Core features, enhancements, compatibility requirements, and other material changes so administrators understand what a release changes.
Chaos MVC version compatibility identifies which framework versions are supported by a release, module, theme, or other component. Compatibility should be established explicitly rather than assumed.
A Chaos MVC update must not assume that an installation can safely move between versions merely because a newer version exists. Applicable compatibility and migration requirements must be considered.
A Chaos MVC release may require a database migration when its changes alter persistent database structures. A release that does not require a database migration should identify that fact in its release information.
Chaos MVC 1.2.1 was released on September 19, 2026 as a Security and Core Feature release. Its minimum supported prior version was 1.2.0 and it required no database migration.
Chaos MVC 1.2.1 introduced filesystem-backed Pages, GitHub Flavored Markdown support, RSS, sitemap.xml, ror.xml, the site.json Site Resource Declaration, Core Updater improvements, and framework integrity fixes.
Chaos MVC preserves release history because previous versions, changes, compatibility information, and security history are part of the technical record of the framework.
A newer Chaos MVC version does not make the historical record of an older release incorrect. Release history records what was true about the framework at that point in its development.
Chaos MVC extends framework functionality primarily through modules and themes rather than placing every capability into Core.
A Chaos MVC module provides functional capabilities that can be installed and maintained separately from the framework Core.
A Chaos MVC theme provides presentation and visual design while remaining separate from the functional responsibilities of modules and Core.
Functionality that properly belongs to a module should remain in the module rather than modifying Chaos MVC Core merely for convenience.
Administration functionality belonging to a Chaos MVC module should remain within that module's controller, model, views, and administrative interface rather than being placed into unrelated Core administration pages.
Chaos MVC modules use module-owned models. A module named developers uses developers_model rather than a generic model shared without clear ownership.
Chaos MVC controllers, models, views, classes, and applicable extension components follow the established lowercase naming convention.
User-facing Chaos MVC modules use routes under /user/modules/{slug}, while user-facing themes use routes under /user/themes/{slug}.
A Chaos MVC extension must respect framework security boundaries. Being installable or executable does not authorize an extension to bypass Core security controls or unrelated application boundaries.
Chaos MVC module signing establishes cryptographic evidence of module origin by associating the module with its developer signing identity.
Chaos MVC uses RSA-3072 with SHA-256 for its established module signing model. The module record pins the public key of the responsible developer.
Chaos MVC uses one developer signing identity for the developer rather than creating a different developer signing key for every module or theme.
A valid Chaos MVC extension signature establishes origin. It does not independently establish security, compatibility, quality, certification, or authorization.
Chaos MVC extension compatibility must be explicitly established against applicable framework versions rather than inferred merely because an extension can be installed.
A Chaos MVC module should define and respect the lifecycle of data it owns. Installation, normal operation, updates, and removal must not casually destroy data whose lifecycle requires preservation.
Chaos MVC modules should keep module-owned functionality and data within clearly defined module boundaries so ownership and responsibility remain understandable.
Removing a Chaos MVC module and deleting the information managed by that module are separate lifecycle decisions. Data must not be assumed disposable merely because its module is being removed.
Chaos MVC development follows established framework conventions and boundaries so extensions remain predictable, maintainable, and compatible with the framework
Chaos MVC Core is distinct from extension development. A module developer should not modify Core merely to make a module work.
A Chaos MVC module should be self-contained within its defined module boundaries whenever the required functionality belongs to the module.
Chaos MVC module controllers, models, views, classes, filenames, and applicable identifiers follow the established lowercase naming convention.
A Chaos MVC module uses a module-owned model. For example, the developers module uses developers_model.
Chaos MVC module administration belongs to the module. Module-specific administrative functionality should not be placed into unrelated Core administration pages.
Chaos MVC module development must preserve framework security controls rather than bypassing them for convenience.
Chaos MVC state-changing actions must use the appropriate security protections. Authentication or administrative access alone does not justify bypassing protections required for the action.
A Chaos MVC module must clearly own the functionality and data for which it is responsible so lifecycle and maintenance responsibilities remain identifiable.
Chaos MVC module installation, operation, updating, disabling, and removal are distinct lifecycle events and should be handled deliberately.
Module removal does not inherently authorize destruction of module-owned data. The applicable data lifecycle determines whether information is preserved or removed.
Chaos MVC distinguishes authorization to create a module from qualification to develop it. Authorization and technical qualification are separate requirements.
Chaos MVC agent qualification requires at least twenty tests, while module qualification requires at least ten tests.
Chaos MVC module qualification requires at least one negative validation test in addition to the required module tests
A negative validation test confirms that a module correctly rejects, prevents, or safely handles an invalid or prohibited condition rather than testing only successful behavior.
Passing positive tests alone is insufficient for Chaos MVC module qualification because required negative validation must also pass.
Chaos MVC module signing and module qualification serve different purposes. Signing establishes cryptographic origin while qualification establishes that required validation has been performed successfully.
Developer certification, module qualification, cryptographic signing, framework compatibility, authorization, and installation are separate properties. One does not automatically establish the others.
Chaos MVC compatibility must be established against the applicable framework version. Successful compilation, signing, qualification, or installation does not independently prove compatibility.
Chaos MVC development favors small, deterministic, understandable implementations over unnecessary complexity.
A Chaos MVC developer should preserve existing framework behavior unless a change is explicitly part of the authorized development objective.
Framework boundaries are part of Chaos MVC engineering discipline. Solving a problem does not justify modifying unrelated components.
Chaos MVC module development should produce behavior that can be validated by evidence rather than relying on assumptions that the implementation probably works.

PHP application security depends on both application code and runtime configuration.

Untrusted text must be escaped for the output context in which it is used.

Authorization must be checked on the server.

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.
HTML is the standard markup language used to structure content on web pages.
HTML describes the structure and meaning of web content.
HTML is a markup language, not a programming language.
HTML documents are interpreted by web browsers.
A web browser parses HTML to construct a representation of the document.
The browser represents a parsed HTML document as the Document Object Model, commonly called the DOM.
HTML elements represent parts of a document.
Most HTML elements are represented using tags.
An HTML element can contain text, other elements, or both.
HTML elements can be nested inside other HTML elements.
Proper nesting helps maintain a valid and understandable document structure.
An opening tag begins most HTML elements.
A closing tag ends most non-void HTML elements.
A closing tag includes a forward slash before the element name.
Some HTML elements are void elements and do not contain child content.
The img element is a void element.
The br element is a void element.
The hr element is a void element.
HTML tag names are conventionally written in lowercase.
HTML attributes provide additional information about an element.
Attributes are normally written inside an element's opening tag.
An attribute commonly consists of a name and a value.

An id value should be unique within an HTML document.
The class attribute associates an element with one or more class names.
Multiple elements can share the same class.

The link element can associate external resources with an HTML document.

The em element represents emphasized content.

Semantic meaning should be considered when selecting HTML elements.
The div element is a generic block-level container.
The span element is a generic inline container.

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.
CSS is a style sheet language used to control the presentation of documents.
CSS is commonly used to style HTML documents.
HTML primarily defines document structure and semantics.
CSS primarily defines presentation and layout.
CSS is not HTML.
CSS is not JavaScript.
CSS is not a server-side programming language.
CSS can control colors, typography, spacing, sizing, borders, backgrounds, and layout.
A CSS rule normally consists of a selector and a declaration block.
A selector identifies the elements to which a CSS rule applies.
A declaration block contains one or more CSS declarations.
A CSS declaration consists of a property and a value.

A property identifies the presentation characteristic being configured.
A value specifies the setting assigned to a CSS property.

The cascade determines which CSS declarations apply when multiple declarations target the same element.
CSS means Cascading Style Sheets because applicable style rules participate in a cascade.
The cascade considers factors including origin, importance, specificity, and source order.
Specificity helps determine which competing selector takes precedence.
Source order can determine the winning declaration when otherwise competing declarations have equal precedence.
The !important annotation changes the priority of a CSS declaration within the cascade.
Using !important unnecessarily can make styles harder to maintain.
Inheritance allows some CSS property values to pass from an element to its descendants.

Layout-related properties are commonly not inherited.

A type selector selects elements by HTML element name.

A class selector begins with a period.

An ID selector begins with a hash character.

An attribute selector can select elements according to attributes or attribute values.
The universal selector * can select all elements within its applicable scope.
Selectors can be combined to express relationships between elements.
A descendant combinator selects elements nested within another matching element.
A child combinator selects direct children of another matching element.

The adjacent sibling combinator is represented by +.
The general sibling combinator is represented by ~.
A selector list allows the same declarations to apply to multiple selectors.
Selectors in a selector list are separated by commas.
A pseudo-class represents an element in a particular state or relationship.
Pseudo-classes begin with a colon.

::after can generate a pseudo-element after an element's content.

ID selectors have greater specificity than class selectors under ordinary specificity comparison.
Class selectors, attribute selectors, and pseudo-classes contribute to specificity.
Type selectors and pseudo-elements contribute to specificity.

CSS source order matters when competing declarations have equivalent cascade priority and specificity.
The box model describes how CSS represents the dimensions and spacing of an element.

The content area contains an element's content.

Memory is storage used by a computer to hold data and instructions.
Computer systems contain multiple forms of storage with different properties.
Processor registers are small storage locations directly available to the processor.
CPU caches store frequently or recently used data close to processor execution units.
Main memory commonly refers to RAM.
RAM stands for Random Access Memory.
Persistent storage includes devices such as solid-state drives and hard drives.
Registers, cache, RAM, and persistent storage have different latency, capacity, and persistence characteristics.
Faster storage is generally smaller and more expensive per unit of capacity.
A memory hierarchy places frequently needed data closer to execution resources.
Registers are generally faster to access than main memory.
CPU cache is generally faster to access than main memory.
Main memory is generally faster to access than persistent storage.
These are architectural tendencies rather than universal timing guarantees.
Memory performance depends on hardware and workload.
RAM normally loses its contents when power is removed.
Persistent storage is designed to retain data without continuous power.
RAM and persistent storage serve different purposes.
A running program requires memory for executable code.
A running program requires memory for data.
A running program can require memory for stacks.
A running program can require dynamically allocated memory.
The operating system manages memory resources available to processes.
A process normally operates within a virtual address space.
A virtual address is an address used by software within a virtual-memory system.
A physical address refers to a location in physical memory according to the hardware memory architecture.
Virtual addresses and physical addresses are not necessarily identical.
The operating system and processor memory-management hardware translate virtual addresses to physical memory mappings.
Virtual memory provides processes with controlled address spaces.
Virtual memory allows different processes to use identical virtual address values without necessarily referring to the same physical memory.
Virtual memory supports process isolation.
Virtual memory can allow memory regions to be mapped with different permissions.
A memory region can be readable.
A memory region can be writable.
A memory region can be executable.
Permissions depend on the mapping and platform.
Memory protection prevents selected invalid accesses.
Memory protection does not make every program memory-safe.
A process can still corrupt memory that it legitimately owns.
A process can still misuse pointers.
A process can still access memory outside an intended object while remaining inside a mapped page.
Hardware memory protection and language memory safety are different concepts.
Virtual memory is commonly divided into pages.
A page is a fixed-size unit used by virtual-memory systems.
Physical memory can be organized into page frames.
A page table records virtual-to-physical mappings and associated properties according to the architecture.
Page size depends on the platform.
Four-kibibyte pages are common on many systems.
Larger page sizes can also exist.
Do not assume one page size universally.
A page fault occurs when a memory access requires operating-system intervention according to the virtual-memory system.
A page fault is not necessarily an application defect.
A page fault can occur because a valid page has not yet been mapped into physical memory.
A page fault can occur when accessing a demand-loaded page.
A page fault can occur during copy-on-write processing.
An invalid access can also produce a fault.
Valid and invalid page faults are different situations.
Demand paging loads or establishes pages when they are required rather than necessarily loading everything immediately.
Virtual memory can allow total mapped address space to exceed physical RAM.
Memory pressure occurs when demand for memory approaches or exceeds readily available physical resources.
Operating systems can reclaim memory.
Operating systems can evict cached pages.
Operating systems can move selected memory contents to secondary storage.
Swap space provides storage used by an operating system for selected memory-management operations.
Paging memory to storage is much slower than accessing RAM.
Heavy paging can severely reduce performance.
Thrashing occurs when a system spends excessive time moving pages rather than performing useful work.
More virtual address space does not create more physical RAM.
Address space and physical memory are different resources.
A 64-bit process can address a very large theoretical address range.
The actual usable address space is constrained by processor architecture, operating system, process limits, and implementation.
A 32-bit process has a much smaller address space than a typical 64-bit process.
A 32-bit pointer and a 64-bit pointer commonly differ in size.
Pointer size depends on the target architecture and ABI.
Do not assume sizeof(void *) equals sizeof(int).
A pointer stores an address or pointer representation according to the language and implementation.
A pointer can refer to an object.
A pointer can refer to a function where the language permits.
A pointer can be null.
A pointer can become invalid.
A pointer can be uninitialized.
A pointer value alone does not establish that dereferencing it is valid.
Dereferencing means accessing the object or function referenced by a pointer according to language semantics.
A null pointer does not point to a valid object.
Dereferencing a null pointer is invalid.
A dangling pointer refers to storage whose valid lifetime has ended.
Dereferencing a dangling pointer can produce undefined behavior in languages such as C and C++.
A wild pointer is an informal term for a pointer containing an invalid or unintended address.
Uninitialized pointers can behave as wild pointers.
Pointers should be initialized before use.
Pointer validity depends on object lifetime.
Pointer validity depends on bounds.
Pointer validity depends on alignment.
Pointer validity depends on access permissions.
Pointer validity depends on language rules.
An address being mapped does not prove a pointer access is valid according to the language.
An object has a lifetime.
Object lifetime determines when storage contains a valid object according to language rules.
Using an object before its lifetime begins can be invalid.
Using an object after its lifetime ends can be invalid.
Storage lifetime and variable scope are related but different concepts.
Scope determines where a name is visible in source code.
Lifetime determines when the object exists.
A local automatic variable commonly has automatic storage duration.
Its lifetime normally ends when execution leaves its defining block according to language rules.
Returning a pointer to an ordinary local automatic variable produces a pointer to an object whose lifetime has ended after the function returns.
That pointer becomes invalid for dereferencing.
A static-storage object exists for the duration defined by the language.
A dynamically allocated object exists until its storage is released according to the allocation model.
Dynamic allocation allows runtime control of storage lifetime.
Dynamic allocation introduces ownership responsibilities.
In C, malloc allocates a block of memory.
calloc allocates storage for an array of elements and initializes its bytes to zero according to C semantics.
realloc changes the size of an allocated block according to C semantics.
free releases storage previously obtained through compatible allocation functions.
malloc returns a pointer to allocated storage or a null pointer when allocation fails.
Allocation failure must be handled where it is possible.
Do not dereference an allocation result before validating success when failure can occur.
malloc does not initialize the allocated bytes.
Reading an uninitialized value can be invalid or indeterminate according to language rules.
calloc performs zero initialization of allocated bytes.
All-bits-zero does not universally represent every possible language value in every historical or theoretical implementation.
On common modern systems, zeroed storage commonly represents integer zero and null-like bit patterns where applicable, but portable code should follow language guarantees.
free does not erase the pointer variable.
free releases the allocation.
A pointer variable can still contain the old address after free.
That pointer is then dangling.
Setting a pointer to null after free can reduce accidental reuse through that particular pointer.
Setting one pointer to null does not invalidate or update other aliases to the same freed allocation.
Aliasing occurs when multiple references or pointers can refer to the same storage.
Aliasing complicates ownership.
One pointer freeing an allocation can leave other aliases dangling.
Ownership defines responsibility for a resource.
An owning pointer or component is responsible for releasing the resource according to the design.
A borrowed pointer or reference accesses a resource without owning its lifetime.
Ownership should be explicit.
Ambiguous ownership causes leaks and premature release.
Exactly one clear owner is often easier to reason about than unrestricted shared ownership.
Shared ownership requires defined lifetime management.
Reference counting is one shared-ownership technique.
A reference count tracks how many owners retain a resource.
The resource can be released when the count reaches zero according to the ownership model.
Reference counting can leak cycles.
If object A owns object B and object B owns object A, both reference counts can remain nonzero even when no external owner exists.
Weak references can break selected ownership cycles in systems that support them.
Garbage collection automatically identifies selected objects that are no longer reachable according to the runtime's model.
Garbage collection reduces explicit deallocation requirements.
Garbage collection does not eliminate all memory leaks.
A program can retain references to objects it no longer needs.
Those objects remain reachable.
Reachable but unnecessary objects can consume memory indefinitely.
Garbage collection does not manage every resource automatically.
Files can still require closing.
Sockets can still require closing.
Locks can still require release.
External resources can have lifetimes independent of memory.
Memory management and general resource management are related but distinct.
A memory leak occurs when allocated memory remains unavailable for reuse even though the program no longer needs it.
Repeated leaks can increase process memory usage.
A small leak in a short-running program can have limited operational impact.
A small repeated leak in a long-running service can eventually exhaust resources.
Memory leaks are correctness and reliability concerns.
A leak does not necessarily cause immediate failure.
Memory growth does not automatically prove a leak.
Caches can intentionally grow.
Buffers can grow.
Workload can increase.
Memory allocators can retain freed memory for reuse.

Use-after-free occurs when code accesses memory after its valid allocation lifetime ended.
Use-after-free is a serious memory-safety defect.
The freed storage can be reused for another object.
The old pointer can then access unrelated data.
Use-after-free can cause crashes.
Use-after-free can cause silent corruption.

Double free can corrupt allocator state.
Double free can cause crashes.
Double free can create security vulnerabilities.
Ownership discipline helps prevent double free.
Buffer overflow occurs when code writes beyond the bounds of a buffer.
Buffer over-read occurs when code reads beyond the bounds of a buffer.
Out-of-bounds access is invalid even when the adjacent memory happens to be mapped.
A program not crashing does not make an out-of-bounds access valid.
Memory corruption can remain hidden.
Memory corruption can damage nearby objects.
Memory corruption can alter control data.
Memory corruption can surface much later than the original invalid write.

An earlier memory write can corrupt state that fails later.

A stack is a runtime data structure commonly used to manage function calls.
A thread normally has its own stack.

A compiler can optimize values away.

Stack size is not unlimited.

A pointer to stack-local storage should not be used after that storage's lifetime ends.
Heap is a common term for memory used for dynamic allocation.
Heap allocation allows objects to outlive the function that allocated them when ownership is transferred appropriately.
Heap allocation has management overhead.

Heap allocation is not automatically slower than every stack operation in every context, but it generally involves more allocator machinery.
Use storage appropriate to the required lifetime and size.
Do not allocate dynamically merely because dynamic allocation appears more flexible.

Allocators use strategies to manage fragmentation.

A memory allocator manages dynamic allocation.
An allocator can maintain free lists.

Examples of memory-safety defects include out-of-bounds access.

A memory-safe program can calculate the wrong answer.

Languages differ in memory-safety models.
C gives programmers direct control over memory.

C++ provides low-level memory control plus higher-level ownership abstractions.

Bounds checking validates that an index or access lies within a valid region.
Some languages perform automatic bounds checking.

The programmer must maintain valid bounds.
A buffer should travel with its length where possible.
A pointer without known bounds is difficult to validate safely.
APIs should include capacity information when writing into caller-provided buffers.
A function receiving a destination buffer should know how much storage is available.
Do not infer buffer capacity from the pointer.
A pointer contains an address representation, not general allocation-size metadata.
sizeof applied to an array can produce the array's size while the array expression remains an actual array in the applicable context.

Arrays and pointers are related in C but are not identical.
An array object contains elements.
A pointer stores a reference.
Array expressions can decay to pointers in many contexts.
Decay does not make arrays and pointers the same type of object.
The number of elements in a true array can often be calculated using sizeof(array) divided by sizeof(array[0]) within a context where array is still an array.
That technique does not work on a pointer as though the pointer contained the original array length.
Array length should be passed explicitly across function boundaries when required.
Strings in C are arrays of characters terminated by a null character according to C string conventions.
The null terminator is part of the storage requirement.
A string containing N visible characters normally requires at least N plus one bytes when characters occupy one byte each in the representation.
Failing to reserve space for the terminator can overflow a buffer.

Binary data is not necessarily a C string.
Binary buffers can contain zero bytes.

Do not use string functions on arbitrary binary data.
memcpy copies a specified number of bytes between non-overlapping memory regions according to C semantics.
memmove copies bytes and supports overlapping source and destination regions.
memcpy should not be used when source and destination overlap.
memset fills bytes with a byte value.
memset operates on bytes.
memset does not assign arbitrary typed values element by element.

It does not generally initialize each integer object to numeric value 1.
Memory operations should use correct byte counts.
Confusing element count with byte count can cause under-copying or overflow.
Multiplying element count by element size can overflow.
Allocation-size calculations should detect arithmetic overflow.
If count multiplied by element size exceeds representable size, the resulting allocation can be smaller than intended.
Writing the expected number of elements can then overflow the allocation.
Validate size arithmetic before allocation.
size_t is an unsigned integer type used to represent object sizes according to C.
sizeof produces a value of type size_t.
Do not assume size_t has the same width as unsigned int.
On common 64-bit platforms, size_t is commonly 64 bits.
Conversion between signed and unsigned size values requires care.
A negative signed value converted to size_t can become a very large positive value.
Validate ranges before conversion.
Integer overflow can become a memory-safety issue when values determine allocation sizes or indexes.
Memory safety therefore depends partly on arithmetic correctness.
A zero-length allocation has implementation-defined or specified special semantics depending on the allocation function and language version.
Do not assume malloc(0) behaves identically on every implementation.
Design code so zero-length cases are handled explicitly.
realloc requires careful ownership handling.
If realloc fails, the original allocation remains valid according to ordinary C semantics.
