Use a temporary pointer when preservation is required.
For example, request the new allocation into a temporary variable.
If the request succeeds, update the owning pointer.
If it fails, retain the original pointer and handle failure.
realloc can move an allocation.
Pointers into the old allocation can become invalid after successful relocation.
Do not assume an allocation remains at the same address after realloc.
Memory ownership should be documented at API boundaries.
If a function returns allocated memory, specify who must free it.
If a function accepts a pointer, specify whether it borrows or takes ownership.
If a function stores a pointer after returning, specify the required lifetime.
If a function copies input data, specify that ownership remains with the caller.
Ambiguous API ownership creates defects.
Allocation and deallocation mechanisms must be compatible.
Memory allocated with malloc should be released using free.
C++ memory allocated with new should be released according to matching C++ deallocation rules.
Memory allocated with new[] should use the matching array deallocation mechanism.
Platform APIs can provide their own allocation and release functions.
Do not assume memory allocated by one allocator can be safely released by another allocator.
Cross-module memory ownership can be especially sensitive on platforms with multiple runtime heaps.
A module interface can avoid allocator mismatch by requiring the allocating component to release its own allocations.
An API can expose a release function.
An API can use caller-provided buffers.
An API can use fixed-layout values instead of transferred ownership.
ABI design should define memory ownership.
A DLL boundary is also a memory-ownership boundary when pointers cross it.
A plugin should not assume the host uses the same allocator unless the ABI guarantees it.
A host should not free plugin-owned memory using an incompatible allocator.
Small stable interfaces reduce memory-lifetime ambiguity.
Memory pools preallocate or manage groups of objects for repeated use.
Pools can reduce allocation overhead.
Pools can improve locality.
Pools can bound resource use.
Pools introduce their own lifetime rules.
An object returned to a pool should not remain in use.
A pointer to a pooled object can become invalid when the object is reused.
Pool reuse can make stale-pointer bugs difficult to detect.
Arena allocation allocates many objects from a common region.

Encode into the target encoding.
Validate the output.
Only then replace or publish converted data.
When debugging garbled text, do not begin by changing characters manually.
Obtain the original bytes.
Determine the expected encoding.
Determine which encoding was actually used to decode them.
Determine whether an incorrect encode-decode cycle already occurred.
Reconstruct only what evidence supports.
Some encoding corruption is reversible.
Some is not.
Do not fabricate lost characters.
A reliable system defines text encoding at its boundaries.
A reliable system distinguishes bytes from text.
A reliable system does not depend on platform-default encodings.
A reliable system uses explicit lengths.
A reliable system validates malformed encoded input.
A reliable system uses the correct encoder for each output grammar.
A reliable system avoids repeated decoding.
A reliable system defines canonical representation when exact bytes matter.
A reliable system preserves authoritative bytes when signatures or hashes depend on them.
A reliable system does not mistake human readability for data identity.
A reliable system does not treat encoding as security.
Encoding answers one fundamental question:
How is this information represented?
It does not answer:
Is this information secret?
Is this information authentic?
Is this information authorized?
Is this information correct?
Those questions belong to other mechanisms.
If the representation is known, decode it according to its rules.
If the representation is malformed, reject it according to policy.
If the representation is ambiguous and no authoritative rule resolves the ambiguity, the correct answer is not to guess.
The encoding is unknown.
DNS stands for Domain Name System.
DNS is a distributed naming system.
DNS maps names to information according to DNS records and protocol rules.
DNS is commonly used to map domain names to IP addresses.
DNS can also publish mail-routing information.
DNS can publish service information.
DNS can publish verification information.
DNS can delegate authority.
DNS can publish cryptographic information.
DNS is not merely a hostname-to-IP lookup table.
A domain name is a hierarchical name in the DNS namespace.
DNS names are composed of labels.
Labels are separated by dots in textual representation.
The hierarchy is interpreted from right to left.
In example.com, com is above example.com in the DNS hierarchy.
The DNS namespace has a root.
The root is conventionally represented by a trailing dot in a fully qualified domain name.
example.com. is an absolute DNS name.
The trailing root dot is commonly omitted in ordinary presentation.
A fully qualified domain name is commonly abbreviated FQDN.
An FQDN identifies a name from the DNS root.
A relative DNS name can be completed using local resolver search rules.
Relative-name expansion can produce different results in different environments.
Do not rely on search-domain behavior for security-sensitive or deterministic naming.
Use the intended absolute name when ambiguity matters.
DNS names are not URLs.
example.com is a DNS name.
https://example.com/path is a URL.
DNS does not resolve the URL path.
DNS does not determine the HTTP resource.
DNS can help locate the network address associated with the hostname portion.
Keep naming layers separate.
DNS names are not IP addresses.
An IP address identifies a network-layer address.
A DNS name can resolve to an IP address.
One DNS name can resolve to multiple IP addresses.
Multiple DNS names can resolve to the same IP address.
A DNS name can exist without an address record.
An IP address can exist without a DNS name.
Name identity and address identity are different.
A hostname is a name assigned to a host according to a system or network naming scheme.
A DNS name can identify a host.
A DNS name can also identify a service or other namespace object.
Do not assume every DNS name represents one physical computer.
A name can represent a load balancer.
A name can represent a cluster.
A name can represent a CDN.
A name can represent a virtual host.
A name can represent a service endpoint.
A name can change addresses over time.
DNS separates naming from network addressing.
This indirection allows an address to change while the name remains stable.
It also means knowing the name does not prove the current address.
Resolve according to current DNS state when current resolution matters.
DNS data is stored in resource records.
A resource record is commonly abbreviated RR.
A resource-record set is commonly abbreviated RRset.
An RRset contains records with the same owner name, class, and type according to DNS semantics.
DNS record types have defined meanings.
An A record maps a DNS name to an IPv4 address.
An AAAA record maps a DNS name to an IPv6 address.
A CNAME record establishes a canonical-name alias according to DNS rules.
An MX record identifies mail exchangers.
A TXT record stores textual data according to applications using TXT records.
An NS record identifies authoritative name servers for a DNS zone or delegation.
An SOA record contains administrative and control information for a DNS zone.
A PTR record is commonly used for reverse DNS mapping.
An SRV record can publish service location information.
CAA records can express certificate-authority authorization policy.
Other DNS record types exist.
Do not infer a record's meaning from its textual appearance alone.
Interpret it according to its DNS type and application protocol.
An A record contains an IPv4 address.
An AAAA record contains an IPv6 address.
A host can have both.
A client can receive multiple A records.
A client can receive multiple AAAA records.
The existence of multiple addresses does not automatically identify one as primary.
Address-selection behavior belongs to the client and network stack according to applicable rules.
Do not assume the first DNS answer is permanently preferred.
Record ordering can vary.
Resolvers can reorder responses.
Authoritative servers can vary response order.
Applications requiring deterministic behavior should not assign unsupported meaning to DNS answer order.
A CNAME record aliases one DNS name to another DNS name.
The CNAME target is another name.
It is not directly an IP address.
Resolution can continue using the target name.
CNAME chains can exist.
Chains should be bounded.
A CNAME loop is invalid for useful resolution.
Resolvers should detect or eventually terminate cyclic resolution according to protocol limits.
Do not recursively follow aliases without bounds.
A CNAME alias does not mean the alias and target are interchangeable in every application context.
Application identity can still depend on the originally requested hostname.
TLS hostname validation commonly uses the requested hostname rather than blindly replacing application identity with DNS canonical names.
DNS aliasing and application identity are separate.
MX records identify mail exchangers for a domain.
MX records include preference values.
Lower preference values are conventionally preferred according to MX semantics.
An MX target is a hostname.
It is not a URL.
It is not an email address.
Mail delivery software resolves the target according to mail and DNS rules.
Do not treat MX records as generic service discovery unless the application protocol defines that behavior.
TXT records contain textual strings.
TXT records are used by many application protocols.
TXT itself does not define the semantic meaning of the text.
SPF-related information can appear in TXT records.
Domain verification tokens can appear in TXT records.
DKIM-related information can appear under selected DNS names.
Other applications can use TXT.
Do not assume every TXT record has the same purpose.
TXT data is application-defined.
An NS record identifies a name server responsible according to zone or delegation semantics.
A delegation directs resolution from a parent zone toward authoritative servers for a child zone.
Delegation is fundamental to DNS hierarchy.
The root delegates top-level domains.
Top-level domains delegate child domains.
Child domains can delegate further subdomains.
No single ordinary DNS server needs to contain the entire DNS namespace.
Authority is distributed.
A zone is an administrative portion of the DNS namespace served authoritatively.
A zone is not necessarily the same thing as a domain.
A domain is a node and descendants in the namespace according to DNS terminology.
A zone contains the portion for which one administrative authority maintains authoritative data, excluding delegated child zones.
A domain can contain multiple zones because subdomains can be delegated.
Do not confuse domain with zone.
A zone apex is the top name of a DNS zone.
For a zone example.com, example.com is the zone apex.
The apex commonly contains SOA and NS records.
Certain aliasing rules at the zone apex differ from ordinary names because required records must coexist there.
Do not assume every provider's proprietary alias feature is a standard CNAME.
Providers can implement ALIAS, ANAME, flattening, or similar features.
These can produce CNAME-like operational behavior without publishing a standard CNAME at the apex.
Distinguish provider features from DNS protocol record types.
The SOA record is the Start of Authority record.
It contains zone control information.
It identifies a primary server name according to SOA semantics.
It contains administrative information.
It contains a serial value.
It contains timing values used by DNS mechanisms.
Exact interpretation follows DNS standards and server implementation.
The SOA serial can be used to determine whether zone data has changed for zone-transfer purposes.
Serial-number handling has defined arithmetic semantics.
Do not treat it as an ordinary unlimited integer without considering DNS serial arithmetic.
Authoritative DNS servers answer using authoritative zone data for names under their authority.
A recursive resolver answers clients by performing or using recursive resolution and caching results.
Authoritative server and recursive resolver are different roles.
One software package can technically provide both roles.
Operationally, the functions remain distinct.
Do not expose unrestricted recursion merely because a server is authoritative.
Open recursive resolvers can be abused.
A stub resolver is the client-side resolver interface commonly used by applications and operating systems.
An application often asks the operating system resolver for an address.
The stub resolver sends queries to configured recursive resolvers.
The application does not necessarily contact authoritative DNS servers directly.
Therefore application-visible DNS behavior can include operating-system and resolver caching.
A recursive resolver accepts a client's recursive query and attempts to obtain the answer.
It can answer from cache.
It can query authoritative hierarchy.
It can return errors.
It can return negative results.
Recursive resolution commonly begins from known root-server information when no useful cached delegation exists.
The resolver can query a root server.
The root can refer it to authoritative servers for a top-level domain.
The resolver can query the top-level-domain servers.
They can refer it to authoritative servers for the requested child zone.
The resolver can query the authoritative server.
The resolver can return the resulting answer to the client.
This process is simplified by caching.
Most lookups do not necessarily begin from the root because useful data can already be cached.
DNS referrals direct a resolver toward another authoritative server.
A referral is not the final answer to the original application question.
It provides information needed to continue resolution.
Resolvers must distinguish answers from referrals.
Glue records provide address information needed to reach delegated name servers in selected delegation situations.
Glue is especially important when a delegated name server's name lies inside the delegated namespace.

Glue records are supplied by the parent zone according to delegation requirements.
Glue is not ordinary authoritative child-zone address data merely because it contains an address.
Its role is to make delegation reachable.
Do not confuse glue with the authoritative A or AAAA RRset for the name.
Caching is fundamental to DNS.
DNS responses contain time-to-live values.
TTL stands for Time To Live.
TTL tells caches how long a DNS record can be retained according to DNS semantics.
TTL is commonly expressed in seconds.
A resolver can cache an answer until its TTL expires.
Changing authoritative DNS does not instantly change every cached answer.
Resolvers can continue returning previously cached data until its caching lifetime expires.
DNS propagation is therefore not one global event traveling across the Internet.
What is commonly called propagation is usually the expiration and replacement of cached DNS information across independent resolvers.
Different resolvers can hold different cached states at the same time.
One resolver can show the new address.
Another can still show the old address.
Both can be operating correctly within their cache state.
Do not declare DNS globally updated based on one resolver.
Do not declare DNS globally broken because two resolvers temporarily disagree during a legitimate transition.
Examine TTL and authoritative state.
TTL begins with the authoritative value but observed remaining TTL can decrease in caches.
A resolver returning a lower TTL can indicate cached data nearing expiration.
Do not assume the returned TTL always equals the zone-file TTL.
Caching layers can exist.
Operating systems can cache DNS.
Browsers can cache selected DNS information.
Applications can cache results.
Recursive resolvers cache results.
Network infrastructure can provide additional resolver behavior.
Clearing one cache does not clear every cache.
A local DNS cache flush cannot force remote recursive resolvers to discard valid cached data.
Authority boundaries matter.
Negative DNS answers can also be cached.
A negative answer can state that a name does not exist.
A negative answer can state that the requested record type does not exist for an existing name.
These conditions differ.
NXDOMAIN indicates that the queried domain name does not exist according to the authoritative DNS result.
A NOERROR response with no requested records can indicate that the name exists but has no records of the requested type.
Do not confuse NXDOMAIN with an empty answer.
Negative caching can cause a recently created name to remain unresolved through some caches until the negative cache expires.
Creating the missing record does not instantly remove every cached negative answer.

SERVFAIL indicates the resolver could not complete resolution successfully.
SERVFAIL does not mean the requested name definitely does not exist.
It can result from upstream failure.
It can result from DNSSEC validation failure.

It can result from resolver failure.
It can result from delegation problems.

The network can be unavailable.

DNSSEC stands for Domain Name System Security Extensions.
DNSSEC provides mechanisms for authenticating DNS data according to a chain of trust.

A signature must validate.
The relevant key must be valid.
The chain of trust must be established.
The signed data must match.
Time validity must be considered.
Algorithm support must be considered.
Presence is not validation.
A validating resolver performs DNSSEC validation when configured and supported.

This can create apparently inconsistent DNS behavior.

A DNSSEC chain of trust commonly begins from a configured trust anchor.
The DNS root trust anchor allows validation to proceed through signed delegations.
Trust does not arise merely because a DNS record says it is trusted.
Cryptographic validation and configured trust establish it.

It does not prove the server at that address is authorized for every application operation.
Application protocols still require their own authentication and authorization where needed.

Low TTL allows faster cache turnover.

Password reuse makes credential stuffing effective.

Users should not reuse passwords across unrelated services.

Brute-force guessing systematically attempts possible credentials.
Online guessing is constrained by the authentication service.
Offline guessing can occur when password verifiers are stolen.
Rate limiting helps online attacks.
Password hashing helps offline attacks.
These are different threat boundaries.
Do not claim rate limiting protects stolen password hashes.
Do not claim password hashing prevents online guessing by itself.
Multi-factor authentication is commonly abbreviated MFA.
MFA requires authentication evidence from more than one factor category according to the system's design.
Common factor categories include:
Something the user knows.
Something the user has.
Something the user is.
A password is something the user knows.
A hardware authenticator can be something the user has.
A biometric characteristic can be something the user is.
Two passwords are not two factors.
Two knowledge-based secrets remain the same factor category.
Do not count multiple pieces of the same category as MFA merely because there are two prompts.
A one-time password can be a possession-related factor when generated from a provisioned authenticator.
Exact assurance depends on the mechanism.
SMS-delivered codes have different security properties from cryptographic hardware authenticators.
Do not treat all second factors as equivalent.
TOTP stands for Time-based One-Time Password.
TOTP generates short-lived codes from a shared secret and time according to its algorithm.
The server and authenticator share secret material.
That secret must be protected.
Anyone possessing the TOTP secret can generate valid codes.
A QR code used to provision TOTP commonly contains the secret or information sufficient to provision it.
Treat provisioning QR codes as sensitive.
Do not store them in public locations.
Do not log them.
TOTP depends on reasonably synchronized time.
Small clock differences can be tolerated according to implementation.
Large clock errors can cause valid-looking codes to fail.
Do not disable TOTP verification because a system clock is wrong.
Correct time synchronization.
TOTP codes expire.
A previously valid code should not remain valid indefinitely.
Verification should follow defined time-window policy.
Do not create arbitrary large acceptance windows merely to avoid user inconvenience.
Larger windows increase the set of currently acceptable codes.
HOTP stands for HMAC-based One-Time Password.
HOTP is counter-based rather than time-based.
TOTP is derived from HOTP concepts using time as the moving factor.
Do not confuse HOTP and TOTP state management.
Recovery codes provide an alternate authentication path.
Recovery codes are credentials.
They should be unpredictable.
They should be stored securely.
They should normally be single-use where designed that way.
They should be invalidated after use.
Do not log recovery codes.

Recovery mechanisms are part of the authentication system.

A reset token should be single-purpose.
A reset token should normally be single-use.
A reset token should be invalidated after successful use.

A password change by an authenticated user should normally require appropriate current authentication according to policy.
A sensitive account can require reauthentication before changing credentials.
An existing session alone might not always provide sufficient assurance for highly sensitive changes.
Authentication age matters in some systems.

A user can have multiple WebAuthn authenticators.
A user can have recovery codes.
A user can have API tokens.
Revoking one credential does not necessarily disable the account.
Credential identity and account identity are separate.
Track which credential authenticated the session when useful.
This enables selective revocation and auditing.
A stolen hardware credential can be revoked without changing unrelated credentials.
A compromised API key can be revoked without changing the user's password.
Credential granularity improves incident response.
Do not make every credential share one irreversible global state unless simplicity requirements justify it.
API keys should have identifiers distinct from secret material.
The system can display an identifier safely while storing a protected verifier for the secret.
This allows operators to identify which key was used without logging the secret itself.
Do not use the complete secret as the key's display name.
API keys can have creation dates.
They can have expiration dates.
They can have last-used information.
They can have scopes.
They can have revocation state.
These improve lifecycle management.
Do not create permanent anonymous secrets with no ownership metadata.
Secret comparison for API keys should use appropriate secure verification.
If API keys have sufficient random entropy, storing a cryptographic hash of the secret can reduce direct disclosure risk.
Exact design depends on lookup requirements and threat model.
Do not assume API secrets must always be stored plaintext.
Authentication keys should be generated using cryptographically secure randomness.
Human-generated API keys are likely to be weaker.
Generate them automatically.
Provide them once where appropriate.
Store only what the server requires for verification.
Authentication tokens should have enough entropy to resist guessing.
Do not use incremental token values.
Do not use account ID plus timestamp.
Do not use predictable database row IDs.
Random credential generation must use a cryptographically secure random-number generator.
UUIDs have different versions and properties.
Do not assume every UUID is an authentication secret.
Some UUIDs contain predictable or structured information.
Use purpose-built random tokens for credentials.
Credential format can include a nonsecret prefix.
A prefix can identify token type.
A prefix can help secret-scanning systems.
A prefix does not reduce security if the remaining secret has sufficient entropy.
Do not treat the visible prefix as secret.
Secret scanners can detect credential patterns in source repositories.
Use them as a defensive control.
They do not replace credential management.
If a credential is committed publicly, assume exposure according to incident policy.
Deleting the commit later may not remove every copy.
Rotate the credential.
Do not merely hide the repository and continue using the exposed secret.
Version-control history can retain deleted secrets.
Credential removal requires history handling where appropriate and credential rotation.
Rotation is the critical security action.
A secret already exposed cannot become secret again by deleting one copy.
Environment variables can provide credentials to processes.
Environment variables are not automatically secure.
Other processes, debugging tools, crash reports, or configuration dumps can expose them depending on platform.
Use the credential mechanism appropriate to the environment.
Do not print environment variables containing secrets.
Secret-management systems can provide credentials dynamically.
They can centralize rotation.
They can control access.
They add infrastructure dependencies.
Use them when requirements justify them.
Do not add a secret manager merely as decoration.
The authentication system itself becomes critical infrastructure.
Administrative authentication should be stronger where risk requires it.
Administrative accounts should not share credentials.
Administrative actions should be attributable.
Default passwords should be changed or eliminated.
Factory credentials should not remain active in production.
Do not ship universal administrative passwords.
Bootstrap authentication requires special care.
A system's first administrator must be established through a controlled process.
Bootstrap credentials should be temporary where possible.
They should be invalidated after initial setup.
Do not leave installation credentials active indefinitely.
Account provisioning establishes an identity record.
Provisioning is not authentication.
An administrator creating an account does not prove the future user is currently present.
Credential enrollment establishes how that user will authenticate.
Keep provisioning and authentication separate.
Credential enrollment should occur through an authenticated or otherwise controlled process.
Adding a new MFA device changes future authentication authority.
Treat it as a security-sensitive operation.
Do not allow a session with insufficient assurance to silently enroll a new authenticator if policy requires stronger verification.
Removing MFA similarly changes authentication strength.
Require appropriate verification.
Log the change.
Notify the account owner where policy requires it.
Do not allow an attacker with a temporary session to permanently weaken authentication without controls.
Authentication notifications can alert users to new logins or credential changes.
Notifications are detection mechanisms.
They are not authentication proof.
An email saying a login occurred does not prevent the login.
Use notification as an additional control, not the primary verifier.
Account enumeration can occur through:
Login error differences.
Password-reset responses.
Registration responses.
Timing differences.
API status codes.
Authentication design should consider information disclosure across all related endpoints.
Do not fix the login message while leaving reset endpoints revealing the same account information.
Authentication endpoints should return appropriate HTTP status behavior according to application design.
HTTP status codes communicate protocol state.
They do not themselves perform authentication.
A 401 response commonly indicates authentication is required or has failed according to HTTP authentication semantics.
A 403 response commonly indicates the server understood the request but refuses it according to authorization semantics.
Exact application behavior can vary.
Do not use status codes as substitutes for internal security logic.
Authorize second.
Then construct the appropriate response.
HTTP Basic authentication transmits a username and password-like credential encoded for HTTP.
Base64 encoding is not encryption.
Basic authentication should use TLS when confidentiality is required.
Do not describe Basic authentication as encrypted because the header is Base64 encoded.
The Authorization header can carry credentials.

Application debugging should redact it.
Bearer authentication commonly uses:

The token is a credential.
The word Bearer is not the secret.
Do not expose the token.
Do not put bearer tokens in public examples using real credentials.
Use placeholders.
Authentication headers can traverse reverse proxies.
Proxy configuration must preserve or deliberately remove them according to architecture.
Do not accidentally forward external credentials to unrelated upstream services.
Credential boundaries matter.
A reverse proxy can perform authentication before forwarding a request.
The upstream application can trust authentication metadata only if the proxy boundary is controlled.
The proxy must remove client-supplied copies of trusted identity headers.
Then it can set its own authenticated identity headers.
Do not trust X-User or similar headers directly from the Internet.
A client can forge them.
Trusted authentication headers require a trusted intermediary.
The upstream should only accept requests from that intermediary or otherwise authenticate the intermediary.
Transport and network controls can establish the boundary.
Do not create header-based authentication without defining who is allowed to set the header.
Authentication middleware can centralize credential validation.
Authorization middleware can then evaluate permissions.
Keep their responsibilities distinct.

It should not silently grant every authenticated user every route.
Authorization remains necessary.
Public routes intentionally require no authentication.
Protected routes require authenticated identity.
Privileged routes require authenticated identity plus authorization.
Do not add authentication to a route and assume privilege separation now exists.
Authentication state should have one authoritative representation within the request context.
Avoid multiple components independently parsing credentials and reaching conflicting identities.
Authenticate once through a controlled mechanism where practical.
Propagate the established principal.
Do not let downstream code replace it using untrusted parameters.
An authenticated user ID should come from authentication context.
It should not come from request parameters for operations acting as the current user.
For example, changing the current user's password should use the authenticated principal.
Do not accept user_id=123 as proof that the requester is user 123.
For administrative operations targeting another account, the target account can come from the request.
The actor identity must still come from authenticated context.
Keep actor and target distinct.
Audit both.
Authentication should not be bypassed because a request originates from localhost unless architecture explicitly defines localhost as a trusted boundary.
Local processes can be compromised.

Use explicit authentication where required.

That identity can be sufficient for selected local services.
The trust root is then the operating system.
Authorization still determines permitted operations.

A hardware module can authenticate a key.
The operating system can authenticate a user.

Authentication is not ownership.

Keep technical identity separate from external ownership concepts.
Authentication is not permanent.
A session can expire.
A credential can be revoked.
A key can be rotated.
An account can be disabled.

Authentication is not trust in every statement made by the authenticated principal.

Authentication establishes identity.
It does not establish correctness.
Authentication is not authorization.
Authentication is not encryption.
Authentication is not hashing.

When implementing password login:
Receive the identifier and password over protected transport.
Locate the candidate account according to the identifier rules.
Perform password verification using the established password-hashing function.
Do not expose whether the account exists when policy requires nondisclosure.
If verification fails, remain unauthenticated.
If additional authentication factors are required, complete them.
Only after all required evidence succeeds should authenticated state be established.
Create or rotate the session credential securely.
Bind the session to the authenticated internal principal.
Return the session credential through the intended secure mechanism.
Record the authentication event according to logging policy.
Do not set authenticated state before verification completes.
When validating a session:
Receive the session credential.
Validate its format.
Locate or verify the session according to the session design.
Confirm it exists.
Confirm it is active.
Confirm it is not expired.
Confirm the associated account remains eligible for authentication according to policy.
Establish the request principal.
Do not trust a user ID supplied separately by the client.
When validating a signed token:
Parse it using a protocol-aware library.
Determine the expected issuer and validation policy from trusted configuration.
Select trusted verification keys according to controlled rules.
Verify the signature.
Verify the allowed algorithm.
Verify issuer where required.
Verify audience where required.
Verify expiration.
Verify not-before conditions where required.
Verify application-specific claims.
Only then establish authenticated identity.
Do not trust claims before validation.
When authenticating a service with a private key:
Provision the service with the intended private key.
Provision the verifier with appropriate public trust information.
Generate a fresh challenge or use a protocol providing equivalent freshness.
Have the service prove possession of the private key according to the protocol.
Verify the proof.
Map the validated key identity to the service principal.
Then apply authorization.
Do not transmit the private key.
When adding MFA:
Define which factor categories are required.
Enroll the additional authenticator through a controlled process.
Verify enrollment before relying on it.
Provide controlled recovery mechanisms.
Protect enrollment secrets.
Log authenticator changes.
Require the factors according to policy.
Do not call the system MFA merely because it displays two screens.
When resetting a password:
Establish the account being recovered.
Issue a cryptographically unpredictable, limited-lifetime recovery credential through the defined recovery channel.
Verify that credential.
Invalidate it after successful use.
Accept the new password.
Hash it using the current password-hashing policy.
Replace the old verifier.
Invalidate other authentication state where policy requires.
Record the security event.
Do not reveal or email the previous password.
When revoking an API credential:
Identify the exact credential.
Mark it revoked or remove its verifier according to design.
Ensure future validation rejects it.
Invalidate derived sessions or tokens where policy requires.
Record the revocation.
Do not disable unrelated credentials unless the incident requires it.
When authentication infrastructure fails:
Determine whether credential verification can still be performed according to an explicitly trusted mechanism.
If not, fail protected authentication attempts safely.
Report authentication infrastructure failure.
Do not report invalid credentials unless they were actually tested and found invalid.
Do not grant anonymous access to protected operations.
Preserve evidence for diagnosis.
When investigating suspicious authentication:
Identify the account.
Identify the credential or mechanism used.
Identify whether authentication actually succeeded.
Identify the session created.
Identify source information available.
Identify subsequent authorized actions separately.
Identify credential changes.
Identify session invalidations.
Do not infer compromise merely from one unusual login.
Do not dismiss compromise merely because a valid credential was used.
A stolen credential can authenticate successfully.
Authentication proves credential possession according to the mechanism.
It does not prove benevolent intent.

Only then implement the mechanism.
Keep authentication small.
Keep authentication deterministic.
Keep credential ownership explicit.
Keep trust anchors explicit.
Keep failure explicit.
Keep authentication separate from authorization.
A reliable authentication system does not guess identity.
A reliable authentication system validates evidence.
A reliable authentication system protects credentials.
A reliable authentication system does not store plaintext passwords.
A reliable authentication system does not trust client claims without validation.
A reliable authentication system uses secure randomness for authentication secrets.
A reliable authentication system limits credential lifetime where appropriate.
A reliable authentication system supports revocation.
A reliable authentication system preserves auditability.
A reliable authentication system fails safely.
A reliable authentication system does not turn infrastructure failure into successful login.
A reliable authentication system distinguishes account identity from credential identity.
A reliable authentication system distinguishes human identity from machine identity.
A reliable authentication system distinguishes authentication from authorization.
Which principal has been established by the evidence accepted under this authentication policy?
If the evidence validates, authenticate according to policy.
If the evidence does not validate, do not authenticate.
If the evidence is missing, do not authenticate.
If the authentication authority is unavailable, do not fabricate an identity.
If the evidence establishes only possession of a credential, do not claim it establishes anything beyond what that credential represents.
Identity is established by evidence.
Permission comes afterward.
Authorization is the process of determining whether an authenticated or otherwise identified principal is permitted to perform a requested action on a resource.
Authorization answers:
What is this principal allowed to do?
Authorization does not establish identity.
Authentication establishes identity.
Authorization evaluates permissions.
Keep them separate.
A user can authenticate successfully and still be unauthorized.
An unauthenticated requester can sometimes be authorized to access a public resource.
Public access is an authorization decision.
Do not require authentication merely to claim that authorization exists.
Authorization requires a decision context.
The context commonly includes:
Principal.
Action.
Resource.
Applicable policy.
Relevant state.
The authorization decision determines whether the requested operation is permitted.
A useful authorization question is:
May principal P perform action A on resource R under policy C?
Every part matters.
Changing the principal can change the result.
Changing the action can change the result.
Changing the resource can change the result.
Changing applicable policy can change the result.
Changing relevant state can change the result.
Do not reduce authorization to a single boolean stored on the user account unless the system is genuinely that simple.
A permission represents authority to perform a defined operation.
Examples include:
Read a document.
Create a record.
Modify a record.
Delete a record.
Publish content.
Manage users.
Change configuration.
Execute an administrative operation.
Permissions should describe actual authority.
Do not use vague permission names when precise operations matter.
A role is a collection or classification of authority according to a system's access-control model.
Examples can include:
User.
Editor.
Administrator.
Operator.
Auditor.
Roles are application-defined.
The name of a role does not inherently define its permissions.
"Administrator" means only what the system's authorization policy says it means.
Do not infer permissions from a role's English name.
Role-Based Access Control is commonly abbreviated RBAC.
RBAC assigns permissions to roles.
Principals are assigned roles.
Authorization can then determine whether one of the principal's roles contains the required permission.
A simplified relationship is:
Principal -> Role -> Permission.
Real systems can include additional constraints.
Do not confuse RBAC with authentication.
RBAC assumes the principal has already been established or otherwise identified.
A role should not be supplied by an untrusted client as authoritative input.
The server determines the principal's roles from trusted authorization state.
Never authorize because a form field says:
role=admin
Never authorize because a URL parameter says:
admin=true
Never authorize because JavaScript hides a button from ordinary users.
Client-side state is not authorization authority.
The server must make the authoritative authorization decision.
Hiding a user-interface element can improve usability.
It does not prevent direct requests.
A user can construct HTTP requests manually.
A user can modify HTML.
A user can modify JavaScript.
A user can call an API directly.
Authorization must be enforced where the protected operation occurs.
Do not rely on the interface to enforce permissions.
Every protected server-side action should enforce the applicable authorization policy.
A page can be protected.
An API endpoint can be protected.
A command can be protected.
A database operation can be protected.
A file operation can be protected.
A message handler can be protected.
A background job can be protected.
Protection belongs at the authority boundary.
Do not assume requests only arrive through the expected user interface.
Authorization should normally occur after authentication when the resource requires an authenticated identity.
A common request sequence is:
Receive request.
Validate request structure sufficiently to identify the intended operation.
Authenticate the requester.
Establish the principal.
Determine the target resource.
Evaluate authorization.
If authorized, perform the operation.
If unauthorized, reject the operation.
Do not perform the protected state change before authorization completes.
Authorization after execution is auditing, not prevention.
A permission check should occur before the protected effect.
Do not write to the database and then ask whether the user was allowed to do it.
Do not delete the file and then evaluate the role.
Do not transmit protected information before checking read authority.
Authorization protects both state changes and information disclosure.
Read access is authority.
Write access is authority.
Execute access is authority.
Administrative access is authority.
Do not focus only on destructive operations.
Unauthorized reading can be a serious security failure.
Least privilege means a principal receives only the authority required for its legitimate function.
Do not grant broad administrative authority merely because it is easier to implement.
Narrow authority reduces the impact of mistakes and compromise.
A service that only reads records should not receive write permission.
A user who only edits their own profile should not receive global user-management authority.
A monitoring process should not receive configuration-changing authority unless required.
Authority should match purpose.
Default deny means access is denied unless policy explicitly permits it.
This is a strong baseline for protected systems.
Unknown permission should not become permission granted.
Missing role should not become administrator.
Missing policy should not become allow.
Ambiguous authorization state should not silently grant access.
When authority cannot be established, deny the protected operation.
Fail closed.
Do not confuse fail closed with crashing.
The application can return a controlled denial.
The application should remain stable.
The protected operation simply does not occur.
Authorization failure is a valid application state.
Handle it deliberately.
An allowlist defines what is permitted.
A denylist defines what is prohibited.
Authorization systems commonly benefit from explicit allowed operations.
A denylist alone can fail when new operations are introduced and are not added to the list.
Default-deny systems reduce that risk.
Do not assume an operation is safe merely because it is not explicitly forbidden.
Authorization policy should define the allowed authority.
Access Control Lists are commonly abbreviated ACLs.
An ACL associates resources or objects with access rules.
An ACL can specify which principals or groups may perform which operations.
For example:
User A can read File X.
Group B can read and modify File X.
User C has no access to File X.
ACLs are resource-oriented access-control structures.
Do not confuse ACLs with filesystem permissions specifically.
Filesystems can use ACLs.
Applications can also implement ACLs.
Discretionary Access Control is commonly abbreviated DAC.
DAC commonly allows an object's owner or another authorized principal to control access according to system rules.
Mandatory Access Control is commonly abbreviated MAC.
MAC enforces access according to centrally defined security labels or policy.
Do not confuse Mandatory Access Control with a network interface MAC address.
They share an abbreviation.
They are unrelated concepts.
Attribute-Based Access Control is commonly abbreviated ABAC.
ABAC evaluates attributes associated with subjects, resources, actions, and environment.
Example attributes can include:
Department.
Resource classification.
Employment status.
Device state.
Time.
Operation type.
ABAC can express policies more flexibly than simple roles.
Flexibility also increases policy complexity.
Do not add ABAC when a small role or ownership check solves the requirement.
Authorization architecture should remain as simple as the actual requirements allow.
Policy complexity creates failure opportunities.
Ownership-based authorization allows operations according to a defined ownership relationship.
A user may modify their own profile.
A user may read their own private document.
A user may delete a resource they created if policy permits it.
Ownership must be established from trusted server-side state.
Do not accept:
owner_id=<current user>
from the client as proof of ownership.
The server should load the resource.
The server should determine its recorded owner.
The server should compare that ownership with the authenticated principal according to policy.
Client claims do not establish ownership.
An object identifier identifies a resource.
It does not authorize access to that resource.
Knowing another user's resource ID does not grant permission to read it.
This distinction is critical.
Authorization must be evaluated after identifying the requested object.
Insecure Direct Object Reference is commonly abbreviated IDOR.
IDOR vulnerabilities occur when an application exposes object identifiers and fails to enforce appropriate authorization on access to those objects.
/documents/100
/documents/101
If User A is authorized for document 100 but can change the URL to 101 and receive User B's document without an authorization check, access control is broken.
The problem is not that identifiers are sequential.
Random identifiers can make discovery harder.
They do not replace authorization.
A UUID does not grant security merely because it is difficult to guess.
If an unauthorized user obtains the UUID, the server must still reject access.
Do not use unguessability as the only access-control mechanism for protected resources.
Capability-based systems intentionally use possession of an unforgeable capability as authority.
That is a specific authorization model.
Do not accidentally create a capability system merely by assuming nobody will discover a URL.
If possession is intended to grant authority, define the credential as a capability and protect it accordingly.
If possession is not intended to grant authority, enforce ordinary authorization.
Object-level authorization checks the requester's authority over the specific target object.
Function-level authorization checks whether the principal may perform a type of operation.
Both can be required.
A user can have permission to edit documents generally while lacking permission to edit a particular document.
Do not stop at function-level authorization when object ownership or scope matters.
Permission: edit_document.
Resource: document 123.
Policy can require both:
Principal has edit_document permission.
Principal is authorized for document 123.
One does not imply the other.
Administrative permission can intentionally override ordinary ownership restrictions.
If so, encode that rule explicitly.
Do not scatter undocumented administrator bypasses throughout the code.
Centralize authorization policy where practical.
Explicit policy is easier to review.
An authorization rule should be understandable.
Allow update when the principal owns the record.
Allow update when the principal has records.admin permission.
Otherwise deny.
This is clearer than:
if ($user)
where authentication is accidentally treated as universal authorization.
Authenticated does not mean authorized.
Roles can be hierarchical.
An administrator role can include permissions from an editor role.
An editor can include permissions from a viewer role.
Role inheritance should be explicit.
Do not infer hierarchy from role names.
A role called "senior_editor" does not automatically inherit "editor" unless policy says so.
Role hierarchies can simplify policy.
They can also create hidden privilege expansion.
Review inherited permissions.
A role change can affect many permissions at once.
Treat role assignment as a security-sensitive operation.
Only authorized principals should assign privileged roles.
Do not let users modify their own role fields unless explicitly permitted.
Mass assignment can create authorization vulnerabilities.
Suppose an account update accepts:
name
email
role
If ordinary users should only modify name and email, accepting role from the request can allow privilege escalation.
Use explicit writable-field allowlists.
Do not bind every request field directly into privileged models.
Privilege escalation occurs when a principal gains authority beyond what policy permits.
Vertical privilege escalation moves toward more privileged authority.
Ordinary user becomes administrator.
Horizontal privilege escalation accesses another principal's resources at the same nominal privilege level.
User A accesses User B's private record.
Both are authorization failures.
Do not focus only on administrator escalation.
Horizontal access-control failures are common and serious.
Authorization boundaries should be tested for both.
For every protected operation, test:
Authorized principal succeeds.
Unauthenticated requester behaves according to policy.
Authenticated but unauthorized principal is denied.
Wrong owner is denied.
Wrong role is denied.
Revoked authority is denied.
Malformed or manipulated identifiers do not bypass checks.
Negative authorization testing is essential.
A test suite that verifies only successful authorized operations does not establish access-control enforcement.
Try to violate the policy.
Authorization tests should operate at the actual enforcement boundary.
If the HTTP endpoint performs the check, test the endpoint.
If the service layer performs the check, test the service layer.
If both are expected to enforce independent boundaries, test both.
Do not test only whether a button is hidden.
UI tests are not sufficient evidence of server authorization.
Middleware can enforce broad authorization rules.
Require authentication.
Require administrator role.
Require a named permission.
Middleware is useful for route-level policy.
Resource-specific authorization can still require application logic after loading the target resource.
Do not force every authorization decision into routing middleware if the decision requires resource state unavailable there.
Put checks where sufficient evidence exists.
Authorization logic can be centralized in policy functions.
can_read_document(principal, document)
can_edit_document(principal, document)
can_delete_document(principal, document)
can_manage_user(principal, target_user)
Clear policy functions improve consistency.
Do not duplicate slightly different authorization logic across many controllers.
Duplicated policy drifts.
One endpoint can be fixed while another remains vulnerable.
Central policy reduces inconsistent enforcement.

A lower-risk application can accept bounded session-cached permissions.

Authorization tokens can contain scopes or roles.

because it arrived as JSON.

Delegated authority should remain bounded.

Avoid vague hierarchy assumptions.

The system must use authoritative qualification state.
A self-declared qualification is not evidence.
Do not let a profile checkbox grant operational authority.

Principal is authenticated.
Principal holds required position.
Principal holds required qualification.
Principal has active assignment.
Requested operation falls within assignment scope.

Do not collapse distinct governance states into one broad role if the policy requires separation.
Eligibility is not authority.
Qualification is not authority.
Assignment is not authority.
Authentication is not authority.
Each can contribute to an authorization decision according to policy.
A principal can be eligible for a role without currently holding it.

No evidence of authority means no authority established.

When implementing a protected endpoint:
Authenticate the requester if authentication is required.
Establish the trusted principal.
Identify the requested action.
Load or identify the target resource using validated input.
Obtain current authorization state.
Evaluate the applicable policy.
If denied, perform no protected operation.
Return the appropriate denial response.
If allowed, perform only the authorized operation.
Record security-relevant activity according to audit policy.
Do not rely on the client to enforce any of these steps.
When implementing ownership authorization:
Establish the principal from trusted authentication state.
Load the resource.
Read the resource's authoritative owner identity.
Compare it with the principal according to policy.
Apply any explicitly defined administrative override.
If neither condition permits access, deny.
Do not accept ownership from request parameters.
When implementing role-based authorization:
Load roles from trusted authorization state.
Resolve role permissions according to defined inheritance.
Determine the permission required by the operation.
Evaluate whether the principal possesses that permission.
Apply resource-specific constraints.
Allow only if every required condition is satisfied.
Do not authorize merely because the principal has some role.
When implementing delegated authorization:
Authenticate the actor.
Validate the delegation credential or record.
Identify the delegating principal.
Identify the actor.
Determine the delegated scope.
Determine expiration and revocation state.
Compare the requested action with delegated authority.
Allow only within that authority.
Preserve both actor and delegation context for audit.
Do not silently elevate delegation to full account authority.
When revoking authority:
Identify the permission source.
Remove or disable that source.
Invalidate relevant caches.
Invalidate sessions or tokens where policy requires.
Ensure future authorization decisions observe the revocation within the defined timeframe.
Record the change.
Do not merely hide the feature from the user's interface.

Determine which resource was accessed.
Determine which authorization rule was evaluated.
Determine whether the authorization check occurred.
Determine the result.
Determine whether an alternate path bypassed the check.
Determine whether policy state was stale.
Determine whether privilege was changed.
Determine what protected effect occurred.
Use evidence.
Do not assume authentication compromise when the actual defect was missing authorization.
Do not assume authorization bypass when stolen valid credentials possessed legitimate authority.
Distinguish the failure.

Authorization answers one fundamental question:
Is this principal permitted to perform this action on this resource under the applicable policy?
If policy permits it, allow it.
If policy denies it, deny it.
If required authority is absent, deny it.
If authority cannot be established, deny it.
If the authorization mechanism fails, do not invent permission.
If the principal merely appears likely to have authority, that is not authority.
Permission must be established.
A session is a mechanism for preserving state across otherwise separate interactions.
HTTP is stateless at the protocol level.
One HTTP request does not inherently remember a previous HTTP request.
Applications frequently require continuity.
A user can authenticate during one request.
Later requests can need to know that the same established session is still active.
A shopping cart can persist across requests.
Application preferences can persist across requests.
Temporary workflow state can persist across requests.
Sessions provide one way to maintain this continuity.
Do not confuse a session with authentication.
A session can carry authenticated state.
A session can also exist for an unauthenticated user.
Authentication establishes identity.
A session preserves state.
Authorization determines what the established principal may do.
These are separate responsibilities.
A typical server-side session uses two components:
A session identifier held by the client.
Session state held by the server.
The client sends the session identifier with subsequent requests.
The server uses that identifier to locate the associated session state.
The session identifier is a reference.
It does not need to contain the complete session state.
A simplified flow is:
Client makes request.
Server creates session.
Server generates session identifier.
Server stores session state associated with that identifier.
Server sends the identifier to the client.
Client returns the identifier on later requests.
Server locates the session.
Server validates the session.
Server uses the session state.
Do not trust a session identifier merely because the client supplied one.
The server must determine whether it corresponds to a valid active session.
A session identifier should be unpredictable.
Use a cryptographically secure random source.
Do not generate session identifiers from sequential numbers.
Do not generate session identifiers from user IDs.
Do not generate session identifiers from timestamps.
Do not generate session identifiers from predictable counters.
Do not create a session identifier by concatenating public values.
An attacker who can predict another session identifier can potentially impersonate that session.
Session identifiers are credentials when possession grants access to session state.
Treat them as secrets.
Do not log full session identifiers.
Do not expose them unnecessarily.
Do not place them in URLs unless a protocol explicitly requires it and the risks are understood.
URLs commonly appear in:
Browser history.
Server logs.
Proxy logs.
Analytics systems.
Referrer information.
Screenshots.
Copied links.
Session identifiers should normally be transmitted using mechanisms intended for credentials.
Web applications commonly use cookies.
A cookie is data associated with HTTP requests according to browser cookie rules.
A session cookie can contain a session identifier.
The browser can automatically send the cookie with matching requests.
The cookie itself does not make the session secure.
Its contents and attributes matter.
A session cookie commonly looks conceptually like:
session=<random identifier>
The identifier maps to server-side state.
Do not put plaintext passwords into session cookies.
Do not put private keys into session cookies.
Do not put unnecessary secrets into session cookies.
A cookie can have a Secure attribute.
Secure instructs compatible browsers to send the cookie only over secure transport according to browser rules.
Use Secure for session credentials when HTTPS is required.
Do not expose an authenticated session over plaintext HTTP.
A cookie can have an HttpOnly attribute.
HttpOnly prevents ordinary client-side JavaScript from reading the cookie according to browser behavior.
This can reduce direct session-cookie theft through some script-based attacks.
HttpOnly does not prevent every consequence of cross-site scripting.
A malicious script can potentially perform requests using the user's existing session even when it cannot read the cookie.
Prevent script injection.
Do not treat HttpOnly as complete XSS protection.
A cookie can have a SameSite attribute.
SameSite controls selected cross-site cookie behavior.
Common values include:
Strict.
Lax.
None.
Their exact behavior depends on browser rules and request context.
SameSite can reduce selected cross-site request attacks.
It does not replace complete CSRF analysis.
When SameSite=None is used, browsers commonly require Secure.
Use cookie settings appropriate to the application's actual cross-site requirements.
Do not weaken cookie policy merely to make an integration work without understanding why.
Cookie Domain controls which hosts can receive a cookie according to browser rules.
Avoid unnecessarily broad cookie domains.
A cookie scoped to an entire parent domain can be exposed to more subdomains than required.
Keep session-cookie scope narrow.
Cookie Path restricts cookie transmission according to URL path matching.
Path can reduce unnecessary exposure.
Path is not a strong security boundary against malicious code within the same origin.
Do not rely on cookie Path as the sole authorization mechanism.
Cookie expiration controls persistence.
A session cookie can expire when the browser session ends according to browser behavior.
A persistent cookie can contain an explicit expiration or maximum age.
Cookie persistence and server-side session lifetime are separate.
Deleting the cookie does not necessarily destroy server-side session state.
Expiring server-side session state does not necessarily immediately remove the cookie from the browser.
The server must validate the session on every request where it is used.
If the server-side session is expired, the request must not regain authority merely because the browser still has the identifier.
Server state is authoritative for server-side sessions.
A session can have a creation time.
A session can have a last-activity time.
A session can have an absolute expiration time.
A session can have an idle expiration time.
These values have different meanings.
Absolute expiration limits total session lifetime.
Idle expiration limits how long the session can remain unused.
A session can use both.
For example:
Absolute lifetime: eight hours.
Idle lifetime: thirty minutes.
The session ends when either applicable limit is reached.
Exact durations depend on application requirements.
Do not invent arbitrary session durations without considering risk and usability.
High-risk administrative sessions can require shorter lifetimes.
Low-risk applications can use different policies.
Session expiration should be enforced by the server.
Do not rely solely on browser cookie expiration.
A copied session identifier can exist outside the original browser.
Server-side expiration limits its validity.
A session can be invalidated before expiration.
Logout is a common reason.
Credential change can be another reason.
Account disabling can be another reason.
Security incident response can be another reason.
Administrative revocation can be another reason.
Session invalidation should make future use of that session fail.
Do not merely hide the application interface after logout.
Destroy or invalidate the authentication state.
A logout operation for a server-side session commonly does the following:
Identify the current session.
Invalidate or delete its server-side state.
Expire the client cookie.
Return the user to an unauthenticated state.
The server-side invalidation is the critical authority change.
Cookie deletion cleans up the client state.
If the cookie is deleted but the server session remains active, a copied identifier can still be usable.
Do not equate client cleanup with server invalidation.
A system can support logging out one session.
A system can support logging out all sessions.
These are different operations.
Logout current session invalidates one session.
Logout all sessions invalidates every applicable session associated with the account.
To support global logout, the system needs enough server-side state or revocation information to identify those sessions.
Do not claim global logout if old tokens remain valid independently.
Session rotation replaces one session identifier with another.
Rotation is important when authentication state changes.
Anonymous session exists.
User logs in successfully.
Application rotates the session identifier.
Authenticated state becomes associated with the new identifier.
The old identifier is invalidated or otherwise prevented from representing the authenticated session.
This helps prevent session fixation.
Session fixation occurs when an attacker establishes or predicts a session identifier and causes a victim to authenticate using that same identifier.
If the application continues using it after login, the attacker can potentially use the known identifier to access the authenticated session.
Rotate session identifiers when privilege state changes.
Login is a common rotation point.
Privilege elevation can be another rotation point.
Sensitive reauthentication can be another rotation point.
Do not retain an externally supplied or previously exposed identifier after authentication without considering fixation.
Session rotation should preserve only state that is intended to survive.
Shopping cart contents may survive login.
Authentication state should be newly established.
Temporary security-sensitive state should be reviewed.
Do not blindly copy every anonymous-session field into an authenticated session.
Untrusted pre-authentication state can become dangerous after privilege elevation.
A session can contain:
Authenticated principal identifier.
Authentication time.
Authentication method.
Session creation time.
Last activity time.
CSRF-related state.
Temporary workflow state.
Selected application preferences.
Other bounded state.
Store only what is required.
Do not turn the session into an uncontrolled dumping ground.
Session state is security-sensitive.
If an attacker can modify server-side session state, they can potentially change identity or authority information.
Protect the session store.
Do not let clients directly modify trusted server-side session fields.
authenticated_user_id
role
authentication_level
must come from trusted application logic.
Do not copy client request parameters directly into trusted session authority fields.
A request containing:
role=administrator
does not become trustworthy because the value is stored in the session.
Untrusted input remains untrusted.
Sessions can be stored in memory.
Sessions can be stored in files.
Sessions can be stored in databases.
Sessions can be stored in distributed caches.
Sessions can be stored using other server-side mechanisms.
Each storage mechanism has operational and security properties.
In-memory sessions are fast.
They can disappear when the process restarts.
They can be difficult to share across multiple application instances without additional architecture.
File-backed sessions are simple.
Filesystem permissions matter.
Concurrent access matters.
Cleanup matters.
Database-backed sessions can persist across processes and servers.
Database availability matters.
Query cost matters.
Distributed cache sessions can support multiple application instances.
Cache availability matters.
Eviction behavior matters.
Replication behavior matters.
Do not select a session store merely because it is fashionable.
Use the smallest mechanism that satisfies requirements.
A single-server application does not automatically need a distributed session cluster.
A multi-server application must ensure a request can access the required session state.
One approach is shared session storage.
Another approach is request affinity.
Another approach is self-contained client tokens.
These are different architectures.
Do not mix their assumptions.
Request affinity is sometimes called sticky sessions.
A load balancer routes a client repeatedly to the same application instance.
This can allow instance-local session state.
If that instance fails, the session can be lost unless state is replicated elsewhere.
Sticky routing is an infrastructure technique.
It is not session security.
Shared session storage allows multiple application instances to access the same session state.
This can simplify failover.
It introduces a shared dependency.
Protect access to the session store.
Only authorized application components should read or modify session state.
Do not expose a session database directly to clients.
Session records should have bounded lifetimes.
Expired records should be removed or marked unusable.
Otherwise the session store can grow indefinitely.
Cleanup can occur:
On access.
Periodically.
Through database expiration.
Through cache TTL.
Through scheduled maintenance.
The exact mechanism depends on storage.
Expiration must still be enforced even if physical cleanup is delayed.
An expired session record remaining in storage must not become valid merely because cleanup has not run yet.
Logical validity and physical deletion are separate.
Session IDs can be stored in a database as hashes rather than plaintext when the design permits.
If an attacker obtains the session database, plaintext active session identifiers can potentially be used directly.
Hashing session tokens can reduce this risk.
The client possesses the random token.
The server hashes the presented token.
The server looks up the hash.
This resembles API-token verification.
Do not confuse session-token hashing with password hashing.
High-entropy random session tokens do not require deliberately slow password hashing.
A normal secure cryptographic hash can be appropriate for random tokens according to design.
Passwords are low-entropy human secrets.
Random session tokens should have high entropy.
Different threat models require different primitives.
Do not apply expensive password hashing blindly to every random session token.
Session identifiers need sufficient entropy.
Entropy makes guessing infeasible.
Length alone is not enough if generation is predictable.
A 128-character sequential identifier is still predictable.
Use cryptographically secure randomness.
Encoding does not create entropy.
Hex.
Base64.
Base64url.
These represent bytes.
They do not make weak random data strong.
Generate strong random bytes first.
Then encode them safely.
Session identifiers should avoid characters that cause transport ambiguity.
Use an established framework's session generation when it provides a secure implementation.
Do not invent a custom token format without need.
Framework session systems should be configured correctly.
Defaults can differ.
Check:
Cookie name.
Secure.
HttpOnly.
SameSite.
Lifetime.
Storage.
Rotation behavior.
Garbage collection.
Domain.
Path.
Do not assume framework defaults match production security requirements.
A framework can manage session lifecycle.
Understand what its session regeneration function actually does.
Some APIs create a new ID while retaining old state.
Some invalidate the old ID.
Some require explicit destruction.
Use documented behavior.
Do not guess.

The application can access session data through $_SESSION.

can hold an authenticated user identifier after successful authentication.

A PHP logout can require:
Starting the session.
Clearing application session state.
Invalidating the session record.
Expiring the session cookie.
Exact implementation depends on configuration.
Do not merely unset one user variable if other authenticated state remains.
Clear the complete security-relevant session state.
Session destruction should not accidentally destroy unrelated server state outside the intended session.
Understand framework and language behavior.
Do not use global destructive operations casually.
Sessions can exist in non-PHP systems.
The principles remain similar.
Generate secure identifiers.
Protect transport.
Validate server-side state.
Rotate after authentication.
Expire sessions.
Support invalidation.
Keep authority explicit.
Do not make security depend on one programming language.
Client-side storage is different from server-side sessions.
Browsers provide mechanisms such as:
Cookies.
localStorage.
sessionStorage.
These have different access and transmission behavior.
localStorage values are accessible to JavaScript running in the origin.
They are not automatically attached to HTTP requests.
sessionStorage is also script-accessible and is scoped according to browser session rules.
Do not assume sessionStorage is equivalent to a server session because the names are similar.
They are different concepts.
Browser storage containing bearer credentials can be exposed through script execution.
Cookie-based credentials with HttpOnly can reduce direct script access.
Architecture determines the appropriate mechanism.
There is no universal rule that every token must always be stored in one specific browser mechanism.
Analyze the threat model.
Do not store credentials casually.
A server-side session and a JSON Web Token are not the same thing.
A server-side session commonly stores state on the server and gives the client an opaque identifier.
A self-contained JWT can carry claims inside the token.
The server can validate the token cryptographically without loading ordinary session state.
Both can represent authenticated continuity.
Their lifecycle properties differ.
Do not call every authentication token a session ID.
A JWT can be used within a session architecture.
A session can be implemented without JWT.
JWT is a token format.
Session is an application-state concept.
Stateless token authentication is not truly state-free in every operational sense.
Keys must exist.
Accounts have state.
Permissions can change.
Revocation can be required.
Security events can require invalidation.
Do not use "stateless" to pretend lifecycle problems disappeared.
Self-contained tokens can make immediate revocation more difficult.
A token can remain cryptographically valid until expiration.
If immediate revocation is required, the system needs a mechanism such as:
Short token lifetime.
Revocation records.
Token introspection.
Account version checks.
Signing-key changes.
Another defined invalidation strategy.
Do not promise session revocation that the architecture cannot enforce.
Server-side sessions make individual invalidation straightforward because the server controls the session record.
They require session storage.
This is a tradeoff.
Do not choose token architecture solely to avoid one database lookup without measuring whether that lookup is actually a problem.
Simple systems benefit from simple sessions.
Performance optimization should follow evidence.
Session state can become stale.
Suppose the session contains:
role=editor
The administrator changes the user's role to viewer.
If the application trusts the old session role until logout, the user can retain editor authority longer than intended.
This is an authorization freshness issue.
Possible approaches include:
Load current role on each request.
Invalidate sessions when role changes.
Store a permission version and compare it.
Use short session lifetimes.
Refresh session authority periodically.
Choose according to requirements.
Do not assume session-cached authorization is current.
Authentication state can also become stale.
An account can be disabled while sessions remain active.
A password can be changed while sessions remain active.
A credential can be revoked while sessions remain active.
Policy should define whether those events invalidate sessions.
Implement that behavior explicitly.
Do not assume password change automatically invalidates sessions unless the system does it.
A session can store an authentication timestamp.
Sensitive operations can require recent authentication.
User logged in six hours ago.
User requests a high-risk security change.
Application requires reauthentication.
After successful reauthentication, the session records a new authentication time or elevated assurance state according to policy.
Do not infer recent authentication from recent activity.
Clicking pages for six hours is not the same as proving the credential again.
Session activity and authentication age are separate.
A session can have an authentication assurance level.
Password authenticated.
Password plus additional factor authenticated.
Hardware authenticator verified.
Exact levels are application-defined.
Authorization can require a minimum assurance level for sensitive operations.
Do not let the client set the assurance level.
It must derive from completed authentication.
Step-up authentication can temporarily elevate session assurance.
Define how long that elevation lasts.
Do not leave elevated state permanent accidentally.
Privilege elevation should have a lifecycle.
Session state can represent impersonation.
If an administrator intentionally impersonates another user, preserve:
Actual authenticated administrator identity.
Effective user identity.
Impersonation start time.
Applicable authorization.
Do not overwrite the actor identity and lose accountability.
A session can carry both actor and effective principal.
Audit logs should distinguish them.
Do not let ordinary users create impersonation state.
Impersonation is a privileged operation.
Session hijacking occurs when an attacker obtains a valid session credential and uses it.
Possible exposure paths include:
Network interception without proper transport protection.
Cross-site scripting.
Malware.
Browser compromise.
Logs.
URLs.
Debug output.
Database compromise if tokens are stored plaintext.
Accidental sharing.
Insecure backups.
Protect the credential throughout its lifecycle.
TLS protects session cookies in transit when correctly used.
TLS does not protect a token after it has been logged to a file.
TLS does not prevent malicious script executing in the application origin.
TLS does not protect a compromised endpoint.
Use layered controls.
Session binding attempts to associate a session with additional context.
Examples can include:
Device information.
Network characteristics.
Client properties.
Binding can detect some anomalies.
It can also break legitimate sessions because these properties change.
IP addresses can change.
Mobile users can move networks.
User-Agent strings can change.
Proxies can alter characteristics.
Do not treat unstable metadata as cryptographic identity.
A changed IP address does not prove session theft.
An unchanged IP address does not prove session legitimacy.
Context can inform security policy.
