Permissions define specific authority granted to a principal, role, group, service, process, or other recognized subject within a system.
A permission answers a narrow question:
Is this subject allowed to perform this action within this scope?
Permissions are part of authorization.
Permissions are not authentication.
Authentication establishes identity.
Permissions describe authority.
Authorization evaluates whether the established authority permits the requested operation.
Keep these concepts separate.

A role can require approval before assignment.
A role can require two approvers.
These are governance requirements layered onto permission management.
Do not add them unless policy requires them.
But if policy requires them, enforce them deterministically.
Approval to grant permission should itself be authenticated and authorized.
An approval record from an unknown actor is not authority.
A valid digital signature can establish who approved.
Policy determines whether that signer had approval authority.
Do not confuse signature validity with permission to approve.
A signed unauthorized grant remains unauthorized.
Permission changes can require quorum.
Two authorized administrators approve a high-risk role assignment.
The system must verify:
Distinct approvers if required.
Each approver's identity.
Each approver's authority.
The target grant.
The required threshold.
Do not merely count approval rows.
Validate them.
Emergency permissions can bypass ordinary restrictions according to defined policy.
They should be:
Explicit.
Limited.
Audited.
Temporary where possible.
Reviewable.
Do not create hidden emergency administrator credentials.
Emergency authority is still authority.
Represent it honestly.
A break-glass role can have broad permissions.
Its activation can require additional authentication.
Its use can generate high-priority audit events.
Its lifetime can be short.
Exact design depends on requirements.
Do not leave break-glass access permanently active.
Permission systems should support removal.
A system that can grant authority but cannot reliably revoke it is incomplete.
Revocation is a first-class operation.
Test it.
Do not treat permission deletion as merely database housekeeping.
Revocation changes security state.
Permission removal can invalidate sessions or tokens according to policy.
If it does not, document the delay.
Do not pretend removal is effective while cached credentials remain valid.
Access reviews can examine effective permissions.
Questions include:
Who can administer users?
Who can change permissions?
Who can read audit logs?
Who can export data?
Who can access production?
Who has wildcard permissions?
Which temporary grants have not expired correctly?
Which service accounts have excessive authority?
Review effective authority, not just role names.
A harmless-looking role can inherit powerful permissions.
A powerful-looking role can have limited scope.
Inspect actual policy.
Permission creep happens when authority accumulates.
A user changes responsibilities.
New permissions are added.
Old permissions remain.
Over time the account becomes overprivileged.
Periodic review can remove obsolete authority.
Do not only ask what access must be added.
Ask what access is no longer required.
Group membership can create permission creep.
A user belongs to multiple old groups.
Each group grants authority.
Removing direct permissions does not remove inherited permissions.
Effective-access analysis must include every grant path.
Do not assume no direct grant means no access.
Nested groups make this harder.
If nested groups are supported, detect cycles.
Group A contains Group B.
Group B contains Group A.
Naive permission resolution can loop forever.
Prevent or safely handle cycles.
Do not allow malformed hierarchy to crash authorization.
Role inheritance can also contain cycles.
Validate role graphs.
A deterministic permission hierarchy should be acyclic unless the engine explicitly supports cycles with well-defined semantics.
Simpler is usually better.
Permission aliases can help migration.
old.permission -> new.permission
Aliases introduce complexity.
They can preserve unintended authority if left indefinitely.
Prefer explicit migrations where practical.
Deprecate old permission identifiers deliberately.
Do not silently interpret unknown old names as broad new permissions.
Permission migration should preserve intended authority.
If one old permission becomes two new permissions, decide which existing users receive.
Do not automatically grant both unless policy requires it.
Migration is a security change.
Review it.
Application upgrades can introduce new permissions.
Default behavior matters.
If a new privileged feature appears, existing ordinary roles should not automatically gain access unless explicitly intended.
Default deny protects new operations.
Add the new permission.
Assign it deliberately.
Do not interpret absence of configuration as everyone allowed.
New permissions can be included in selected existing roles through an intentional migration.
Record the change.
Do not hide privilege expansion inside a software upgrade.
Module installation can introduce permissions.
module.reports.read
module.reports.manage
Register them explicitly.
Do not give every installed module unrestricted administrative authority.
Module permissions should integrate with the host authorization model when architecture supports it.
Removing a module should handle its permission records safely.
Historical audit references can remain.
Active grants to nonexistent permissions should not become wildcard authority.
Unknown means no authority.
Permission names can be namespaced to avoid collisions.
core.users.read
reports.reports.read
sentinel.events.read
Exact namespace convention depends on the system.
The goal is unambiguous identifiers.
Do not let two modules define the same permission name with different meanings.
Collision creates unpredictable policy.
Permission registries should reject conflicting definitions.
Configuration permissions should be particularly narrow.
Changing authentication configuration can affect security.
Changing authorization configuration can affect security.
Changing network configuration can affect exposure.
Changing logging configuration can affect evidence.
Do not hide all of these behind one generic edit_settings permission unless broad authority is intentional.
High-impact configuration can require separate permissions.
settings.general.update
settings.authentication.update
settings.authorization.update
settings.logging.update
This can support separation of duties.
Again, do not over-fragment without need.
Permission design is a balance between clarity and manageability.
File permissions are a separate authorization domain.
Unix-like filesystems commonly use owner, group, and other permission classes.
Common bits include:
Read.
Write.
Execute.
Application permission names do not automatically map to filesystem bits.
A web user with documents.read can still require the application process to have OS read access to the underlying file.
Both layers must permit the operation.
Do not confuse application permissions with operating-system permissions.
Unix root can bypass many ordinary filesystem restrictions.
That does not mean a remote application user should receive application administrator permissions.
Authority domains differ.
Database permissions are also separate.
A database account can have:
SELECT.
INSERT.
UPDATE.
DELETE.
EXECUTE.
CREATE.
ALTER.
DROP.
Application-level users can have different authority even though queries use one shared database account.
The application must enforce its own permissions.
Do not assume database access control automatically provides per-user application authorization.
Cloud permissions can use policies, roles, and resource scopes.
The same principles apply:
Narrow authority.
Explicit scope.
Deterministic evaluation.
Auditable grants.
Revocation.
Do not copy cloud permission complexity into a small local application unless needed.
Use architecture appropriate to scale.
Permissions can be represented in configuration files.
Protect those files.
If an untrusted user can edit the permission configuration, they can potentially grant themselves authority.
Filesystem permissions become part of the authorization trust boundary.
Do not secure the application UI while leaving policy files world-writable.
Permissions can be represented in source code.
Changing them then requires software deployment.
This can be appropriate for fixed roles.
Dynamic applications can store assignments in a database while keeping permission definitions in code.
There is no universal storage requirement.
Choose based on how often policy changes and who is authorized to change it.
Static policy can be easier to audit.
Dynamic policy can be easier to administer.
Both require integrity protection.
Permission state should have one authoritative source.
Do not maintain conflicting permission truth in:
Database.
JSON file.
Session.
Cache.
Configuration.
without defining precedence and synchronization.
Caches are derived state.
Sessions can contain cached state.
The authoritative policy should be identifiable.
When sources disagree, behavior must be defined.
Do not guess.
Permission decisions should be explainable.
For an allow:
Allowed because User 42 has Editor role in Project 7, which grants documents.update in Project 7.
For a denial:
Denied because documents.update is required and no active grant exists in Project 7.
This level of reasoning makes systems debuggable.
Do not return internal explanations to unauthorized users if they reveal sensitive structure.
But make them available to authorized diagnostics.
A permission engine can return:
ALLOW
DENY
It can also return structured reason information internally.
missing_permission
scope_mismatch
expired_grant
explicit_deny
inactive_assignment
unknown_permission
Do not make security behavior depend on human-readable error strings.
Use stable machine states.
Human-readable messages can be generated separately.
Permission enforcement should be consistent across interfaces.
Web UI.
REST API.
GraphQL.
CLI.
Background jobs.
Message queues.
Administrative tools.
If they perform the same protected operation, they should enforce equivalent policy.
Do not protect only the web route while leaving the CLI remotely exposed through another mechanism.
Know the trust boundary of each interface.
Internal function calls can still require policy enforcement if untrusted paths can reach them.
Place enforcement where bypass is difficult.
A service layer can centralize policy.
Controllers can also enforce route-level rules.
Defense in depth can be appropriate.
Do not duplicate inconsistent policy everywhere.
One source of authorization semantics is easier to maintain.
Permission checks should use current principal context.
Do not pass arbitrary user IDs into:
has_permission(user_id, permission)
from client-controlled input and assume that user is the requester.
The authenticated principal comes from trusted authentication state.
Administrative operations can intentionally check another principal's permissions for diagnostics.
That is a separate authorized function.
Do not confuse subject inspection with requester identity.
Permission simulation can be useful for administrators.
What could User 42 access?
Simulation should not actually execute the protected operation.
It should evaluate policy.
Protect simulation interfaces because they can reveal security structure.
Do not allow ordinary users to enumerate every administrator permission unless intended.
Permission enumeration can disclose capabilities.
A user can often be allowed to see their own effective permissions.
This can help interfaces adapt.
The server still enforces them.
Do not rely on the permission list sent to the browser as authoritative.
It is presentation data.
An attacker can modify it.
Server-side enforcement remains required.
UI permission checks improve usability.
Hide Publish if user lacks documents.publish.
Disable Delete if user lacks documents.delete.
These are interface conveniences.
They are not security controls.
Direct requests must still be denied.
Never write:
if button is hidden, endpoint is safe.
The endpoint must check permission.
Client applications can cache permission lists.
Those lists can become stale.
A stale UI might show an action the server now denies.
That is acceptable if the server remains authoritative.
The client can refresh state after denial.
Do not weaken server policy to match stale client state.
A stale UI can also hide newly granted actions.
Refresh appropriately.
Security favors server truth.
Permission evaluation can be expensive in highly complex systems.
Optimize after correctness.
Possible optimizations include:
Role-permission caching.
Effective-permission caching.
Scope indexes.
Precomputed grants.
Policy compilation.
Do not optimize by skipping checks.
Do not optimize by granting broad permissions.
Do not remove object-level checks because they require another query without measuring alternatives.
Correctness first.
Performance second.
Measure.
Permission data structures should support the actual lookup pattern.
If every request asks:
Does principal P have permission X in scope S?
index accordingly.
Do not scan every permission record for every request if a simple index solves it.
Efficiency can remain deterministic and simple.
Permission evaluation should not depend on database row order unless policy explicitly defines priority.
SQL result order without ORDER BY is not guaranteed.
If rule priority matters, store and evaluate explicit priority.
Do not let accidental storage order decide authority.
Policy precedence must be intentional.
If explicit deny wins, implement that rule.
If specific scope overrides parent scope, implement that rule.
If temporary emergency authority overrides ordinary denial, define exactly when.
Do not let different modules implement different precedence rules for the same policy.
Centralize semantics.
Permissions can have conditions.
reports.export allowed only during assigned operation.
deploy.execute allowed only in staging.
payments.approve allowed below a defined amount.
Conditions should use trusted state.
Do not trust client claims such as:
environment=staging
amount_under_limit=true
Load or calculate authoritative values.
The client requests.
The server decides.
Location-based permissions can exist.
Network-based permissions can exist.
Time-based permissions can exist.
Device-based permissions can exist.
These are contextual policy conditions.
Use them only if requirements justify them.
Do not infer strong identity from weak context.
An IP range can be one condition.
It is not automatically a person.
A time window can restrict authority.
It does not authenticate the actor.
Keep evidence types distinct.
Permissions can depend on active assignment.
A principal is qualified to perform maintenance.
The principal receives maintenance authority only while actively assigned to that system.
Qualification alone does not grant access.
Assignment alone might not be sufficient if qualification is also required.
Policy can require both.
Do not collapse separate states.
A useful relationship can be:
Identity.
Position.
Qualification.
Assignment.
Access decision.
Each stage has distinct meaning.
Do not infer one from another unless policy explicitly defines the relationship.
A principal can hold a position without a particular permission.
A principal can be qualified without active access.
A principal can have an assignment with narrowly scoped authority.
Permission is not a social title.
It is operational authority.
Human-directed policy determines that authority.
Software should enforce the defined decision.
Do not reinterpret policy to make an operation convenient.
If permission is absent, deny.
If an authorized human changes the policy, enforce the changed policy.
Software does not invent organizational authority.
Permission models should preserve explicit human decisions.
Do not silently expand authority because a new feature appears similar to an old feature.
Ask whether the existing permission semantically covers it.
If not, define a new permission.
Do not silently narrow authority either if established policy grants it.
Implement the actual policy.
No speculation.
No implied permission without defined inheritance.
No implied denial beyond defined policy.
Use evidence from the permission state.
A permission decision can be expressed as:
Required permission P.
Principal S.
Scope C.
Applicable conditions K.
Evaluate whether S possesses active authority P within C while K is satisfied.
If yes, permit the operation.
If no, deny the operation.
Do not replace that evaluation with:
S seems trustworthy.
Trustworthiness is not a permission.
Do not replace it with:
S is an administrator-like user.
Check actual authority.
S performed this operation before.
Historical behavior is not current permission.
The request came from inside the network.
Network origin is not automatically application authority.
The request contains role=admin.
Client claims are not authoritative.
The ID is hard to guess.
Identifier secrecy is not permission.
Permission must be established.
When adding a permission:
Define its identifier.
Define its exact operation.
Define its scope.
Define any conditions.
Define which roles receive it.
Define who may grant it.
Define whether it can be delegated.
Define whether it can expire.
Define how revocation works.
Add enforcement at the protected operation.
Add positive tests.
Add negative tests.
Document the semantics.
Do not merely add the name to a database table.
When granting a permission:
Identify the target principal.
Identify the exact permission.
Identify the scope.
Verify the grantor has authority to grant it.
Apply required approval policy.
Set expiration if temporary.
Record the grant.
Invalidate stale authorization state where required.
Audit the change.
Do not grant broader authority than requested.
When revoking a permission:
Identify the grant source.
Remove or deactivate it.
Consider inherited grants.
Invalidate caches where required.
Invalidate sessions or tokens where policy requires.
Verify future authorization no longer receives the permission.
Audit the revocation.
Do not assume deleting one direct grant removes authority if another role still grants the same permission.
Effective authority matters.
When changing a role:
Identify all affected principals.
Identify permissions added.
Identify permissions removed.
Evaluate scope.
Review privilege expansion.
Apply the change.
Invalidate derived permission state where required.
Test effective permissions.
Do not treat role editing as cosmetic configuration.
When investigating unexpected access:
Identify the principal.
Identify the required permission.
Enumerate active direct grants.
Enumerate roles.
Enumerate group memberships.
Enumerate inherited permissions.
Check explicit denies if supported.
Check temporary grants.
Check expiration.
Check cached authority.
Check token scopes.
Check resource ownership.
Check contextual conditions.
Determine the exact path that produced the allow decision.
When investigating unexpected denial:
Confirm the principal identity.
Confirm active roles.
Confirm scope.
Confirm the permission exists.
Confirm role mappings.
Confirm temporary grants have not expired.
Confirm no explicit deny applies.
Confirm authorization state is current.
Confirm the resource is within scope.
Confirm the enforcement point requires the intended permission.
Do not solve the problem by granting unrestricted administrator access.
Find the missing authority.
When designing permissions, ask:
What operations exist?
Which operations require protection?
Which operations have materially different security consequences?
What resources exist?
What scopes exist?
Which roles exist?
Which permissions belong to each role?
Can permissions be granted directly?
Can groups grant permissions?
Does inheritance exist?
Can explicit deny exist?
What is the precedence rule?
Can permissions expire?
Can permissions be delegated?
Who can grant them?
Who can revoke them?
How quickly does revocation take effect?
How are effective permissions calculated?
Where are permission checks enforced?
How are changes audited?
How are permissions tested?
Then build only what is required.
Keep permission names precise.
Keep scopes narrow.
Keep roles understandable.
Keep grants explicit.
Keep inheritance visible.
Keep revocation reliable.
Keep policy deterministic.
Keep privilege minimal.
Keep enforcement server-side.
Keep authority explainable.
A reliable permission system can identify why authority exists.
A reliable permission system can identify its scope.
A reliable permission system can revoke authority.
A reliable permission system rejects unknown permissions.
A reliable permission system does not trust client-supplied roles.
A reliable permission system does not use UI hiding as enforcement.
A reliable permission system does not silently convert scope-specific authority into global authority.
A reliable permission system does not infer authority from identity alone.
A reliable permission system does not infer authority from position alone.
A reliable permission system does not infer authority from qualification alone.
A reliable permission system does not infer authority from historical behavior.
A reliable permission system does not grant authority because the requester seems trustworthy.
A reliable permission system does not guess.
Authentication establishes the principal.
Permissions establish defined authority.
Authorization evaluates that authority against the requested operation.
Sessions can preserve the principal's authenticated continuity.
None of these concepts replaces the others.
For every protected operation ask:
What permission is required?
Who is the principal?
What trusted evidence establishes the permission?
Is the permission currently active?
Do additional policy conditions apply?
If the required permission is established, continue according to policy.
If it is not established, deny.
If permission state cannot be determined, do not invent authority.
If multiple grants conflict, apply the defined deterministic precedence rule.
If the permission is scoped elsewhere, it does not apply here.
If it expired, it is not active.
If it was revoked, it is not active.
If the client merely claims it, it is not established.
Permission is explicit authority.
Probable permission is not permission.
Input validation is the process of determining whether supplied data satisfies the requirements defined for that input.
Applications receive input from many sources.
Examples include:
HTML forms.
URLs.
Query parameters.
HTTP headers.
Cookies.
JSON requests.
XML requests.
API clients.
Command-line arguments.
Configuration files.
Environment variables.
Uploaded files.
Databases.
Message queues.
Network protocols.
Other applications.
Hardware devices.
Users.
Do not assume input is trustworthy because it came from a familiar source.
Input crossing a trust boundary must be treated according to the receiving system's requirements.
A trust boundary is a point where data moves between components or contexts with different trust assumptions.
Browser to server.
Client application to API.
Internet to application.
Application to database.
Plugin to host application.
External service to internal service.
Configuration file to privileged process.
Message queue to worker.
User-controlled file to parser.
Do not trust data merely because it is inside the application now.
Its origin still matters.
Input validation answers:
Does this input satisfy the requirements for this field or operation?
Validation does not answer:
Is this user authorized?
Is this input safe in every possible output context?
Is this data true?
Is this data trustworthy?
Is this request legitimate?
Keep these questions separate.
Valid input can still be unauthorized.
Valid input can still be malicious in another context.
Valid input can still be factually false.
Valid input can still violate a business rule.
Validation establishes conformance to defined input requirements.
A useful validation process is:
Identify the expected input.
Define its type.
Define its format.
Define its allowed values.
Define its length or size constraints.
Define its range where applicable.
Define whether it is required.
Define any structural relationships.
Parse it.
Validate it.
Reject it if the requirements are not satisfied.
Do not begin with arbitrary transformations intended to make unknown input acceptable.
Know what valid input means first.
Validation should be explicit.
For example:
Expected:
Integer from 1 through 100.
Valid:
1
42
100
Invalid:
0
101
-5
hello
12.5
The validation rule is clear.
Do not write:
if value looks roughly numeric, accept it.
Define the accepted domain.
Types matter.
Common input types include:
Boolean.
Integer.
Floating-point number.
String.
Enumeration.
Date.
Time.
Timestamp.
Identifier.
Array.
Object.
Binary data.
File.
Do not treat every input as an arbitrary string forever.
Parse into the intended type when appropriate.
If an API requires an integer, validate an integer.
Do not accept:
"twelve"
because application code might later convert it unpredictably.
Type conversion can hide invalid input.
"12abc"
might be partially interpreted as 12 by permissive conversion routines.
Do not rely on implicit conversion.
Use strict parsing where possible.
Parsing and validation are related but distinct.
Parsing determines whether input can be interpreted according to a grammar or representation.
Validation determines whether the parsed value satisfies application requirements.
"2026-10-01"
can parse as a date.
The application can still reject it if only future dates are permitted.
Syntactically valid does not mean semantically acceptable.
Syntax describes structure.
Semantics describe meaning.
Validate both where required.
A syntactically valid email-shaped string does not prove the mailbox exists.
A syntactically valid IP address does not prove the address belongs to a trusted system.
A syntactically valid user ID does not prove the requester may access that user.
A syntactically valid URL does not prove the destination is permitted.
Do not infer more than validation establishes.
Allowlist validation defines what is accepted.
status must be one of:
pending
active
disabled
Anything else is rejected.
This is preferable when the valid set is known.
Do not attempt to enumerate every possible invalid status.
Define the valid domain.
A denylist identifies known prohibited values or patterns.
Denylisting can be useful in selected contexts.
It is generally weaker than defining the valid input when the valid domain is known.
A denylist can miss new or unexpected forms.
Rejecting:
<script>
does not define valid HTML.
Many other representations can exist.
Do not build general input safety from a small list of bad strings.
Prefer positive validation when possible.
A field with a fixed vocabulary should use an enumeration.
method:
GET
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE
if those are the only accepted values for the application context.
Reject unknown values.
Do not silently interpret:
POTS
as:
Validation should not guess intent.
A boolean should have a defined representation.
For example, an API can define:
true
false
Do not accept arbitrary values such as:
yes
on
enabled
unless the interface explicitly defines them.
Different languages interpret truthiness differently.
Explicit representation prevents ambiguity.
An integer field should define range.
port:
1 through 65535.
Do not merely validate that it contains digits.
999999 is digits.
It is not a valid TCP or UDP port number.
Type validation and range validation are separate.
A quantity can require:
minimum.
maximum.
Both.
Neither.
Define the actual domain.
Do not use arbitrary limits without a requirement.
Length validation constrains strings, arrays, files, or other collections.
username:
1 through 64 characters.
Do not allow unlimited input when the application has a finite requirement.
Unbounded input can create:
Memory pressure.
Storage growth.
Processing cost.
Log flooding.
Rendering problems.
Protocol failures.
Denial-of-service conditions.
Set meaningful limits.
Do not choose tiny limits that reject legitimate data merely for convenience.
Validation should reflect the actual system.
Character count and byte count are different.
A Unicode string can contain characters represented by multiple bytes.
If a protocol limits bytes, validate bytes.
If an application limits characters, validate characters.
Do not confuse the two.
A database column size can be measured according to database semantics.
Understand the storage model.
Do not assume a 255-character application limit matches every database type automatically.
Unicode requires deliberate handling.
Input can contain:
ASCII.
Accented characters.
CJK characters.
Emoji.
Combining characters.
Other Unicode sequences.
Do not reject non-ASCII input unless the specification requires ASCII.
Do not assume one byte equals one character.
Normalization can matter when equivalent-looking Unicode sequences have different binary representations.
Unicode normalization can convert defined equivalent representations into a canonical form.
Use normalization only when the application's semantics require it.
Do not normalize blindly if exact byte preservation matters.
Identifiers can have stricter rules than human-readable text.
For example, a module slug can require:
lowercase ASCII letters.
digits.
hyphen.
Maximum length.
That is valid if the identifier specification defines it.
Do not apply identifier restrictions to ordinary prose fields without reason.
Different fields require different validation.
Do not create one universal string validator.
A username is not an email address.
An email address is not a filesystem path.
A filesystem path is not a URL.
A URL is not a shell argument.
A shell argument is not SQL.
Context matters.
Validation should be field-specific.
Regular expressions can validate some formats.
They are not automatically the best tool for every input.
Use a regular expression when the accepted language is appropriately expressed by one.
Do not create enormous fragile expressions for formats that already have reliable parsers.
A parser can be clearer.
Regular expressions can also have performance risks.
Certain expressions can exhibit excessive backtracking on crafted input.
Keep expressions bounded and understandable.
Do not accept a complex regular expression merely because it passes ordinary examples.
Test adversarial lengths and patterns.
A regular expression matching format does not establish meaning.
^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$
can match:
2026-99-99
The string has the expected shape.
It is not a valid calendar date.
Use semantic validation after format validation.
Dates should use defined formats.
YYYY-MM-DD
If that is the interface contract, reject ambiguous alternatives unless explicitly supported.
Do not guess whether:
01/02/03
means:
January 2, 2003.
February 1, 2003.
January 2, 1903.
Ambiguous date formats create errors.
Use explicit formats.
Validate actual calendar rules.
February 30 is not valid.
Leap years matter.
Use reliable date libraries where appropriate.
Time zones matter for timestamps.
Define whether timestamps are:
UTC.
Offset-aware.
Local to a specified zone.
Do not accept ambiguous local times where the protocol requires a global instant.
Daylight-saving transitions can create nonexistent or repeated local times.
Use appropriate time representations.
Do not invent timezone assumptions silently.
Numeric validation should consider overflow.
A value can contain valid digits and still exceed the receiving type.
999999999999999999999999999999999999
may exceed a fixed-width integer.
Check conversion errors.
Check range.
Do not allow overflow to wrap into another value.
Signed and unsigned ranges differ.
A negative value can be invalid for an unsigned quantity.
Do not cast negative input to unsigned and accept the resulting large number.
Validate before unsafe conversion.
Floating-point values require care.
NaN.
Infinity.
Negative infinity.
Signed zero.
Very large exponents.
These can be accepted by some parsers.
If the application requires ordinary finite numbers, explicitly require finite values.
Do not assume every parsed floating-point value is suitable.
Money should not casually use binary floating-point when exact decimal behavior is required.
This is a representation issue beyond validation.
Input validation should still enforce permitted monetary format and range.
Amount must be nonnegative.
Amount must have no more than two decimal places if policy requires cents.
Do not silently round arbitrary user input unless the interface defines rounding.
Identifiers should be validated according to their actual format.
